K-Pop Demon Hunters star Ejae has admitted she feels “haunted” by her performance at the Baftas earlier this year – claiming a poker-faced A-lister unwittingly put her off.

Ejae, Audrey Nuna and Rei Ami – who provided the singing voices for the HUNTR/X girl group in Netflix’s animated film – performed the movie’s hit track “Golden” for the star-studded audience at the London ceremony in February.

But Ejae, real name Kim Eun-jae, has now confessed that she wasn’t too pleased with her own vocals, telling The Times: “The Batas haunt me. I made mistakes. I cracked a little bit on the high notes.”

Explaining what happened, the 34-year-old continued: “Leonardo DiCaprio was [in the audience] right in front of me, and he was not smiling.”

Ejae added that as she was singing one of the song’s highest notes, she looked directly at the One Battle After Another actor.

open image in gallery It was the first time the trio were performing ‘Golden’ outside the US ( Bafta/YouTube )

“That’s what put me off,” she said. “He made me so nervous. It was already so nerve-racking to be in front of all these celebrities, and then I look up and lock eyes with Leonardo DiCaprio? Come on.”

Both the HUNTR/X singers and Titanic star DiCaprio were fixtures on the awards season circuit this year.

Released in 2025, K-Pop Demon Hunters fast became the most-watched film in Netflix’s history, amassing over 325 million official views, according to the streaming service. It followed up the astonishing viewing figures with plenty of accolades and Netflix has confirmed that a sequel is on the way.

open image in gallery DiCaprio at the Baftas ( Getty )

While K-Pop Demon Hunters was deemed ineligible for the Baftas because it wasn’t released in cinemas, it was named Best Animated Film at the Golden Globes, with “Golden” – co-written by Ejae – winning Best Original Song from a Motion Picture.

The film and its songwriters walked away with the same accolades at the Oscars, where Ejae also got a second chance at performing in front of Leo. That time around, things went a little better and the 51-year-old actor was even spotted waving a K-Pop lightstick as he stood to applaud.

DiCaprio’s star turn as Bob Ferguson in Paul Thomas Anderson’s acclaimed thriller One Battle After Another resulted in best actor nominations at all of this year’s major award ceremonies.

open image in gallery Ejae with her Academy Award ( AFP/Getty )

The actor didn’t manage to get his hands on any major statuettes, though, with Robert Arayamo (I Swear) pipping him to the post at the Baftas, before Michael B Jordan (Sinners) was victorious at the Oscars.

The Golden Globes splits its acting awards into Drama, and Musical or Comedy categories, with DiCaprio’s performance submitted in the latter. On the night, he lost out to Marty Supreme’s Timothée Chalamet.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

News.title: Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG
News.content:
His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

News.title: Advice, cookbooks and emergency pot noodles: Your best gifts for university students
News.content:
When it comes to sending a child or grandchild off to university, it can be tempting to fill their room with every conceivable gadget.

So to help, we asked the Telegraph Recommended Community for their best gift recommendations and their suggestions ranged from desk lamps to cookery books and supermarket gift cards.

Here are the essentials worth buying.

Kitchen basics

From cupboard essentials to electrical appliances and cookbooks, most readers say they’d gift kitchen equipment.

Thinking back to his university days, reader TJ, 43, from London, says “the main essentials are around kitchen items and good long lasting food”.

“It’s nice to have some bits to cook for others as well and to make friends quickly,” he adds.

Susan, 54, from the West Midlands, agrees, recommending “basic cooking equipment” as a key staple and “distinctive cutlery, plates and cups that are easily identified”, which are particularly useful for shared accommodation.

“A box of store cupboard ingredients such as olive oil, soy, stock cubes and spices to use when cooking,” is also well-received, she says.

News.title: Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check
News.content:
Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

Sports.title: Swiatek beats Rybakina to end title drought in Toronto
Sports.content:
Iga Swiatek claimed her first title of the season with a dominant 6-2 6-3 win over Elena Rybakina in the final of the National Bank Open in Toronto.

The Polish seventh seed gained an early advantage in the first set when the world No 2 gave up a break point on back-to-back double faults.

That was all the room Swiatek needed as she continued her stellar form from earlier in the tournament to race away with the opening set.

Unforced errors continued to cost Rybakina into the second set, as two missed backhands gifted Swiatek another break.

Rybakina was able to stave off one championship point, but Swiatek converted on her second opportunity to clinch her first title since last September.

Speaking at the post-match awards ceremony, Swiatek dedicated her victory to "everyone who is dealing with unfair judgement and hate".

She said: "Just keep pushing, keep growing, keep focusing on yourself because you know what's best for you.

"Always remember what's ahead and what might be possible."

Shelton retains crown

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Canadian Open men's final between Ben Shelton and Brandon Nakashima.

In the men's draw, American Ben Shelton retained his crown by eclipsing compatriot Brandon Nakashima 6-3 7-6 (7-4) in Montreal.

Shelton did not drop a set throughout the tournament and is just the fourth man this century to go back-to-back at the event, joining Andy Murray, Novak Djokovic and Rafael Nadal.

Image: Ben Shelton completed his flawless Canadian Open title defence with victory over Brandon Nakashima

He told atptour.com: "For me to play the way that I played this week to go through this draw speaks to the work I have been putting in.

"It also speaks to my mental toughness, my ability to focus through everything that was going on this week."

Sports.title: Super League leaders Leeds beaten by Leigh after late drama
Sports.content:
Innes Senior scored twice as Leigh Leopards inflicted a first home defeat of the season on Betfred Super League leaders Leeds Rhinos by winning 20-16 at Headingley.

Wing Senior went over twice in the first half after team-mate Josh Charnley's effort had cancelled out Ryan Hall's opener for Leeds, for whom Brodie Croft also touched down before the break.

In balmy, energy-sapping conditions after the hottest day in the UK this year, Leigh scored a fourth try through centre Umyla Hanley early in the second period and then withstood heavy pressure to seal a deserved win.

Ryan Hall thought his late effort for Leeds had tied the scores, but his foot was clearly in touch as he grounded the ball in the corner and Leigh clung on.

Hall touched down in the corner for the opening try in the second minute after taking Jake Connor's quick pass following a high kick, but Leigh's response was immediate as Charnley raced over following Hanley's line break.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Leigh Leopards head coach Adrian Lam reflects on their Super League win at Leeds Rhinos.

Connor's penalty in front of the posts for a shoulder barge on Kallum Watkins edged Leeds 8-6 ahead, but Leigh piled on the pressure midway through the first half and got their reward.

Senior powered over near the touchline and despite Leeds full-back Lachlan Miller's brilliant tackle, the video referee ruled the Leigh winger had dotted down before going out of bounds to put his side 10-8 up.

Leeds came roaring back when Croft burst through a gap under the posts for a converted score to nudge them 14-10 in front.

Rhinos centre Jack Bird went off for a head injury assessment following a clattering tackle and was replaced by teenager Zak Lloyd, whose terrific last-ditch tackle halted Charnley soon after.

But quick hands saw Leigh spin the ball left for Senior to go over on the outside to level the scores at 14-14 at half-time after Cook had missed his second conversion attempt.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur reflects on their Super League defeat to Leigh Leopards.

Connor landed his second penalty to give Leeds a two-point advantage soon after the restart following Cook's off-the-ball block on Ash Handley.

Leigh responded again though, carving open the Rhinos' defence via another slick handling move that sent Hanley over for the visitors' fourth try of the match, with Cook adding the extras to put them 20-16 in front.

The visitors were reduced to 12 men when second row Andy Badrock was sin-binned for his dangerous tackle on Harry Newman with 17 minutes to go.

Leeds threatened to make their extra man count, but they lacked composure and failed to execute in the face of some desperate, scrambling defending from Leigh.

Image: Umyla Hanley (R) celebrates scoring Leigh's final try

With three minutes remaining, Leeds thought they had drawn level when Handley sent Hall over in the corner following Connor's high kick.

But the video referee revealed the winger's foot was in touch as he grounded the ball and Leigh held firm before celebrating an impressive win.

Leeds' defeat gives Wigan Warriors the chance to move level with them at the top of the table on 36 points when they visit struggling Bradford Bulls on Sunday.

The victory kept Leigh on course for the playoffs as they tightened their grip on sixth by moving six points clear of St Helens, who can claim a maximum of 10 points from their five remaining games.

Warrington beat York to go third

Warrington Wolves beat York Knights 30-10 at the Halliwell Jones Stadium to move back up to third.

York had taken an early lead after Warrington failed to deal with a high kick and Paul McShane went over in the corner.

The Wolves - looking to edge ahead above play-off rivals Wakefield - then got themselves in front after nine minutes when Josh Thewlis darted through to slide in under the posts and Ewan Irwin added the extras.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League clash between Warrington Wolves and York Knights.

The Knights, though, soon responded again when Cody Hunter's low kick was not gathered by the Warrington backline and Jon Bennison latched onto the loose ball in the right corner.

Sam Stone, returning to the side following a three-month injury lay-off, chased George Williams' kick on the left wing and dived full length to just touch the ball down as he slid off into the advertising boards, before 18-year-old Irwin scored a fine individual try, stepping inside to burst clear, and his penalty then put Warrington 18-10 ahead at half-time.

York were punished for giving away penalties early in the second half when hooker Danny Walker took the ball a couple of yards out to spin under the posts.

Image: Ewan Irwin (R) celebrates scoring one of Warrington's five tries

Irwin then picked up a loose ball to sprint clear and run in a 60-yard try - but his celebrations were cut short after a lengthy video review decided James Bentley had knocked Denive Balmforth's arm, which caused him to fumble possession.

After a breakaway from Hunter, which looked set for a York try, was called back for what looked a tight offside call, Warrington made sure when Aaron Lindop went over in the corner after Albert Hopoate had tapped back a high kick and Irwin then slotted over a late penalty.

Hull KR maintained their push for a home play-off with a comfortable 28-10 victory over Catalans Dragons.

The home side led 22-6 after a dominant first half that saw Jack Broadbent touch down twice as Jez Litten and Joe Burgess also scored.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League clash between Hull KR and Catalans Dragons.

Tyrone May all but sealed victory with the first score of the second half after 62 minutes, before Tommy Makinson hit back with a late consolation try for Catalans.

The victory kept Hull ahead of Leigh in fifth on points difference, and moved them within just two points of Warrington and Wakefield in third and fourth.

Sports.title: Gay out for duck as Pakistan impress against County Select XI
Sports.content:
England opening batter Emilio Gay was out for a duck as Pakistan made a strong start to their tour against a Professional County Club Select XI.

Concerns over Gay's fitness for England's first Test against Pakistan, which starts on August 19, were allayed by the left-hander's inclusion for the game at Beckenham, but he made the worst possible start.

The 27-year-old, who had suffered a shoulder issue playing for Durham last week, was caught off the bowling of Mohammad Abbas by Salan Agha at second slip, having failed to score from his 12 balls faced.

PCCSXI would go on to be bowled out for 305, with captain Tom Haines, Caleb Falconer and Saif Zaib contributing half-centuries before Matthew Fisher, who is in England's 16-player squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan, made a crucial unbeaten 62 batting at 10.

James Rew, who made his England Test debut against New Zealand in June, was also dismissed cheaply as he fell for just four to Abbas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England Test captain Joe Root explains why he has removed the curfew that was previously imposed on his team.

Abbas (3-37) and Mohammad Ali (3-23) were the pick of the Pakistan bowlers, while Khurram Shahzad (2-55) also chipped with a couple of wickets despite being more expensive.

There was also a wicket apiece for Aamer Jamal (1-32) and Ali Usman (1-38).

Pakistan then put themselves in a strong position in the three-day contest by reaching 44-0 at the close, with Azan Awais (15*) and Imam-ul-Haq (26*) seeing out the final 13 overs of the day.

Fisher was economical as he went for just seven runs from his four overs, while the other PCCSXI player who is in England's Test squad, spinner Shoaib Bashir, bowled two overs at the end of the day.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England selector Marcus North reflects on the latest decisions around the Test side and explains the involvement of Stephen Fleming.

Both sides are fielding more than XI players in the match, with Pakistan attempting to give as many of their touring squad as possible match practice ahead of Tests at Headingley, Lord's and Edgbaston.

England will be led captained by Joe Root following his reappointment as captain after Ben Stokes retired from international cricket during the final Test of the 2-1 series defeat to New Zealand in June.

England also have a new head coach in Stephen Fleming, who has replaced Brendon McCullum but is not taking charge of the side during the Pakistan series, for which Marcus Trescothick will be in interim charge.

Sports.title: McIlroy makes woeful start to FedExCup Playoffs as Spieth shares lead
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy made a woeful start to the FedExCup Playoffs as he shot four-over par opening round at the FedEx St. Jude Championship in Memphis.

Playing for the first time since finishing tied for 40th at The Open at Royal Birkdale almost a full month ago, McIlroy was level par going into the final three holes before a disastrous streak left him towards the rear of the field.

Dropped shots at 16 and 17 were followed by a double bogey at TPC Southwind's final hole, which came after McIlroy found the water with his tee shot to the closing par four.

The 74 left McIlroy nine shots adrift of the first-round leaders, with Jordan Spieth among a group of five Americans to finish on five-under par.

Spieth, who started the week outside of the top 50 players in the FedExCup standings that will go through next week's BMW Championship, is joined in the lead by Michael Thorbjornsen, Kurt Kitayama, Jake Knapp and Michael Kim.

Spieth said: "I just tried to come into this week and just be as patient, non-reactive as possible, dumb it down to try to win the golf tournament and not worry about anything else."

England's Tommy Fleetwood, who was paired with Spieth, was a shot off the lead after opening up with a 66 that included a delightful chip in for eagle at the par-five third hole.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy had an eighteenth hole to forget at the FedEx St. Jude Championship.

Fleetwood said: "I feel good. I didn't really play very good in the practice days. Game's not really been that great. I've been showing a lot, like some good and some really not so good.

"Hit it great off the tee today. Still my iron play was iffy, but I did a good job of managing it for the most part. Still hit some really good shots, and you can never underestimate how good - I think shooting under par on this golf course is very good."

World No 1 Scottie Scheffler, who played alongside McIlroy in the marquee group for the opening two rounds, put himself in a solid position by delivering a 68.

Scheffler said: "I felt like I hit a lot of quality shots with my irons.I did a good job of being patient and not trying to force it too much.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tommy Fleetwood produced this eagle on third hole at the FedEx St. Jude Championship.

"I feel like I was right on the edge of having a good day, kind of all day is how I would describe it. So, I felt like patience-wise, I did a pretty good job."

Fleetwood had European company towards the top of the leaderboard, with Ludvig Aberg, Viktor Hovland and Sepp Straka joining Scheffler on two-under.

Shane Lowry posted a solid one-under round to start the week, while Matt Fitzpatrick was left frustrated by a closing double bogey that dropped him back to level par.

McIlroy could at least take consolation from not having the worst round of the day, which belonged to Scotland's Robert MacIntyre, who shot a 12-over par 82.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the Sky Sports Golf Podcast, Jamie Weir and Brad Faxon debate whether Rory McIlroy's extended break since The Open will help him win a record-extending fourth FedExCup title.

Justin Rose also made a slow start as he finished on three-over, with fellow Englishmen Aaron Rai and Harry Hall faring little better as they finished two over.

Memphis is hosting the first of three FedExCup Playoffs events, with only the top 50 in the overall season standings at the end of Sunday's final round progressing to the BMW Championship, and then the top 30 qualifying for the season-ending Tour Championship.

McIlroy's position of 12th out of the 70-player field means there is no concern about his progress to the BMW Championship, while the fact the events have no cut gives him plenty of time to climb the leaderboard over the weekend.

How do the FedExCup Playoffs work?

All season long, players have earned points based on how they have performed in PGA Tour events, with extra points available for the signature events and majors.

Only the top 70 in the standings have reached the FedEx St Jude Championship (August 13-16), with just the top 50 then progressing to the BMW Championship (August 20-23) and then only the top 30 making it to the finale, The Tour Championship (August 27-30).

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brooks Koepka was extremely disappointed after failing to make the FedExCup playoffs.

Sports.title: Steelers rookie Allar stars as McCarthy beats Packers on debut
Sports.content:
Rookie Drew Allar starred in Mike McCarthy's first game as Pittsburgh Steelers head coach, throwing two touchdown passes and running for another in a 28-9 preseason win over the Green Bay Packers.

The third-round pick completed 10 of 13 passes for 154 yards and impressed McCarthy with his poise and decision-making.

Will Howard also caught the eye, completing seven of nine passes for 86 yards and directing a touchdown drive as the Steelers outgained Green Bay 385-160.

Mason Rudolph was similarly efficient in his brief outing, heightening competition for the backup quarterback spots behind Aaron Rodgers.

Jordan Love made a short appearance for the Packers, while rookie kicker Trey Smack was a bright spot, converting field goals from 58, 38 and 37 yards.

Cardinals 27-14 Raiders

Image: Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza threw a touchdown in a debut defeat to the Arizona Cardinals

No 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza threw a touchdown pass in his preseason debut but the Las Vegas Raiders fell 27-14 to the Arizona Cardinals.

Mendoza completed 10 of 16 passes for 97 yards and found rookie receiver Jack Bech for a six-yard score, becoming the first top draft selection since Baker Mayfield in 2018 to throw a touchdown in his first preseason appearance.

Veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins also threw a touchdown in a sharp one-series cameo for Las Vegas.

Arizona built its advantage behind flawless passing from Jacoby Brissett and former Raider Gardner Minshew, while third overall pick Jeremiyah Love impressed with 58 rushing yards on 11 carries.

Colts 13-13 Patriots

Image: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Anthony Richardson was denied victory by the Patriots on his return from injury

Anthony Richardson returned from injury with a mixed display as the Indianapolis Colts drew 13-13 with the New England Patriots in their preseason opener.

The former first-round pick threw for 145 yards and scored on a one-yard quarterback sneak, but also lost a fumble and had a pass intercepted as Indianapolis committed four turnovers.

Tommy DeVito led New England's offence, completing 13 of 22 passes for 128 yards and a touchdown to Kyle Williams.

The Colts rescued the tie with a 61-yard field goal from Spencer Shrader late on, while Anthony Borregales missed a potential game-winner for the Patriots.

Titans 19-13 49ers

Image: Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward is pressured by San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Titus Leo

No 1 overall pick Cam Ward endured a mixed preseason debut as the Tennessee Titans beat the San Francisco 49ers 19-13 in their exhibition opener.

Ward led a 95-yard touchdown drive on Tennessee's opening possession but finished with just 25 passing yards, completing five of 10 attempts while failing to connect with fellow rookie Carnell Tate.

Tony Pollard scored the Titans' only touchdown and Joey Slye kicked four field goals, including three from beyond 50 yards.

San Francisco backup Kurtis Rourke impressed on his return from injury, completing 12 of 14 passes for 101 yards before leaving with a rib injury, while rookie receiver De'Zhaun Stribling caught seven passes for 63 yards.

Chargers 27-7 Texans

Image: Los Angeles Chargers running back Amar Johnson scored a stunning 55-year touchdown against the Houston Texans

Amar Johnson scored twice and produced a spectacular 55-yard reception as the Los Angeles Chargers opened their preseason campaign with a 27-7 victory over the Houston Texans.

The undrafted running back, entering his second season, rushed for two touchdowns and added a two-point conversion as the Chargers pulled away in the second half.

With starters Justin Herbert and C.J. Stroud rested, Trey Lance completed 12 of 20 passes for 164 yards for Los Angeles, while Davis Mills threw Houston's only touchdown pass.

DJ Uiagalelei also impressed, throwing a late touchdown, as the Chargers dominated after the break in Houston.

Lions 14-16 Bengals

Image: Quarterback Joe Flacco threw the Cincinnati Bengals to preseason victory in Detroit

Joe Flacco threw a touchdown pass in relief of Joe Burrow as the Cincinnati Bengals opened their preseason with a 16-14 victory over the Detroit Lions.

Burrow completed five of six passes for 39 yards in two early series before giving way to Flacco, who found rookie tight end Jack Endries for a score.

Evan McPherson added three field goals, including a 56-yarder, while the Bengals capitalised on three Detroit turnovers.

Undrafted rookie Luke Altmyer threw for 130 yards and a late touchdown for the Lions, who threatened a comeback before Russ Yeast sealed the result with a late interception.

Sports.title: Oceania declares support for Infantino in boost for Fifa president but New Zealand breaks ranks
Sports.content:
The Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) has declared their support for Gianni Infantino following demands for the Fifa president to resign from Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation in a development that further highlights world football’s civil war.

After a meeting of its executive committee in Fiji on Wednesday, the OFC issued a statement on Friday praising “the progress achieved over the last decade” by Fifa in its first public comments since the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan emerged this month.

In another sign of division however, the OFC’s biggest member and only nation to qualify for this summer’s World Cup, New Zealand, broke ranks with the confederation by withdrawing their backing for Infantino and calling for an independent review of the Fifa Forward Enterprise plan, which has been demanded by the three rebel groups.

The OFC is the smallest confederation in world football with just 11 full members, but with Infantino facing a leadership challenge for the first time in a decade at next year’s presidential election those votes could prove crucial.

Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC provide 143 of Fifa’s 211 members, but powerful countries within those blocks most notably Mexico and Qatar have already made it clear that they still support Infantino, while others may also defy the orders of their confederation.

The OFC is the last confederation to declare its position and their stance completes the symbolic division of world football, with the Confederation of African Football (Caf) and South American confederation (Conmebol) also backing Infantino.

In addition their stance illustrates the continued backing for Infantino among smaller nations such as American Samoa and the Cook Islands, which is likely to emerge as a theme of the presidential election.

View image in fullscreen New Zealand were the only OFC team to qualify for this summer’s World Cup. Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images

“The OFC Executive Committee welcomes Fifa’s decision to withdraw the FFE (Fifa Forward Enterprise) proposal and its commitment to review the issues surrounding the project,” the OFC said in a statement.

“OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under Fifa’s leadership and encourages Fifa to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary.”

The OFC has repeatedly declined to answer questions from the Guardian on its position over the last fortnight, and delayed releasing a statement until two days after its ExCo meeting.

New Zealand’s decision to break ranks goes some way towards explaining their reticence to commit in a move that has added significance given the federation have benefited from Infantino’s leadership of Fifa as co-hosts of the 2023 Women’s World Cup with Australia.

“After careful consideration, New Zealand Football has formed the view that decisions and actions within Fifa have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust,” NZF said in a statement.

“NZF believes this point in time represents an opportunity for all Fifa member associations to advocate for stronger governance, accountability and transparency which are fundamental in maintaining confidence of the administration of the global game.”

The NZF chief executive, Andrew Pragnell, said that their decision to withdraw support from Infantino was based on their values.

“Everyone who’s connected to the game around the globe deserves to know where we stand,” he said. “New Zealand is a country that’s always led based on its values, and we’re really proud to put those first and put the fans and the football community first, because I think right now there are some pretty strong calls for change.

“There are an incredible group of hard-working professionals at that organisation who’ve been amazing to work with and actually our thoughts are with them at this time, because it’s a difficult time for them to be in this situation as well, and that’s concerning for us.

“So, while we reflect on a lot of positives that have come out of the organisation, ultimately, this type of proposal should never have emerged in the way it did.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 9: Everton
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 10th (NB: this is not necessarily Andy Hunter’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 13th

Prospects

A season stripped of the fear of relegation, featuring more proactive, front-footed football and the return of some hope: had Everton been offered that package before their relocation to Hill Dickinson Stadium last summer it would have been accepted gratefully given the turmoil of the previous four years. For four fifths of last season it was accepted gratefully, but then came a collapse that transformed perceptions of David Moyes’s first full season back in charge. Talk of progress requires more supporting evidence this time around.

Everton were three points off the fifth and final Champions League qualification spot on 21 March having dismantled Chelsea in their finest performance at the club’s new stadium. They did not win another game all season and slumped to 13th on the final day – the same position as the previous campaign under Sean Dyche and Moyes, with only one point more but an inferior goal difference. European football may well have been an ambitious target for a club adjusting to a new home and the loss of 10 players following the expiry of their contracts, loans included. But the opportunity presented itself to Moyes’s team and they blew it.

Without the upheaval of last summer, with midfield resources improved and young players having had the benefit of a year’s experience of the Premier League, European qualification could be a more realistic proposition this season. Provided a few glaring holes in Moyes’s squad are finally filled. An upgrade on the limited centre-forward options of Beto and Thierno Barry is essential, although the latter has shown more promising signs in pre-season. Likewise a successor to Séamus Coleman – one of several big Evertonian losses behind the scenes recently. Everton’s quest for a new right-back is their very own Odyssey, while central defence was another area of concern last season. Genuine progress, the measure of which is not open to debate, rests on the final moves of the window.

Off-field picture

The consequences of Farhad Moshiri’s calamitous ownership are still being felt with Everton ordered to pay almost £40m in compensation to Burnley over the latter’s relegation in 2021-22. Everton are appealing against the can-of-worms verdict by a Premier League independent disciplinary commission, along with the biggest financial penalty ever imposed on a Premier League club, but claim their latest punishment has not affected this summer’s transfer plans. Many season ticket holders have been hit by above-inflation price increases – in some instances of almost 10% – and the club have extended a sponsorship deal with Stake, despite the UK government pledging to crack down on unlicensed gambling operators sponsoring British sports teams.

Owner-fan relationship

The Friedkin Group (TFG) has brought the financial stability that Everton desperately needed but it would be a stretch to suggest fans have connected with a low-key ownership group that rarely attend games. The man they appointed to run the club, chief executive, Angus Kinnear, annoyed supporters at the end of last season by claiming the hierarchy was “happily dissatisfied” with the first campaign at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The comment was portrayed as fresh evidence of Everton accepting mediocrity but in fairness to Kinnear, who was writing about TFG’s determination to banish the threats of financial instability, relegation and regulatory sanction, he did add: “The progress is clear but we have not achieved anything yet.”

The manager

David Moyes turns 64 in April and, while the Premier League’s oldest manager clearly retains the hunger and ambition to rebuild Everton on a stronger footing, it will be interesting to see whether he retains the appetite for a fight with his critics in the event of a poor start. Particularly as the Scotland job remains available and he would appear the ideal candidate to succeed Steve Clarke. Moyes was exceeding his brief until the dismal end to last season cost Everton a shot at Europe and placed his team selections under an unforgiving spotlight. Talk of a contract extension has since gone quiet.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Brennan Johnson struggled at Crystal Palace but could have just the attacking qualities Everton need. Photograph: Everton FC

It has been a sensible window rather than a sexy one from Everton so far – see replacing Idrissa Gana Gueye with the £7m Christian Nørgaard – but they might have delivered in swapping Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. No one would dispute that the Wales’ international’s move from Tottenham to Crystal Palace in January fell flat, least of all Palace who were willing to take a significant hit on their £35m, one-time record investment only seven months later. But if the 25-year-old recaptures the form he showed at Nottingham Forest, or when scoring 18 goals for Spurs in 2024-25, he could prove a steal who addresses several problems in the Everton frontline.

Stat attack

David Moyes loves to keep a settled side. Everton averaged the fewest changes to their starting XI of any team in the 2025-26 Premier League. With the squad looking largely the same as last season, this trend should continue. But what if injuries bite?

Set for a breakthrough

Tyler Dibling would have been a strong candidate for this category last summer following his arrival from Southampton for an initial £35m. It reflects a nonevent of a debut season on Merseyside that he can be nominated 12 months on. Everton invested a lot of time and money into their pursuit of the England Under-21 international, who remains the most expensive signing of Moyes’s second spell in charge, but the return was a huge disappointment. The attacking midfielder started only four league games and was not given a single minute after the 2-0 win over Burnley on 3 March. The manager did not hide his frustration with what he was seeing on the training ground.

World Cup impact

The longest World Cup in history should not have too onerous an impact on Moyes’s squad. Only three of his players were involved and, of those, only Jordan Pickford was in action after 1 July. Pickford came in for familiar criticism following his performances against Ghana and Argentina despite reinforcing his status as England’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper across the tournament. Iliman Ndiaye started once for Senegal and was subbed in the 73rd minute with his country leading Belgium 2-0 in the last-32 tie. They ultimately lost 3-2. Nathan Patterson, whose Everton future is uncertain, featured in all three of Scotland’s forgettable group campaign.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Arsenal offered Osimhen in exchange deal? Newcastle to make Baleba bid?
Sports.content:
As these glorious pages reported on Thursday, Galatasaray wanted Gabriel Martinelli. In the following 24 hours things changed a bit, creating greater complexity, something we do not approve of. Arsenal have supposedly been offered the chance to involve the Nigeria striker Victor Osimhen in exchange for the Brazilian, which could be temptong for a side looking for a new No 9. To further sweeten any potential, Ethan Nwaneri could be chucked into it too to make it a mega swap.

Tijjani Reijnders may struggle to find a perfect role within Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City. The Dutchman has already been linked with Nottingham Forest, which has stirred some interest in Saudi Arabia from Al Qadsiah, who are managed by Brendan Rodgers and are willing to cough up £51m for the midfielder.

Newcastle are also searching for a central midfielder after losing Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães to Spurs and Arsenal. They did at least get around £175m for the pair, so are eyeing up a deal for Brighton’s Carlos Baleba. Rafik Belghali could head to St James’ Park if the Magpies are willing to stump up £12m for the right back.

Leeds are trying to progress a move for Nico Elvedi from Borussia Mönchengladbach, where the centre-back played under Daniel Farke. The 29-year-old wants out and only has a year remaining on his current contract, so will almost certainly end up at Elland Road.

There is very little like the signing of a third-choice goalkeeper to get fans excited. Nottingham Forest are giving their people what they want by bringing in the former Swansea stopper Steven Benda for nothing. One assumes he will be met at East Midlands Airport by thousands of excited supporters eager to welcome their new hero.

Down at Crystal Palace, getting greater strength in depth is part of the plan. Anan Khalaili is set to help out with that by joining from Union Saint-Gilloise to provide competition for Daniel Munoz at right-back. Palace could be involved in a battle royale for the services of Lecce centre-back Tiago Gabriel, who is valued at £25m. Bournemouth are also tracking the defenders who was previously the subject of a bid from Benfica.

It transpires that Wilfried Zaha is out of work so is back training at Crystal Palace to keep fit. Would he be worth a punt for the Eagles? He came through the ranks at Selhurst Park and returned for a second spell after things did not work out at Manchester United.

The winger is wanted by numerous teams but the Premier League has plenty of allure. The Tigers are also in the market for a central midfielder and have sent a £15m to Everton for Tim Iroegbunam.

Sports.title: Rangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes on
Sports.content:
Derek McInnes’s fledgling tenure as Rangers manager is in disarray after his side exited the Europa League qualifiers with a 3-2 aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok after drawing 1-1 at Ibrox.

Rangers had lost 2-1 in the first leg in Poland last week but there was optimism when the captain, Lawrence Shankland, levelled the tie on aggregate with a penalty on 19 minutes.

However, in the 65th minute, the visitors deservedly equalised through the attacker Nik Prelec and the disjointed home side could not get a foothold in the game again despite changes in formation and personnel, with the boos ringing out around the ground at full time from fans frustrated at the dismal start to the season.

McInnes has failed to register a win in four competitive matches since moving from Hearts in the summer and the dispiriting performance means Rangers will take on Jablonec, from Czechia, in the Conference League playoff round.

Hearts, meanwhile, restored some pride in a 1-1 draw with Benfica as they too dropped out of the Europa League.

Tómas Magnússon had the home fans dreaming of a famous win over their illustrious opponents after firing in the opener in the 77th minute. But the Portuguese giants, cruising from a 6-1 first leg win a week earlier, levelled less than a minute later through Dodi Lukébakio to wrap up a 7-2 aggregate triumph.

View image in fullscreen Tómas Magnússon (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring for Hearts against Benfica. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

It was nevertheless an encouraging display from Wouter Vrancken’s side against a team who made seven changes from the first leg.

The consolation for Hearts is a place in the Conference League playoffs, where they will face Rapid Vienna of Austria.

David Gray revealed his Hibernian players had their heads in ice buckets as he lauded them for “an incredible achievement” after closing out a 2-1 aggregate victory over Shkendija to set up a Conference League playoff round showdown with the Belgian side Gent. The two teams played out a tightly contested 0-0 draw in the second leg in the searing heat of the Todor Proeski National Arena.

View image in fullscreen Hibernian fans in the stands at the Todor Proeski National Arena. Photograph: Nikola Krstic/Shutterstock

“I’m delighted for the players,” the Hibs manager told BBC Sport. “It’s a brilliant time to get your first clean sheet of the season.

“I just said to the players, don’t underestimate how big an achievement that is against a really good side who made it to the knockout stages of the competition last season.

“Added to that, the conditions, the heat, we had to deal with all these things. I don’t think it was a brilliant game, but we put our bodies on the line and the attitude was there.”

Sports.title: Lincoln have faith in double act as they return to second tier
Sports.content:
The last thing the Championship needs is another spying scandal, so when a lorry emblazoned with KGB parked up alongside Lincoln City’s training ground on Tuesday lunchtime there was laughter as staff pondered whether the Soviet Union were examining their set pieces. It shows the relaxed atmosphere at one of the second tier’s newest clubs, one that has witnessed a summer of change yet maintained continuity by appointing joint head coaches.

Tom Shaw and Chris Cohen have replaced Michael Skubala, who led the Imps to 103 points and promotion to this level for the first time in 66 years before leaving for Bristol City. It was a symbiotic appointment because while the former assistants were devising a sales pitch to the club’s hierarchy, the wheels were already in motion to promote from within. Their plan is to banish English football’s memories of Liverpool’s ill-fated pairing of Roy Evans and Gérard Houllier. The duo are doing final preparations for Saturday’s season opener at the Riverside against Middlesbrough, who have spent over £20m on summer signings – Lincoln have spent a quarter of that across their 142-year history, indicating the task ahead.

“The difference is that they’re put together by a football club, Evans and Houllier being the prime example, it’s two men just put together and told to go and do the same job,” says Cohen in the office he shares with Shaw. “Me and Tom have formed a relationship over the last few years where the club has seen our relationship as a pair of coaches and blokes evolve. We drive in together, we drive home together, we spend all of our days together, when we’re off, we’ll have a game of golf together.

“They understand that if it is going to work with any two coaches, then this is probably the one with the best chance because we see football the same way, we see life the same way, we see our principles are very, very similar. We obviously have differences in small decisions and nuances within everything, but principally we see the way that a football club should be run and the team should play very, very similarly. That gives us a really good chance.”

Lincoln is a forward-thinking club but the latest major decision is not about experimentation. The duo fit the club’s philosophy, having worked within academies giving them the skills to develop players, as they did with Jack Moylan who was sold to Cardiff for a record fee. Shaw and Cohen were key members of Skubala’s staff, taking on great responsibility and Lincoln were keen to reward their progression and give the squad continuity. The players have been told not to call them “gaffer or boss”.

They complement one another, with Cohen’s focus on the defence and Shaw the attack to share the workload. The pair are rarely side-by-side on the training ground, as they seek different perspectives, whether watching a session taken by the other head coach or the former Hull defender Paul McShane, while David Preece oversees goalkeeping.

“We do get to the end of some days and we look at each other and go: ‘Thank God we’ve got each other,’” says Cohen. “Thank God there’s two of us to do that, what we’ve just created on that day on the training pitch or gameplans. I’ve been an assistant for a long time, so I’ve had that relationship with managers where I’ve had their full trust, but there is a different feel about having the final decision and being sure that you’re making the right one. To have two of us to check and challenge each other and then come out with hopefully the best logical decision for the team.” The bickering, they say, is left for golf.

View image in fullscreen Lincoln’s analysts preparing data after a training session. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian

The club has handed out 14 new contracts since promotion, in addition to two permanent signings and three loans to maintain momentum. The 2016-17 run to the FA Cup quarter-finals brought prize money which was invested in a purpose-built training ground, having not had one before, which sits between a former RAF base and a potato field. Promotion means more income, allowing a £9m upgrade of the ground and training site, with further expansion planned.

One of the few things the pair do apart is holiday, which is when they found out they would be taking over, with Shaw in Greece and Cohen in Spain. “The first two or three days of our holidays were very hectic,” says Shaw. “We signed the paperwork and then enjoyed the last few days in the swimming pool. There was some emotion in our families,” says Shaw, looking at a photo of Cohen and him celebrating promotion with their children. “It was just a really nice moment in our journeys and our families know each other and really get on. So just really nice for us to be doing this together and a big moment in our careers.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The visit to Sincil Bank has been jokingly used to illustrate the impact of relegation on West Ham but Lincoln are far more than a punchline. They are in the Championship on merit, despite being the bookmakers’ favourites to go down. A deserved 2-1 away win was secured over divisional rivals Derby in the Carabao Cup last weekend further proved their credentials.

“We hope we’re underestimated, we hope the big clubs in the division when they turn up at Sincil Bank underestimate how good our players are, how good our fans are, how good our stadium is to come to,” Cohen says. “We’re hoping that clubs take us for granted or underestimate us because it just goes back to that group of players in there that we back to the absolute hilt.

“We’re bringing a couple more recruits hopefully to help with the volume of the squad but as I said all along they’re an amazing group, amazing technically, tactically but the thing they’ve got is heart and passion which wins you games of football.”

The Riverside will be a key test of their credentials. “We will check and challenge each other through the week,” says Shaw. “We’ll have minor disagreements throughout the week to get to what we think is the right plan. And then by Thursday, Friday we’re super aligned and massively behind whatever decisions we’ve come to, with the support of all the people as well.”

Sports.title: High-flying Sirius chase shock Allsvenskan title despite losing ‘best player in league’
Sports.content:
For most teams, losing a forward with 15 goals in 15 games midway through the season, amid a historic title chase, might be cause for panic. Sirius, the runaway Allsvenskan leaders, are not most teams.

“I’m actually really confident,” says Henrik Castegren, the club captain, when asked about the team’s ability to adapt after Robbie Ure’s move to Sevilla for a club-record fee, reported to be £5.6m plus add-ons. “I’m really happy for Robbie, but also quite sad because I enjoyed playing with him a lot. I think he was by far the best player in this league for the first six months [of the season] … but, with that being said, I’m feeling quite comfortable with us moving forward.”

It helps that Sirius have been here before. They loaned last season’s top scorer, Leo Walta, to Swansea in February before the deal became permanent this summer for a fee of around £3m. Like Ure, Walta arrived at a young age, developed rapidly, caught the eye of a wealthier club and earned Sirius a significant profit, which they reinvested. That has become the blueprint for their success, allowing a club with no major honours to their name, having spent most of their existence in Sweden’s lower leagues, to compete for a first Allsvenskan title against storied rivals with far greater resources.

“One important part of our strategy is to have a lot of sellable players,” says Jonathan Ederström, Sirius’s sporting director. “We’re not the biggest in Sweden, we’re not the richest in Sweden, we don’t have the fanciest history in Sweden, but we decided that we were going to aim to become the best in terms of development. Having the best development culture, but also building a squad with mostly young players that we saw big potential in.”

In that sense the departure of Ure, a former Scotland youth international who came through Rangers’ academy and Anderlecht’s reserves before moving to Sweden at the start of last season, is a sign that Sirius’s model is working exactly as intended. “It’s such a good thing for all parties,” says Ederström. “It’s a fantastic journey for Robbie, but it’s also fantastic for Sirius.”

As well as allowing for reinvestment in the squad – Sirius have already signed Jesper Uneken, a promising 22-year-old forward from PSV Eindhoven, as Ure’s replacement, along with the Finland Under-21 midfielder Otso Liimatta from Famalicão – the fee will be ploughed back into the club’s infrastructure and facilities. “[The other advantage] is that we become more attractive as a club for other players around the world,” says Ederström. “It can be close by in Sweden but it can also be Belgium, or Netherlands, or Scotland obviously. Hopefully it helps us getting the next Robbie here.”

View image in fullscreen Robbie Ure (left) shrugs off Halmstad’s Gustav Friberg. The forward, who has now moved to Sevilla, scored 31 goals in 50 games for Sirius in all competitions. Photograph: Anders Bjurö/TT/Shutterstock

No one is expecting Uneken to match Ure’s numbers immediately and, if there is a period of adjustment, Sirius have plenty of breathing room. They are 12 points clear of second-placed Hammarby and undefeated in the league with just under half the season to play. Isak Bjerkebo, their left winger, has also been prolific, tallying 14 goals and nine assists in all competitions. They also have one of the tightest defences in the league buttressed by Mohamed Soumah, a goalscoring centre-back brought in with money reinvested from the deal that took Walta to Swansea, and a high-tempo midfield capable of harrying opponents to exhaustion.

Holding it all together is Andreas Engelmark, who was appointed head coach in January last year. The team’s ascent is all the more impressive given that his early days in charge were hard going. Sirius spent a significant portion of last season looking nervously over their shoulders, dropping to 14th, the Allsvenskan’s relegation playoff spot, for several weeks. Engelmark battled on and, despite sustaining the heaviest defeat of the season, an 8-2 loss at Djurgården in September, Sirius ended strongly. In fact, they have not lost in the league since.

“Even though he went tough when the results weren’t there last summer, he stuck to what he thought was the best going forward,” says Castegren. “That, I would say, is his biggest strength, to not give that up and start doing other short-term stuff.

“He really sees you as a player and adjusts small things to get the most out of you, and also how you can complement the team as a collective. I really feel comfortable, in that sense, now Robbie has left us, that we can find ways to get results, to perform well and play well.”
