View image in fullscreen Sirius fans display their scarves in the stands with the club’s meteoric rise a source of huge excitement. Photograph: Staffan Claesson/TT/Shutterstock

For people in Uppsala, the city where Sirius are based, the club’s meteoric rise has been a source of huge excitement. Attendances at their ground, Studenternas, have leapt up, while there is a buzz around the place that has energised staff and players alike. “With the results that have come, I think the city has really turned it on,” says Castegren. “You can see blue and black shirts wherever you go … you can tell also by the numbers we have at the games, in the audience. It’s a packed house every game, which you couldn’t even think would be a reality three years ago when I first came here.”

While Sirius winning the title might have seemed unthinkable a few seasons ago, there is an encouraging precedent: last season’s Swedish champions, Mjällby, were also rank outsiders who had never won a major trophy before. All three Scandinavian leagues have been won by dark horses in recent seasons, with Viking, for the first time in 34 years, the reigning champions of Norway, and Aarhus, after a 40-year wait, triumphant in Denmark.

Asked why the Allsvenskan, in particular, has been so unpredictable over the past few years, Ederström gives a concise answer: “Because the big teams underperform.” That has created an opening for insurgent clubs who scout well, recruit smartly and are willing to innovate.

There is still a way to go for Sirius, but they have good reason to believe they can finish the job. “The biggest thing for me this season is what we have created in Uppsala as a city,” adds Ederström. “To have something to believe in, to have something so important in [people’s] life … we really appreciate that.”

Sports.title: Championship spending hits record levels and likely to go higher as playoffs expand
Sports.content:
The Championship’s collective wage bill grew to a record £903m in 2024-25, according to Deloitte’s latest Annual Review of Football Finance. Clubs are paying players enormous sums in their pursuit of Premier League football. With the playoffs expanding this season, the number of owners willing to risk even more money in the hope of securing promotion is only likely to increase.

In isolation, the figure of £903m does not signify much. Compared to the Premier League’s £4.4bn salary outlay, it almost looks small. But England’s top division can afford that gargantuan commitment to wages whereas the second tier cannot. The 24 clubs in the Championship earned £942m, meaning salaries consumed 96% of revenue. If there was any surprise in their collective net debt being £1.4bn at the end of 2024-25, it was only that it had reduced from the £1.5bn it was a year earlier.

While qualifying for European competitions is not on the immediate agenda for clubs at that level, Uefa’s financial sustainability regulations restrict spending on wages, transfers and agent fees to 70% of club revenues. Luton and Sheffield United spent about 59% of their income on salaries in 2024-25, with the parachute payments they received for being relegated from the Premier League the previous season helping them keep a grip on their finances.

But only four other clubs were below 80%, with 13 – more than half the division – spending more on wages than they earned. Cardiff spent £39m on salaries against £26m income, giving them the worst wages to revenue percentage in the division (150%). The reward for their ambition was to finish bottom of the table.

The reason for such risk-taking is obvious. Deloitte estimates that the newly promoted Coventry and Hull will see their revenue rise by at least £210m over the next three seasons, with the windfall potentially reaching £365m if they can retain their Premier League status into 2027-28. Ipswich’s figures are lower thanks to receiving parachute payments last season, but they are still thought to be around £170m and £325m respectively.

These sums are helping to form a strata of clubs that regularly flit between the top two tiers of English football. Burnley have either enjoyed promotion from the Championship or suffered Premier League relegation for five consecutive seasons. The Clarets are fourth favourites with bookmakers to go up once again next May, with their fellow relegated sides West Ham and Wolves leading the Championship promotion market.

Their advantage is obvious. Capology estimates West Ham have the 15th highest wage bill in the world outside the Premier League and Saudi Pro League. Wolves are only two spots behind them in these amended standings, with Burnley a further six places back.

The majority of top division teams in France, Germany, Italy and Spain can’t keep pace with the salary spend of these clubs so how can most Championship teams expect to compete? Jarrod Bowen alone is thought to earn £7.8m per year at West Ham, more than the entire squads of Lincoln (£5.8m) or Bolton (£6.3m).

The new playoff system in the Championship at least offers more clubs the chance of a Premier League golden ticket. The teams that finish between third and eighth will qualify, with third and fourth going straight through to the traditional two-legged semi-finals. Their opponents in those ties will be decided by one-legged quarter-finals that feature the teams in fifth and sixth at home to those in eighth and seventh respectively.

This will leave the tantalising possibility of a playoff berth open to plenty of clubs until very late in the season. Few will be entirely out of the running in January, when the transfer window offers an opportunity for squad investment. The fate of Leicester highlights the possible risks though. When the winter window closed earlier this year, they were six points from eighth, nine above the bottom three. Clubs in a similar position next January may gamble on going for a playoff spot but could end up being relegated as Leicester were.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The National League also highlights how unlikely it is that teams that take the additional playoff spots go up. The highest tier of non-league football has employed a six-team playoff format since 2017-18, with only the division winner earning automatic promotion. The club finishing seventh have yet to win the playoffs, with the side in sixth succeeding only once. Even then, the team in question (Grimsby in 2022) were in their only season outside League Two in the past 10. They were below their regular level, not climbing up to reach sixth.

The Championship has a similar theme for playoff success. No team finishing sixth have gone up since 2010, with Aston Villa the most recent fifth-placed side to earn promotion, in 2019. None of the previous seven teams that finished eighth in the second flight averaged more than 1.5 points-per-game or won more than 43.4% of their matches. If they can’t win every other game at that level, how can they hope to compete in the Premier League in the unlikely event they go up?

No one cares about that when there’s a reward in the region of £200m simply for getting there. Supporters might care if the owner drives their club’s finances further into the red chasing an unlikely playoff dream though.

Sports.title: Kieran Trippier: ‘The Championship is relentless … it’s totally different to the Premier League’
Sports.content:
When the question inevitably comes, Kieran Trippier is happy to set the record straight. Fresh from training, head to toe in Wolves kit – vest, shorts and club-branded sliders – he walks into a suite at their Compton Park base, conversation soon shifting to an episode that rocked supporters and stopped outsiders in their tracks: three days after signing, the manager Trippier cited as a significant driver behind his decision to drop into the second tier, Rob Edwards, was sacked. All the while, a deal for his replacement, César Peixoto, was being accelerated.

“I’m not going to sit here and lie, I wasn’t expecting it,” Trippier says. “But it’s the club’s decision. I had good chats with Rob, of course, but I’m here to play for Wolves. There are many surprises in football and that certainly was a surprise, I’m not going to deny that. But I just cracked on, I was with my kids on holiday, training in Mallorca and just looking forward to day one in pre-season.”

Other reports followed the bombshell news. “I’ve read it all: that I was looking to rip my contract up, and all this nonsense. I was just looking forward to reporting back to Wolves. I don’t know where it even came from to be honest, that I was looking to rip my contract up – it certainly didn’t come from me, otherwise you would have heard it from me, that’s just the player that I am.”

It is a line in keeping with Trippier’s endearing straight-talking character that has made him a big hit everywhere he has been. He left Newcastle at the end of last season after playing an instrumental part in their rise under Eddie Howe, the crowning glory the Carabao Cup win last year. He spent three seasons at Atlético Madrid under Diego Simeone, where he won La Liga, after four at Tottenham under Mauricio Pochettino, culminating in a Champions League final appearance. He represented England at four major tournaments, playing every game en route to the Euro 2024 final.

Now he is back in the second tier for the first time since promotion with Burnley 12 years ago, poised to start Wolves’ Championship opener against Blackburn on Friday. He accepts it is not a natural segue. Instead of entertaining Barcelona at St James’ Park last September, here comes Bolton at Molineux in October.

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier in a huddle with his new teammates during Wolves’ 3-0 friendly win against Racing Santander. Photograph: WWFC

“I’m not ashamed to go to the Championship because I played in it for many years,” Trippier says, recalling his first taste of the division: defending alongside Darren Moore while a teenager at Barnsley. “I had a good chat with Eddie Howe and Ross Wilson [Newcastle’s sporting director] and made my decision at the end of the season that I wanted to try something new. There were a few [interested] clubs but it was important for me that I was close to my children.”

Trippier, who calls Manchester home, knows what to expect from an unforgiving league. He recalls being part of a Burnley side that triumphed 2-1 at Wolves in the penultimate game of 2012-13, to extinguish lingering fears of relegation and all but condemn Wolves to League One. “I’ve been speaking to my teammates because the majority of them have never played in the Championship, so it’s important for myself and the lads who have to help them and try and make them understand that it’s going to be difficult.

“I’ve just said: it’s relentless, because it is … and it’s totally different to the Premier League. Going to Lincoln away is going to be a difficult game, but they’re good lads who have listened to me, Tommy [Doyle], Adam [Armstrong]. The lads will be ready.”

This is Trippier’s first external interview since joining Wolves on a two-year contract with the option of a further 12 months. He canvassed the opinions of Doyle, Conor Coady, John Ruddy and Sam Johnstone, with whom he was on holiday in Turkey before signing, to tap into “the insides of the club”. Edwards’ sudden departure – a month after André committed his future to the club and 48 hours after Raúl Jiménez returned to enhance the feelgood factor generated by Trippier’s arrival – warrants discussion, but the full-back is well placed to talk on numerous fronts, including Howe’s exit after four and a half years.

“He helped the club stay in the Premier League, twice qualified for the Champions League, won a trophy, but the most important thing he did was reconnecting the supporters with the team. I was told before the [Saudi Arabia-led] takeover that it was not a good place to be – the fans were against the owners, the board etc – but when the new owners came in, and the manager, he [Howe] connected everyone, just like Gareth Southgate did with England.”

Is Howe’s legacy deserving of a statue? “He’s won a trophy, hasn’t he?” Trippier says with a smile, “but that’s not for me to decide … the parade was incredible, the big banner of the manager showed the love the supporters had for him and still have now. When I first went there, it was a tough place [to play], especially after getting beat by Cambridge [in the FA Cup third round], but maybe that was a blessing, really, so we could just focus on [staying in] the Premier League … he will go down in history there, for sure. I’m gutted to see him go.”

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier holds the Carabao Cup trophy aloft with Alexander Isak on board the open-top bus with their teammates and manager Eddie Howe (front row, left) as they pass St James’ Park. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Then there is England’s World Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina, when their low block crumbled late on. “I’ve been in that position many, many times with Simeone – I could name 30 games when he’s done it and we’ve managed to see it out, typical Simeone for you. He’s the master of the dark arts and seeing out games. Thomas Tuchel has been in that position many, many times, won a Champions League trophy with Chelsea, did unbelievably with Bayern Munich … it just didn’t happen. We were against one of the greatest players ever who can flick a switch,” Trippier says of Lionel Messi, clicking his fingers. “I’ve played against him many times where he just walks for 60 minutes, but then he can score a hat-trick. That’s just the magic of him.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Peixoto is unknown to most but Trippier says he was aware of the Portuguese’s pedigree before the 46-year-old, who spent last season in charge of Gil Vicente, succeeded Edwards. Peixoto’s command of English has meant Trippier has not needed to dip into his Spanish to converse. “When the postman used to come in Madrid, I used to get my son to answer because he was fluent,” Trippier says, smiling.

So, what’s Peixoto like? “Really demanding. Honest. On the training field he is 100mph, nuts – in a good way – but he’s really, really demanding and I think that’s what we need as players if we want to be successful. He’s very demanding, like Pochettino and Simeone. He has his own rules: don’t break his trust, don’t be late. I wouldn’t like to be on his bad side, let’s put it that way.”

View image in fullscreen The Wolves manager, César Peixoto (second right), slows down from his 100mph on the training pitch to speak with Kieran Trippier (left), Andre (centre) and Toti Gomes at a pre-season training in Faro, Portugal. Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty Images

Trippier turns 36 in September, twice the age of Mateus Mané, an exciting talent who Trippier witnessed first-hand when marking him with Newcastle last season and one of those Wolves hope will illuminate a positive season. “I feel good, I feel probably in the best shape I’ve been in for many, many years. I’m not as fast as I used to be but I always believe I am clever and fast up here,” Trippier says, tapping his temples. “I feel like I’ve still got many years left in the tank.”

For Wolves, his signing was a coup. “It’s similar to when I went to Newcastle, when I left Atlético Madrid … There were a lot of eyebrows raised, but throughout my whole career I’ve had no regrets.”

Trippier, who is part of Peixoto’s leadership group, acknowledges he and his teammates will begin the campaign with a target on their backs. “Going into the Blackburn game, the first game of the Championship season, all eyes will be on us,” he says.

“When teams get relegated from the Premier League, everybody wants to beat them. It was a tough year for Wolves last year, but this season is a new season, like a reset. The reality is now we’re in the Championship, so you have to forget what happened and look forward, be positive. Our goal has to be to go straight back up to the Premier League.”

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo unveils shock new look just days after marrying Georgina Rodriguez at intimate wedding ceremony
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo unveils shock new look just days after marrying Georgina Rodriguez at intimate wedding ceremony

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cristiano Ronaldo has revealed an astonishing new hairstyle in the wake of his wedding to Georgina Rodriguez.

Gone is the black, slicked-back hair and in its place is a hairdo we never thought we'd see on him: a ginger buzz cut with a high skin fade.

The 41-year-old has been remarkably consistent with his look over the years but, with his fresh trim, it would now be hard to distinguish him from his old Manchester United team-mate Paul Scholes.

This could well be the haircut with which he passes his coveted 1,000 career goals mark.

The Al-Nassr star is on 976 goals for club and country and has a year left on his £488,000-a-day contract in Saudi Arabia.

Ronaldo was pictured returning to training, preparing for the season under new manager Ange Postecoglou alongside the likes of Sadio Mane and Kingsley Coman.

Cristiano Ronaldo debuted a bold new look as he returned to training with Al-Nassr

Just days ago he married Georgina Rodriguez in an 'intimate and private' ceremony in Cascais, Portugal, alongside their five children

CR7 finally broke his major trophy duck with Al-Nassr last campaign as they got their hands on the Saudi Pro League.

And on Tuesday he finally achieved his long-time dream of marrying Georgina in an 'intimate and private' ceremony with their five children present, a year after they first got engaged.

Ronaldo shared that he and Georgina had tied the knot after ten years together by sharing a snap of their wedding bands on Instagram.

A representative for Ronaldo also confirmed news of the union, saying: 'Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez were married today in a civil ceremony in Cascais, Portugal, and are now officially husband and wife.

'The ceremony was a private and intimate moment attended by their five children.'

Their wedding news came just days after it was thought the couple were set to marry in Funchal Cathedral, leading to thousands of fans gathering outside the church.

However, it was then revealed that the couple were not getting married there at all, and the ceremony turned out to be for an entirely unconnected Portuguese couple from Madeira called Fabio Ramos and Fatima Nicole Cunha Teixeira.

Georgina was working at a Gucci store in Madrid, earning £10 an hour, when she and Ronaldo met in 2016.

The Portugal star announced that he and Georgina had tied the knot by sharing a snap of their wedding bands on Instagram

The pair have two biological children, though she helps raise all five of his kids. Cristiano Jr. (pictured left) hugs his baby sister Eva while Georgina cradles Mateo on her lap, Cristiano (pictured right) holds his two daughters baby Bella and Alana Martina

Ronaldo, 41, is aiming to score 1,000 career goals and has a year left on his deal at Al-Nassr

Recalling their meeting, Georgina said: 'I was finally able to leave the shop to go home three hours later than I should have and as I was getting ready to leave Cristiano came in with his eldest son and some friends.

'Let's just say it was butterflies in my stomach.'

Cristiano would then pick Georgina up from work in his £1.5million Bugatti – after she had arrived at the shop on the bus.

'Many times he'd come after work', she said in her Netflix series I Am Georgina.

'He would come, I remember once, once in a Bugatti. My coworkers went crazy. They get there on the bus, and I would leave in a Bugatti. I mean people couldn't believe it.'

By December, she quit her job shortly after fans began crowding outside the store.

The following month, the pair made their first public appearance at The Best FIFA Football Awards, confirming speculation that they were a couple.

Cristiano and Georgina made their Instagram debut as a couple in March 2017 when the footballer posted a sweet snap of them cuddling on a couch.

Ronaldo proposed to Georgina last year with a huge diamond engagement, having previously said he 'waited' before popping the question

Georgina joked that the soccer star popping the question with an 'enormous' diamond ring was 'the least he could offer' after waiting for so long to propose

In June of that year, the footballer welcomed twins Mateo and Eva via surrogacy and then five months later, Georgina gave birth to their daughter, Alana Martina, in November.

The following month, Georgina posed for photos with her newborn daughter Alana for the cover of HOLA!

Revealing how they came up with the name for their daughter, she said: 'We both chose the name. Cristiano chose Alana and I chose Martina.

'We decided to give her both names that each of us chose. We thought it was even more special.'

In 2022, the couple welcomed twins; however, their baby boy tragically died during childbirth, while his sister, Bella Esmeralda, survived.

Opening up about how he and Georgina coped with the heartache of losing a baby, the footballer told Piers Morgan at the time: 'I feel that we always support each other. Sometimes it's like in a relationship you have good moments, bad moments it is part of the journey.

'But probably in that period, we consolidated it more, the relationship, but even in the worst moments you have to meet, you have to make the thing smooth.

'I learned so many things. I saw the other perspective of the life. My daughter, now who is three years old, she is the queen of the family, who made the house happy.

Cristiano met Georgina in 2016 after he saw her in the Gucci store where she was working

'Everything happens for a reason. I believe in that. So, we are a blessed family. I am proud of that.'

After nearly a decade together, fans were then desperate to know when Georgina and Cristiano would marry, with their family now complete.

However, in an interview with Marca last year, the Portuguese admitted he hadn't yet married Georgina because he hadn't felt the 'click'.

He said: 'I always tell her, "when we get that click". Like everything with our life, and she knows what I'm talking about.

'It could be in a year or it could be in six months or it could be in a month. I'm 1000 per cent sure that it'll happen.'

In August, the footballer finally popped the question with a giant diamond ring.

Fans speculated the pair got engaged the month before after the model shared pictures of a bridal-themed dinner, complete with 'C heart G' pillows, a six-piece band and stunning white flower arrangements.

She also wore a giant sparkler on her wedding ring finger, hinting at the pair's secret engagement.

Georgina gleefully shared the news on Instagram with a photo of her glitzy engagement ring. 'Yes I do. In this and in all my lives,' she wrote in a heartfelt caption.

Cristiano then revealed that two of his children inspired him to give Georgina a 'not-so romantic' and off-the-cuff proposal.

He revealed that he didn't plan to propose to the 'woman of his life' the night they got engaged, but it felt like the 'right time'.

'It was like 1am. My daughters were in bed sleeping,' the 41-year-old told Piers Morgan in part one of their new interview.

He said: 'One of my friends gave me the ring to offer Gio (Georgina) and as I was giving her the ring, my two kids come in and say "Daddy, you're going to give the ring to mum and you're going to ask her to get married."

'I said, "Wow, this is the right moment to say yes." It was the time. I knew that I was going to do it one day but I hadn't planned to do it then.

'Because my daughters said that and my friends were filming, it was what I wanted and I offered (the ring). I didn't (get on one knee) because I wasn't prepared but it was a beautiful moment. I made a speech.

'It was simple, I'm not a very romantic guy. Well, I am, but I'm not very romantic, not the kind of guy who brings flowers every week to the home. But I'm romantic in my way. It was beautiful and I knew that it's the woman of my life so I did that and I hope that I did it well.'

Asked about when they plan to tie the knot, the footballer joked: 'Not yet. We plan to do it after the World Cup with the trophy! But she is not the person that likes big parties. She doesn't like it. She likes private things. So I will respect these decisions.

'One thing that I love, she didn't care about the ring. She asked me if I was honest and I said, "I want you and I want to marry you." I didn't cry but I had tears on my eyes.'

Experts estimated that Cristiano splashed out an astonishing £1.5million on Georgina's engagement ring.

Sports.title: Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge
Sports.content:
Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez got married at their new £30million mansion near Lisbon in front of just four witnesses and their children, it emerged today.

Cristiano's doting mum Dolores Aveiro and his three siblings Hugo, Elma and Katia, were not present at the intimate civil ceremony, which took place at 1.30pm on Tuesday.

Georgina's sister Ivana, Cristiano's long-time friend Miguel Paixao and a Spanish couple named as Jose Rodriguez Sangil and his wife Monica Goncalez Martinez were the only witnesses.

Registrar Maria Manuel Ferreira de Campos Folhadela de Oliveira travelled from the northern Portuguese city of Porto to Cascais to officiate the ceremony.

And the star couple, who married exactly one year to the day after they announced their engagement on social media, have decided to keep their prenuptial assets separate despite tying the knot after a decade-long romance.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez married with four witnesses in Cascais, Lisbon

The marriage certificate for Ronaldo and Georgina's wedding has now emerged

The couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings after the small ceremony

They signed a prenup agreement to define their property regime on August 10, a day before the ceremony, at a public notary's office in Lisbon.

Cristiano Ronaldo's representatives confirmed earlier this week the footballer and his long-time partner married on August 11 in an 'intimate' ceremony in Cascais after the couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings on social media.

It followed speculation which turned out to be false that they were due to marry at Funchal Cathedral in Cristiano's native island of Madeira on Saturday.

No details had emerged about where in Cascais they had wed or who exactly was at the ceremony apart from their children.

Overnight respected Portuguese newspaper Jornal de Noticias published a copy of the marriage certificate showing it took place at Cristiano's massive mansion in the upmarket residential area of Quinta da Marina.

And it also evidenced the fact so few people were invited there appeared to be no place for Cristiano's mum, who gave the union her blessing shortly afterwards by posting a heart emoticon on her son's Instagram in response to his wedding announcement, or the rest of his family apart from his children.

Jose Rodriguez Sangil was described as a Spanish jeweller by Portuguese press.

The marriage document listed Cristiano's full name and age of 41 as well as his birthplace and the names of his parents, including his late father Jose Dinis.

Cristiano's massive built-from-scratch mansion in Quinta da Marina was the venue

The home boats an impressive infinity pool, underground car park and a private cinema room

Ronaldo wore his wedding ring on his finger as he returned to training in Saudi Arabia

The same details were listed for 32-year-old Georgina, born in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires, and referenced by her full name of Georgina Luisa Rodriguez Hernandez. They will both keep their pre-marriage names.

The marriage certificate was recorded as number 1,493 of this year but appears to have been listed at Porto's Registry Office instead of Cascais which is the municipality where the wedding took place.

Cristiano and Georgina are now back in Saudi Arabia where the Portuguese international plays his club football for Al Nassr ahead of the start of the new season tomorrow.

Sports.title: Aryna Sabalenka reveals how tennis 'saved' her from depression following the apparent suicide of her ex-boyfriend
Sports.content:
Aryna Sabalenka reveals how tennis 'saved' her from depression following the apparent suicide of her ex-boyfriend

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Tennis sensation Aryna Sabalenka has opened up on the 'tough' aftermath of the death of her ex-boyfriend.

The world No 1's former partner, former NHL player Konstantin Koltsov, died from apparent suicide aged 42 in March 2024.

Sabalenka, who was no longer in a relationship with the hockey player at the time, was practising nearby ahead of the Miami Open.

Despite the unthinkable tragedy, Sabalenka continued to immerse herself into her on-court grind and competed at the tournament to the dismay of many friends.

While her decision to continue playing was met with reproach on social media, the Belarusian star has now revealed that sport was a coping mechanism for her at the time through her grief.

Sabalenka told Time Magazine that her coach Anton Dubrov had suggested she take some time off from tennis in the wake of the devastation, but she insisted that the sport was her escape.

Aryna Sabalenka has said tennis helped save her from depression after the death of her ex

The tennis sensation appears on the cover of Time Magazine's September edition

Former NHL player and Sabalenka's fellow Belarusian Konstantin Koltsov died in March 2024

'Tennis really saved me from depression,' she told the outlet in an interview for their September cover issue.

'I was just trying to focus on training, just so I spend less time with myself in my thoughts. I would cry in practice a lot. It was a very tough moment in my life.'

Koltsov died after falling from a balcony on the 23rd floor of a Miami five-star hotel in an apparent suicide.

Police officers approached Sabalenka on the courts during a practice session ahead of the Miami tournament to inform her of Koltsov's death.

She previously shared to Vogue that she was 'fighting' with the cops, unable to come to terms with the heartbreaking loss.

Days after Koltsov's death, Sabalenka took down close friend Paula Badosa in the tournament, before exiting against Ukrainian Anhelina Kalinina in the Round of 32.

'I feel like in this situation, there is no right and wrong,' she told Vogue in May, claiming there is no 'cliche' on how to grieve. 'We all need different things. For me, going back to work is the only way. I'm 28, but sometimes I think I've had everything in life that you could imagine.'

Sabalenka has since become engaged to fiance Georgios Frangulis, who popped the question in March this year.

Koltsov died aged 42 after falling from a hotel balcony on the 23rd floor in Miami

The world No 1 is now engaged to Brazilian entrepreneur Georgios Frangulis (pictured)

'He was really supportive and really helpful for the team,' her coach Dubrov told Time of the Brazilian entrepreneur. 'He was always asking us, "What do you think, guys? Should I be at practice? Should I be at the matches?" Sometimes relationships can be not helpful. But he was asking, "What do you think would be the best for her?"'

Sabalenka suffered another personal tragedy in 2019 when she lost her father suddenly to meningitis, at the age of just 43.

Her father was the first to introduce her to the sport after driving her past some empty tennis courts when she was just six years old. Interest piqued and he began to teach her, handing down his own athletic ambition after a car accident when he was 19 shattered his career as a professional hockey star.

Sabalenka was scarcely older when she suffered the shock tragedy in November 2019, forced to digest her bereavement during her sport's offseason.

If you or someone you know needs help, please call or text the confidential 24/7 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the US on 988. There is also an online chat available at 988lifeline.org.

Sports.title: 'I want to be an extension of his legacy': New Salford City boss Peter Cklamovski on making Ange Postecoglou 'proud', leading David Beckham's club-wide reboot - and the League Two promotion race
Sports.content:
To most English football fans, Peter Cklamovski is a name that needs some introduction.

The highly rated Australian coach took over as Salford City boss this summer after building an impressive career across continents and in some hugely demanding environments.

He was a long-term assistant to Ange Postecoglou in Australia, Japan and Greece, before striking out on his own, winning plaudits for his attacking, high-energy football and work with young players at Shimizu S-Pulse, Montedio Yamagata and FC Tokyo in Japan. He also impressed with the Malaysia national team.

Now, at 47, he has arrived in League Two as one of the most intriguing EFL appointments in recent years, and with a clear objective – to get Salford promoted after seven seasons in the division.

‘I’ve loved English football from afar and now I’m in the middle of it,’ Cklamovski tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘I’m honoured and privileged to be here, and it’s been fantastic so far.’

His relationship with Postecoglou naturally attracts plenty of interest. The pair spent 15 years working together, including a spell in the lower divisions in Greece as the former Tottenham boss built his managerial career.

Salford City appointed Australian coach Peter Cklamovski as their new manager this summer

Cklamovski was a long-term assistant to former Tottenham boss Ange Postecoglou

Together, they won the AFC Asian Cup with Australia and took the Socceroos to the 2014 World Cup. Their partnership was credited with helping reshape coaching standards, methodology and tactical identity in Australia and Asia, and only ended when Cklamovski took the managerial job at Shimizu in 2020.

The pair remain in constant contact, with Postecoglou acting as a mentor and ‘sounding board’ while Cklamovski was applying for the Salford job.

‘Fifteen years with Ange… it’s a long time with anybody,’ says Cklamovski. ‘We’ve got a special connection and synergy. I take a lot from him, and I can't speak highly enough of him.

‘Whatever I’ve done in my career over the last eight years, and however long I've got left, I want it to be an extension of his legacy. That's how much he means to me.

'If we're successful, I know that's going to make him very proud sitting in Saudi Arabia, and hopefully he can do the same in 12 months.’

Cklamovski certainly shares some similarities with his former boss, particularly in his mannerisms and the way he communicates. But his route to English football has been distinctly his own.

‘Mate, this is going to get deep, but for a long time I didn’t really have that aim to get to England as a manager,’ he says. ‘Ange had a motivation to get to English football so as a loyal soldier to him, I pushed hard for that.

‘When I went out on my own, my ambition was to be a dominant manager in Asia. But in the last couple of months, the ambition for me personally, the fire and flame of English football just switched. And here I am.

‘The timing of it was natural. Trust the universe. I’ve got a really strong motivation to do something special with a football club that has great people and an inspiring mentality in the playing group.’

Cklamovski gained rave reviews for his work as a manager in Japan and with Malaysia

He has taken over a Salford side desperate to get promoted from League Two this year

How Cklamovski ended up in the English fourth tier, at a club whose ownership group includes David Beckham and Gary Neville and where Paul Scholes serves as the chief football adviser, is an interesting story.

Its origins date back eight years, when he was working alongside Postecoglou at Yokohama F Marinos, part of the City Football Group.

Salford CEO Gavin Fleig spent 17 years with CFG, including seven as director of talent management, and came across Cklamovski during his time in the Far East.

At the end of a family holiday to the UK earlier this summer, the pair met up. Fleig promised to get in touch if he ever needed a manager.

This was no favour to an old colleague, however. Cklamovski – who didn’t speak to Beckham or Neville during the process – emerged as the outstanding candidate after impressing across various data metrics and during the interview process.

‘The aim is to chase promotions and that resonates with me,’ he says. ‘I'm not afraid of that. I have a strong belief we can achieve it with special people and play a brand of football that's going to entertain our fans and bring pride and excitement to the Salford community.’

Scholes had to google Cklamovski as he didn’t know who he was, but was particularly impressed, although Salford’s decision to appoint a manager with no experience of English football is undoubtedly a risk.

That move came after the club sacked Karl Robinson despite only missing out on automatic promotion on the final day of last season, before they lost to Notts County in the play-off final.

The hierarchy admitted the decision to part company with Robinson was a difficult one. But with Salford’s budget understood to have increased this season, the club are determined to finally make the step up to League One.

Cklamovski intends to build on Robinson's work, rather than rip everything up and start again.

‘Whatever sort of team you take over, you can’t stand still,’ he says. ‘We've got the benefit of the work done over the years, especially last year, and we’ve used that as a foundation. But you’ve got to go to another level. We’ll use the heartache from last year as motivation as well.’

Salford missed out on automatic promotion last season before losing in the play-off final

Salford, whose ownership group includes Gary Neville and David Beckham, have reverted to their traditional orange colours ahead of a big season for the club

His arrival at Moor Lane coincides with a significant season of change for Salford.

The club have increased their playing budget, reverted to their traditional orange colours as part of a rebrand in which Beckham played a key role, improved their Man United-owned Littleton Road training ground and overhauled their medical department.

There have also been statement signings, including Millwall striker Macaulay Langstaff, the League Two Golden Boot winner in 2023-24, and Doncaster Rovers winger Luke Molyneux, who was named in the division’s Team of the Season in 2024-25.

‘It’s a sign of the club’s ambition,’ Cklamovski says. ‘But it also shows the commitment to building something special long-term. We’ve made some great signings but there's a super core group here as well, and that's exciting.’

Salford begin their league campaign at Barnet on Saturday after losing on penalties to Shrewsbury in the EFL Cup last week.

It promises to be the first proper acid test of Cklamovski’s reign – and whether his aggressive style can translate into the results and entertainment he has promised supporters.

‘We want to play a brand of football that's going to make every Salford fan and everyone at the club proud and excited,’ he says. 'We want to have a goalscoring mentality, but we'll also have a real strong mentality to roll our sleeves up and keep clean sheets.

‘We've got to stay humble, work hard, and commit to that. Some really good work has started, but there's a lot more work to do.’

Sports.title: Is Enzo Fernandez really good enough to replace Rodri? And is he worth £120million? Enzo Maresca thinks so - and this is why
Sports.content:
So, the deadline is set. Friday 5pm. If Enzo Maresca is so keen on his reunion with Enzo Fernandez, he has until then to make his move. Oh, and it’ll be £120million please. Relations between the two club have been better. Maresca resigned as Chelsea manager in January with his heart set on the City job and his former team couldn’t even bring themselves to refer to him by name when they released a scathing statement in June to confirm they had agreed compensation that meant he could replace Pep Guardiola at the Etihad Stadium. So, what would City get for their £120million if they choose to pay up? Well, what some might call a ‘character’. One who gets himself sent off in a World Cup final, one who tries to get his Chelsea team-mate Marc Cucurella sent off for Argentina in the same game. One who was frequently booked for dissent throughout the season, one who taunted England fans by cupping his ears after his equaliser in the World Cup semi-final, and one, most damningly, who was accused by his own club-mates of racism after live-streaming himself and team-mates chanting after Argentina won the Copa America two years ago. Maresca, though, gets a player he trusts more than any other. And if he is to succeed, he will need players he can trust. It said a lot that despite the racism row in 2024, Maresca still handed Fernandez the captain’s armband for the Premier League season opener against City. Maresca joked recently that Erling Haaland could not possibly be his captain at City because he demands that his skipper race over to him after every goal to receive fresh instructions, unless it was the captain who scored it. Haaland would clearly score too many. At Chelsea, though, even when club captain Reece James was on the pitch, Maresca would often still call Fernandez over once they scored. So, what would Manchester City get for their £120million if they choose to pay up for Enzo Fernandez? Well, what some might call a ‘character’ This is a player who got himself sent off in a World Cup final. One who tried to get his Chelsea team-mate Marc Cucurella sent off for Argentina in the same game

Your browser does not support iframes.

Fernandez was so often Chelsea’s engine room. Last season, albeit one Maresca left halfway through, the club ranked rock bottom for how far their players ran in the Premier League yet Fernandez sat inside the top 10 for distance covered individually. Across Maresca’s 18 months at the club, no one played more league matches for Chelsea than Fernandez and only Mo Salah and Bruno Fernandes created more chances from open play across the division. It looks like Maresca will have to take on the most daunting succession in world football without the most influential midfielder in City’s recent history, Rodri. Barcelona are deep in talks over bringing him back to his homeland. Without the most reliable metronome in world football, Maresca is going to have to find another way to make City’s midfield tick. The club have already paid £116million for Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest but he alone isn’t enough. City are also in talks to sign Morocco’s £85million World Cup star Ayyoub Bouaddi, who is a superb ball-winner and tidy on the ball. Fernandez certainly isn’t a like-for-like replacement. Both are hugely authoritative and dominant but in different ways. Like Rodri, Fernandez is always at the heart of his team’s attacking play but more frequently at the business end of it. In his full season under Maresca in 2024-25, he played a part in 200 attacking moves that ended in a Chelsea shot, either taking it himself, creating the chance, or being a part of the build-up. Nearly 60 per cent of them were him having the shot or setting it up. Among midfielders last season, too, he ranked first for expected goals. By contrast, Rodri’s influence in the previous 2023-24 campaign, the one before he suffered his serious injury, was such that while he topped the list for involvements in his side’s attacking play, only 37 per cent of them were shots or chances he created. Across Maresca’s 18 months at the club, no one played more league matches for Chelsea than Fernandez and only Mo Salah and Bruno Fernandes created more chances from open play In Maresca's only full season at Chelsea, Fernandez was involved in attacking play as much as any player bar Cole Palmer Rodri was also heavily involved in City's offensive work - but earlier on in the build-up That season, Rodri averaged more than twice as many passes as Fernandez in 2024-25 and at a far higher completion rate with more than three times as many splitting opposition defensive lines. The Chelsea man, however, was much more direct when he got the ball, playing a higher percentage of his passes forward than Rodri and more of them into the box. Unsurprisingly, Fernandez commits more fouls. As one colleague who watches Fernandez often put it: ‘Rodri is like the dishwasher, keeps everything nice and clean. Enzo then smashes those dishes.’ One of the biggest differences, and one that Maresca will hope to make the most of, is Fernandez’s superb knack of crashing into the box. Rodri averages less than half a run into the penalty area per game. Fernandez usually makes at least five, and they frequently end up with him scoring. Like another Chelsea star who made the move to City, he’s Lampard-esque in his ability to find the net following his late runs into the box. See these examples below, beginning with a trip to Burnley in November, when he bursts forward late as team-mate Marc Guiu charges into the box. With Burnley’s Josh Cullen (24) distracted by the ball, Fernandez is able to sprint past on his blind side, get to the cutback before him, and strike a first-time shot into the net Against Brighton, Joao Pedro drops deep to collect the ball, drawing defenders. The ball is played out to Reece James on the right and Fernandez gets on to the end of a cross to head it in Against Liverpool at the end of the 2024-25 season, Fernandez calls for the ball from Pedro Neto, who cuts it back, by which time Fernandez is there to collect it, take a touch and score When Rodri was fit and at his peak, Guardiola prefered to use him as a single midfield pivot able to give others like Bernardo Silva the freedom to roam forward, safe in the knowledge that Rodri was there to clean up any mess. When he wasn’t fit, Guardiola would often switch to a two-man midfield. Maresca has done the same in pre-season with Mateo Kovacic and Tijjani Reijnders there against Atletico Madrid in South Korea. The former sitting, the latter primed to burst forward. It will be interesting to see which of those slots, if any, Anderson takes against Arsenal in the Community Shield on Sunday. In terms of style, Fernandez is much more similar to out-of-favour City midfielder Reijnders, who looks set to leave for Saudi side Al Qadsiah. If you compare their heat maps (below), they are both at their most content getting on the ball in the channels. Rodri proved at the World Cup that he still has what it takes to be the best player on the biggest stage, but so much of the tournament was played at a slower pace due to the heat and altitude in the United States, Canada and Mexico. That allowed him to thrive. The Premier League is a less forgiving landscape with monsters more effective these days than metronomes. So, if he is to depart, Maresca seems to have found his way to replace him. It’ll only cost them more than £300million to do it.

Sports.title: 'I'm not a huge fan of Viktor Gyokeres - any Arsenal striker should get minimum 20 goals a season. I didn't sleep in the summer if I hadn't': MICKY QUINN on Coventry, his Highbury hat-trick, assault courses, army training and the Funky Chicken
Sports.content:
Micky Quinn spent the weeks after this season's Premier League fixtures were released impatiently checking his phone and waiting for the Sky Sports booking that never came.

With Coventry City back from a 25-year exile and launching their campaign at Arsenal no less, the defending champions, live on Sky on the opening Friday night, he would have been the perfect studio guest.

Picture Quinn regaling an armchair audience with tales of his hat-trick for the Sky Blues in a 3-0 win at Highbury on the opening day of the 1993-94 season and his expertise in the art of scoring goals with his polished comic timing.

'Can't believe they haven't called,' quips Quinn, only half-joking. 'Their loss.'

His roguish wit will instead be available on Friday at Mr Shenanigans in Coventry for a pre-match Q&A followed by a live screening of the game and a late bar until 3am, which sounds like more fun than a night on Holloway Road with Roy Keane and Gary Neville.

'I'm looking forward to seeing how Coventry go,' he says. 'They play a lovely brand of football, there's a harmony at the club and a great spirit under Frank Lampard. Are they going to be strong enough? I don't know. They can take heart from Leeds and Sunderland staying up last season. Hopefully, they can surprise a few.'

Micky Quinn spent the weeks after this season's Premier League fixtures were released impatiently checking his phone and waiting for the Sky Sports booking that never came

It is 33 years since Quinn scored an opening-weekend hat-trick at Highbury, as Coventry ran out 3-0 winners

That's what Coventry did 33 years ago with Quinn in his pomp. 'Arsenal weren't ready for us,' says the 64-year-old. 'They'd won the FA Cup and League Cup the season before and didn't expect Bobby Gould to go 4-3-3 against the England back five.

'I was up front with two fantastic players, Peter Ndlovu and Roy Wegerle. They were so mobile, dropping deep, going wide. The likes of Tony Adams couldn't handle them.'

Ndlovu won a penalty for the first after being brought down by Lee Dixon, which was converted by Quinn in front of a Clock End closed for renovation. Wegerle set up the other two on the break in the second half.

'Roy backheeled one to me and it was one of the best finishes of my career,' says Quinn. 'I guided it, left foot. Just passed it into the top corner past David Seaman. Ian Wright came up and said it was one of the best finishes he'd ever seen.

'The hat-trick goal wasn't too shabby neither. Bit wider this time and I hit it with enough power. It swerved a little bit. He got his fingers to it but couldn't stop it going in.

'I was told I was the first (visiting player) to score a league hat-trick at Highbury for more than 70 years. I don't know if anybody has done it since because they knocked the ground down.'

Online footage includes Quinn and team-mate John Williams celebrating this momentous occasion with a chicken dance.

'I took the lads on a bonding session,' Quinn explains. 'We were in a '70s disco night in a club outside Coventry and this song called Funky Chicken came on. We were laughing and said whoever scored the first goal at Highbury we'd all do the funky chicken dance.

Arsenal goalkeeper David Seaman is helpless as Quinn fires in his second goal - 'one of the best finishes of my career'

Quinn celebrated with a chicken dance when he completed his hat-trick

'They either forgot because they were too p***ed to remember or they were too embarrassed because when me and John Williams attempted this stupid dance no one else did it.'

Arsenal boss George Graham was not impressed either, although for different reasons.

'Paul Merson always says George had a go at him for going out on Thursday night and not preparing right,' says Quinn. 'Merse's response was, "Well, Quinny was out on Friday night and he scored three goals". I wasn't really. He was just trying to get himself out of the s***e.'

Pre-season wasn't all disco chickens for Gould's Coventry. They had done their fitness training with the army in Aldershot.

'Assault courses, night manoeuvres, everything,' says Quinn. 'Camping out in the woods, pitching tents in the woods in the dark, building campfires. The army lads were skinning rabbits.'

Quinn joined Coventry at the age of 30, a £250,000 snip from Newcastle in November 1992, and started with a spectacular eruption of goals, setting records for a new competition which stood for years until Erling Haaland stormed into Manchester City.

'Bobby Gould was great for me,' says Quinn. 'We got on like a house on fire. He said I reminded him of himself, an aggressive goalscoring centre forward.

'When I signed, he said, "We've got a decent team here but we can't score any f***ing goals. That's why you're here. So don't come back for corners or free-kicks, conserve your energy and get in the box". And I did. I exploded.'

Quinn joined Coventry at the age of 30, a £250,000 snip from Newcastle in November 1992

He scored ten goals in his first six games for the Sky Blues, a record that stood until Erling Haaland arrived at Manchester City

Quinn scored ten goals in his first six games. 'Sergio Aguero and Diego Costa got to nine in six, but then Haaland came along. I'm not one of them who says records are there to be broken.

'They survived nearly 30 years. I remember being in a pub one Saturday when Haaland arrived and he's scored again and the graphics come up showing you the records with all these world-class players and there's me among them.

'There is one he didn't break. I scored in all my first six Premier League games from debut. No one else has done that. Haaland didn't score in his second game against Bournemouth. That's the only one left.'

Manchester City were a very different club back in 1984, when they tried to sign Quinn after his 39 goals in 63 appearances for Stockport, where he won the first of his three Golden Boot awards in the old Division Four.

'Oldham, Man City and Blackpool came in,' he says. 'I spoke to Blackpool who were in the same division as Stockport. City and Oldham were in the second, but the chairman said I couldn't speak to City. The fee was £52,000 and City wanted to pay catalogue style, over two or three years. They were that skint.

'Oldham and Blackpool fronted up the money. I went to Oldham with Joe Royle and he took me under his wing, nurtured me and got rid of the rough edges. Between Joe and Alan Ball at Portsmouth they crafted a striker.

'I just dreamed about goals, like every goalscorer. I didn't sleep in the summer if I hadn't banged in 20 league goals.'

He had a predator's instinct like other strikers of his era and does not see it when he watches Viktor Gyokeres, the former Coventry striker who scored 14 Premier League goals in his first season at Arsenal after moving for £64million from Sporting Lisbon.

'Not a huge fan, to tell you the truth,' says Quinn of Viktor Gyokeres, who scored 40 goals in 97 games for Coventry before joining Sporting Lisbon in 2023

'Workmanlike at Arsenal but doesn't get the goals he should. If you're the centre forward in an Arsenal team you need to be getting 20-plus a season'

'Not a huge fan, to tell you the truth,' says Quinn. 'Workmanlike at Arsenal but doesn't get the goals he should. If you're the centre forward in an Arsenal team you need to be getting 20 a season minimum with the chances they create.

'The one thing they need if they are going to cement their status among the very best and go on and win a Champions League is a goalscorer. If they get Julian Alvarez he is different class and I think they'll win the Premier League again.

'In the main, Gyokeres has been massively disappointing. I hope that doesn't come back to haunt me on the night.'

Quinn's opening goal spree in Coventry colours included two against Liverpool.

'My family are all Liverpool supporters, so I got them five or six tickets and some passes for the players' lounge,' he recalls. 'Their psyche was: "We'll go down and see our Mick, hopefully Liverpool batter Coventry and he has a good game and scores."

'We beat them 5-1 and I got a couple. I went in the players' lounge and found them all with faces longer than Ruud van Nistelrooy. You could've picked their jaws up off the floor. They didn't even say well done!'

Back at his dad's pub on the Cantril Farm estate in Liverpool though, Quinn was the toast of jubilant Evertonians. He didn't buy a drink. Not until he scored twice against Everton later in the same season.

He had 17 by the end of the campaign and when he started the next with a hat-trick at Arsenal, there was talk of an international call-up. England's fading World Cup hopes were resting on an eight-goal winning margin against San Marino, though still requiring a favour from elsewhere.

Bobby Gould motivates his Coventry players during their 5-1 demolition of Liverpool in 1992, in which Quinn scored twice on an electric start to life in the Midlands

'Coventry were never a sexy club compared to some and there was a lot of bias - that's the closest I came to an England cap but I never had a phone call'

'Coventry were never a sexy club compared to some and there was a lot of bias, but for once the Press were pushing me to play against San Marino because England needed to score eight,' he says.

'Some of the strikers were injured and they were all saying: "Play Quinny for a one-off game." Graham Taylor was the manager. He totally ignored it. I knew then it wasn't about talent. That's the closest I came but I never had a phone call or nothing.'

Some things never change.

Sports.title: Amy Hunt clinches European Championships sprint double: Team GB golden girl beats rival Dina Asher-Smith in 200m final
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt completed a brilliant sprint double by landing 200m gold in Birmingham – but warned there will be no celebrating until her target of four is complete.

The 24-year-old is seeking a historic quadruple this week and is now halfway there after blitzing the field in 22.19.

Dina Asher-Smith was the last sprinter to double up at this competition eight years ago but could only manage bronze on this occasion.

The home hopefuls were in adjacent lanes and Asher-Smith got the better start around the bend as she sought a seventh European gold.

But Hunt reeled her compatriot in on the home straight as the domestic duel lived up to expectations in front of an improved crowd of more than 20,000 at the Alexander Stadium.

'The 100 is the hardest mentally and the 200 is the hardest physically,' Hunt told the BBC.

Amy Hunt completed the sprint double by adding 200m gold to her triumph in the 100m

Hunt clinched victory ahead of her rival Dina Asher-Smith, who claimed the bronze medal

'I've had a lot of health things going on this year, some really low blood pressure, and the 200s have been really scary. I have been fainting after some of my 200s this year.

'I just had to go into that one, get on the bend and be really brave. It was an amazing race.'

Asher-Smith has now won nine European medals, putting her one shy of the all-time record, but this was the latest sign of a changing of the guard.

Hunt retained her national 100m title by beating Asher-Smith on this track in June before dethroning her over the same distance on the opening night of these Championships.

Asher-Smith still leads the 200m head-to-head between the two but Hunt has come of age in the last 12 months and now set her sights on completing a remarkable quadruple as she looks ahead to the women's and mixed 4x100m relays over the weekend.

'This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life,' she said.

'There is no celebrating or champagne until Sunday night. I have a debt to the ladies, we have to come out here and show them who the best sprint nation is in Europe. It's not over yet – I hope you're not sick of my face.'

Asher-Smith said: 'Obviously, I'm disappointed to have a bronze, but I think 10 years after my first one it is such an achievement to be in a place to come back year after year.

Hunt signalled that she had won two of her targeted four golds, with her focus now turning to the relays

'It doesn't matter what's going on in my life, I just want to continue to be one of the fastest women in the world. I'm happy to have done that and it is great to be part of a successful British team.'

The hosts' pair finished either side of Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who won silver in a 22.28 national record.

Keely Hodgkinson kept her bid for a European hat-trick on track on a dramatic afternoon which saw her main rival Audrey Werro take a tumble – before being reinstated for the final.

Hodgkinson won the second semi-final in 1:57.38, holding off Femke Broeders-Bol to safely advance to one of the most eagerly-awaited events of the week tonight.

It was a far more serene race than the opening semi, which was dominated by Werro before she hit the deck on the final bend.

Werro picked herself up to stumble over the finish line and a successful appeal means the 22-year-old, who holds this year's world lead, will also be on the start line.

Hodgkinson was relieved to avoid the chaos and said: 'You can't worry about what happened to other people, but I hope she's ok.

'The excitement makes me excited. I love a good challenge and I hope for a clean race with no falling over and no wind.'

Scot Jemma Reekie took advantage of Werro's slip to cross the line first and advance in 1:58.61.

Novuna is the Official Finance Partner of British Athletics and proud sponsor of the GB & NI Athletics Team.

Sports.title: Rangers suffer latest European humiliation after  crashing out of Europa League qualifying with embarrassing defeat by Polish minnows: Pressure already growing on Derek McInnes
Sports.content:
Rangers suffer latest European humiliation after crashing out of Europa League qualifying with embarrassing defeat by Polish minnows: Pressure already growing on Derek McInnes

In the build-up to this Europa League qualifier against Jagiellonia Bialystok, Rangers manager Derek McInnes had spoken of how the club were ‘playing with fire’.

His words were in reference to the lack of bodies in key positions. Down to the bare bones at left-back, it was a hurry-up aimed at the club’s board and recruitment department.

Yet, on a night when McInnes was chasing his first win as manager, the unfancied Poles turned up at Ibrox, doused the place in petrol and lit a match.

Make no mistake, McInnes is in serious danger of being engulfed by the flames even this early in his tenure. The vitriolic reaction from fans at full-time made that abundantly clear.

His team are nothing short of a shambles. He can moan about a lack of cover in certain positions all he wants. The reality is that he is not getting the best out of those players under his command.

The blame for this Europa League exit lies squarely at his door. No one else’s.

Cammy Devlin, Findlay Curtis and Lawrence Shankland react to a bitterly disappointing result

Rangers will now drop down into the Europa Conference League qualifiers, where they will face Jablonec of Czechia.

Given the way the atmosphere turned toxic towards the end, this had echoes of Russell Martin against Club Brugge last season.

At least Martin had the excuse that Brugge were actually a very decent Champions League side. Jagiellonia are second-rate opposition – and Rangers still couldn’t beat them.

At the end, many of the Rangers players slumped to their knees, before awkwardly circling around the pitch to applaud the supporters.

There was no gratitude to be found from those who stayed. Instead, torrents of abuse and boos rained down from a fanbase already at their wits end even this early in the campaign.

A long, long season lies in store on the evidence Rangers have produced over their first four matches, none of which have yielded a win.

Nico Raskin was posted missing again last night and was hooked shortly after the Poles had equalised midway through the second half.

Other players such as Manny Fernandez and Ryan Naderi are miles – absolutely miles – off the required standard to succeed at a club like Rangers.

Nik Prelec heads home the goal that silenced Ibrox and ended Rangers' Europa League hopes

It may still be early in the season but this was a horribly damaging night for McInnes on the back of the home defeat to Hibs last weekend.

The injury to Tuur Rommens, along with the absence of any other competent left-sided defender, forced McInnes into another reshuffle and change of system. He opted for a back three of Fernandez, Dujon Sterling and Olwethu Makhanya, with Djeidi Gassama and Daisuke Yokota deployed as the wing-backs.

The chopping and changing between systems and personnel has been a prominent feature of these early weeks of the McInnes era, albeit this one was forced upon him.

After only coming off the bench for the final five minutes of last week’s first leg in Poland, Lawrence Shankland was restored to the starting XI.

This felt like a big night for the newly appointed captain, both in terms of proving he can cut it at a higher level than the SPFL Premiership and also his ability to lead by example.

Jagiellonia were having a fair amount of joy down the flanks in the early stages. Particularly down their right flank, with Gassama guilty of switching off far too often.

Rangers were fortunate not to fall behind on 14 minutes when a slick move from the Poles cut the home side wide open straight through the middle.

Jesus Imaz latched on to a neat through ball and only had Ivor Pandur to beat, but his shot came back off the post and the ball was eventually scrambled clear.

Rangers players were left to contemplate a season in the Conference League... at best

That was the cue for a section of the Ibrox crowd to erupt in anger, clearly less than enamoured at what they were watching and with Europa League qualification in serious danger of slipping away.

There was no question the stadium was growing tense and nervy even so early in the contest. It was a timely boost, then, when Rangers took the lead on 18 minutes.

Operating from the right wing, Yokota was comfortably Rangers’ brightest player in attack and he was instrumental in the move which eventually led to the award of a penalty.

A handball against former Celtic defender Yuki Kobayashi was spotted by the VAR and the referee was called over to the monitor. Shankland stepped up and calmly clipped the ball straight down the middle as Ibrox breathed a much-needed sigh of relief.

Dan Neil was having a decent game in midfield, with his energy and ability to read the play leading to Rangers winning the ball high up the pitch on a number of occasions.

Neil has been one of nine new summer signings thus far. For all that McInnes may bemoan the lack of options in certain positions, the reality is that he has still been well backed by the board.

With the tie now poised at 2-2 on aggregate, Rangers still had plenty of work to do and Thelo Aasgaard flashed a low shot just wide of the target on 35 minutes as they chased a second goal.

However, at the back, Rangers still looked far from convincing. There was a huge let-off seven minutes before half-time when Jagiellonia forward Nik Prelec skewed a shot wide after a good cross from Rodrigo Conceicao.

Even though his side had the lead on the night, McInnes clearly was not overly impressed with what he had seen in the opening 45 minutes. Aasgaard was hooked at half-time and Ross McCrorie was brought on at left-back as the manager reverted to a back four.

Decked out in their red-and-yellow kit, and backed by a decent travelling support, Jagiellonia sensed this was there for them.

Daichi Yokota was Rangers' most creative player but in truth they were very poor on the night

It had been noted by a pundit on radio that ‘they kind of look like Partick Thistle a little bit’, in reference to the colour of jerseys worn by the Poles. Sadly for Rangers, the same reference could be made about them in terms of their performance levels. Plainly, this was a very tough watch.

Dull, nervy and laboured throughout, it was no surprise when Rangers finally caved and conceded an equaliser on 65 minutes.

Jagiellonia switched the play a couple of times to stretch the home defence, before Andrea Klynge swung over a good cross to the back post. Having fluffed his lines in the first half, Prelec made no mistake on this occasion as he bulleted a header past Pandur and into the net.

With the Poles now leading 3-2 on aggregate, this was utterly desperate from Rangers. No substance, no backbone, no leadership, no quality, no style of play – and absolutely no idea about what they were being asked to do.

On as a substitute, Bojan Miovski glanced a header just wide of the target with only a couple of minutes left to play.

The truth is that Rangers didn’t deserve to go through. They have regressed from last season. A League Cup tie with St Mirren on Sunday is a match McInnes dare not lose.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
