World.title: The job Zelenskyy can’t fill: Ukraine’s envoy to Trump’s Washington
World.content:
Zelenskyy moved his reshuffle plans forward so he could offer the ambassadorship to Yulia Svyrydenko, the outgoing prime minister, according to a former senior Ukrainian official and a Republican foreign expert familiar with the background to the shake-up. But she declined, disrupting his plans.

“It is no secret that I counted on and offered Yulia Svyrydenko the post of ambassador to the United States,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference in late July. He added that he was looking for a candidate with the highest possible qualifications: “a person at the level of a deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister.”

Since then, however, other prospective candidates have proved equally reluctant, spurning what would in any case be the difficult job of handling Donald Trump’s unpredictable White House.

Ukrainians with sufficient heft and skill for the ambassadorship are looking at it askance, “worrying that they would not enjoy the conditions they would need to do the job properly,” said Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a prominent Ukrainian opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister who is a regular critic of Zelenskyy.

“Certainly that would be the case without having the ear of the president or his trust,” she added. That narrows Zelenskyy’s options sharply. The person would likely have to come from his tight inner circle of trusted aides, Klympush-Tsintsadze said, but there is no one there who seriously fits the bill.

“Framing it as if nobody wants the job would be a kind of oversimplification,” said a former Ukrainian diplomat who was granted anonymity in order to speak freely. “Of course, there are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it. Zelenskyy is having a hard time filling the position.”

World.title: EU leaders are on holiday. The crises affecting the bloc aren’t.
World.content:
“Physical presence can signal much more effectively that these emotions are taken seriously and are heard,” she added.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was just hours away from kicking off his weeks-long summer break when 72,000 migrants surged into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on July 30. The Socialist leader duly postponed his plans and traveled to the North African coastal city, where he delivered a televised address pushing back against criticism from other EU leaders.

But as soon as the emergency was deemed to be under control, Sánchez resumed his scheduled vacation at a state-owned villa on the island of Lanzarote.

His decision to take time off, even as the political aftershocks continued to roil the bloc, drew criticism from opposition politicians like Elías Bendodo, deputy secretary of the center-right People’s Party, who this week accused the prime minister of “unprecedented selfishness” for taking time off while the situation in Ceuta is “far from normal.”

“Sánchez insults the Spanish people by remaining on his beach vacation,” he added.

The Spanish government rejected the criticism, noting the prime minister is not only reachable but actively participating in remote meetings, and insisted the state remains fully operational even when its top leaders are away.

World.title: Magyar casts doubt on Hungary-Russia nuclear power deal
World.content:
Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev wrote that the Russian state nuclear company was still on schedule with two new reactors at Paks despite Hungary’s change of government in April, which saw Magyar oust Russia-friendly incumbent Viktor Orbán.

Concrete preparation for Unit 5 is more than 80 percent complete, he said, while work on Unit 6 is advancing and reactor components are already being manufactured.

“We are ready for dialogue,” Likhachev said, adding that Rosatom had received no questions from Hungary’s new government.

Magyar challenged that account hours later. Under the original contract, Paks II should have been operating by 2024, he told reporters in a press conference Thursday. Instead, Hungary has spent roughly 1,000 billion forints (€2.8 billion) on a site he described as little more than depots and “two large concrete pits.”

“I don’t really see that they have adhered to the contract,” Magyar said. His government is now carrying out a full review of the project, including its financing and cooling arrangements.

The review cuts at one of Orbán’s signature deals with Russia. Orbán struck the Paks II agreement in Moscow in 2014, handing Rosatom the two-reactor expansion backed by up to €10 billion in Russian state financing. Two years later, he called it the “deal of the century.”

Those ties survived Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. As recently as March this year, Orbán’s foreign minister Péter Szijjártó admitted to discussing EU sanctions with senior Russian officials after leaked calls showed him boasting that a bank linked to Paks had been kept off a sanctions list.

Downstream, Romania shut the second and last operating reactor at Cernavodă on Thursday after the Danube fell too low to supply its cooling pumps.

World.title: NATO’s plan for a drone-infested battlefield: Let AI fly while humans decide who dies
World.content:
For NATO, AI-assisted drones would be part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative — a digital battlespace network the alliance is building to track threats along its borders with Russia and Belarus, which stretch from northern Finland to the Black Sea.

The new concept includes thousands of drones, sensors and satellites linked with AI to detect potential breaches of allied territory and repel attacks as the first line of defense. Conventional military forces, such as tanks, fighter jets and artillery, will remain the backbone.

U.S. Army Maj. Ben Schiff, a software operations officer, told Bild — which, like Business Insider and POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — that both Ukraine and Russia still rely on humans to control drones.

While some systems have AI or machine-learning capabilities that allow brief moments of autonomy in flight, piloting is primarily performed by operators on the ground. Schiff said that “the most boring parts of flying”— drones loitering above the battlefield looking for targets — should be automated. But when it comes to deciding what the drone should strike, that’s where a human comes into play.

“So the humans are deciding what the drone does, but they don’t necessarily need to take the action of flying it because we don’t have a million pilots. We can’t fly a million drones at the same time,” said Schiff at the U.S. Army Europe and Africa headquarters in Wiesbaden, Germany.

Schiff is a product manager for the EFDI Data Backbone, a developing framework designed to help NATO forces detect, classify, share and act on information at speed and scale. The backbone bridges incompatible computer and command systems across multiple allied nations, allowing real-time data to flow from forward-deployed sensors all the way back to headquarters.

World.title: Unprecedented rainfall in Japan leaves at least four dead in Chiba prefecture
World.content:
Nearly 26,000 households were left without power, while 45 homes were flooded and another 39 reported water entering below floor level. Hundreds of people spent the night in shelters or at Chiba station after rail services were suspended.

 

The disruption was particularly severe around Narita Airport, where about 7,000 travellers were stranded overnight after trains were cancelled, with many sleeping on terminal floors. In rural Chiba, more than a dozen cars were abandoned on flooded roads. A man in his 60s or 70s was found dead in floodwater, while a 66-year-old woman died after becoming trapped in her submerged car, according to the Chiba disaster management office.

The Japan Meteorological Agency warned that the rainfall could be unprecedented. The highest-level warning was downgraded to level four on Friday morning, although the risk of further flooding and landslides remained.

World.title: 18-year-olds spend more and more time online, especially on social media
World.content:
A study by Portugal's Institute for Addictive Behaviours and Dependencies (ICAD) has found that 18-year-olds are spending more time on the internet, especially on social media.

 

The findings are based on a survey of young people taking part in the 2025 National Defence Day.

Most young people (60%) use the internet for an average of four or more hours a day, with intensive use (five hours or more) on the rise compared with previous years.

"In itself, this indicator is not necessarily a sign of problems, but rather of a life lived both physically and virtually, often intertwined, with new ways of behaving, acting and being," the study concludes.

Social networks are the platforms most used by young people, who prefer to access them via their mobile phone. But most of those surveyed, almost 45%, say they spend around two to three hours on platforms such as TikTok, Facebook and Instagram. Thirteen percent of young people said they spend around six or more hours on social media.

Besides social media, online searches - for reading or studying - gaming (including betting) and watching films, videos and tutorials are other reasons contributing to the increase in the time young people spend on the internet.

It was also striking that in 2025, 99% of young respondents said they had started using the internet before the age of 16 and 39% said they started before the age of 10.

This is a particularly important figure, as this proportion has been increasing, showing that the internet is entering people's lives at an ever earlier age. The study stresses that this rise is slightly more marked among young women than among young men.

Young women seem to spend more time on social media or searching online, while young men appear to spend more time gaming.

In the case of online gambling, the level of use among young people also seems striking: 17% of 18-year-olds (30% of young men and 5% of young women) place bets online.

Problems linked to internet use

Excessive internet use is associated with a range of problems, especially among adolescents. ICAD's study therefore set out to find out whether its sample had already experienced any of these, such as poor performance at school or work; health problems requiring medical care; behavioural problems at home; financial difficulties; incidents of violence or disorderly conduct; unprotected sex; and episodes of emotional distress.

Overall, 35% of young people said they had experienced at least one of these seven problems in the 12 months prior to the survey.

The most frequently mentioned problem (20%) was emotional distress (lack of motivation, sadness, dissatisfaction, loneliness, anxiety), followed by poorer performance at school or work (17%).

This study ties in with one of the big issues being debated in EU policymaking on young people's and children's use of social media.

A World Health Organization (WHO) report published at the start of last year identified the dominance of the digital world in young people's lives as one of the main drivers of loneliness worldwide.

Excessive screen time has been linked to lower levels of physical activity and poorer sleep, as well as anxiety, depression, stress and social isolation.

The United Kingdom's plans to ban teenagers from accessing social media have reignited a debate that is playing out across Europe. Countries such as France, Spain, Austria, Greece and Denmark are discussing measures to restrict minors' access, amid concerns ranging from cyberbullying and the addictive design of platforms to tragedies such as suicide and self-harm.

World.title: Pop-Tarts, Tupac and marriage: Marco Rubio opens up in rare podcast appearance
World.content:
As US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio is used to answering questions about wars, diplomacy and national security.

 

But there's been a change of pace... In a wide-ranging interview on The Katie Miller Podcast with his wife Jeanette, the 55-year-old career politician touched on everything from Pop-Tarts and late rapper Tupac Shakur to college football and watching scary movies with his children.

There were other personal details revealed. Rubio is colour-blind, enjoys EDM, has a sweet tooth and, if he could assemble a dream political dinner party, would invite Margaret Thatcher, Ronald Reagan and Winston Churchill.

The conversation offered a glimpse of Rubio beyond his polished political persona, as a husband and father with an eclectic playlist, a weakness for Pop-Tarts, and a wife who was not shy about correcting him.

Three decades of marriage

Rubio and Jeanette, who have been married for more than 30 years and have four children, frequently joked with each other during the interview.

Asked for the secret to a happy marriage, Jeanette began with "faith".

Rubio had another answer.

"Compliance. For the husband," he joked.

At another point, Rubio reflected on what he had learnt about family life as he got older.

"Probably one of the things I learned over time is you try to appreciate the moment that you are in right now because that moment is not going to come back," he said.

"Every stage and every season of life has its things that you should enjoy."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his wife Jeanette sit down with Katie Miller. The Katie Miller Podcast

Jeanette Rubio calls out Marco's Pop-Tart habit

One of the exchanges that attracted attention online came when host Katie Miller asked Rubio whether he supported Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA.

"I'm in favor of MAHA. Like I think people should be healthy," Rubio began before Jeanette interjected.

"No, he's not," she said.

Asked what her husband eats, she replied: "Pop-Tarts. He eats all the things he should not be eating."

"No. I don't eat Pop-Tarts every day," Rubio replied, before adding, "The Pop-Tart is one of the great American innovations in the history of the world. It comes in a beautiful foil package."

Reaction on social media was mixed. Some viewers enjoyed the exchanges as light-hearted marital banter, while others focused on how often Jeanette corrected her husband.

One Instagram user commented “Wow, his wife is totally putting him down and corrects him on every question”, while another posted on X: "Watched the interview of Marco Rubio and his wife and one thing is crystal clear, she hates Marco!"

Later on, Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth came up, although the story had little to do with politics.

Rubio recalled one of his dogs wandering over to Hegseth's home on the military base where they are neighbours, only to encounter the defence secretary's cats.

"I never took Pete for a cat guy," Rubio said.

Pete and Jen Hegseth appeared on Miller's podcast about eight months ago.

What Rubio says about Cuba’s future

The conversation briefly touched on politics, including Cuba, with Rubio saying he believes the country "will be on an irreversible path towards a much different future".

The son of Cuban exiles cautioned that change would take time.

"You can't have something in place for 70 years, it grows roots and then think overnight you're just going to rip out the whole thing and put something new into the ground," Rubio said. "There's a transition that has to happen, a process to get there."

He pointed to the experience of eastern European countries, saying it took several years for their political systems to change.

"Poland is probably the best example," he said.

The interview was conversational in tone, with no challenging questions, and focused largely on Rubio's personal life and views.

It is worth noting that podcast host Miller is married to Stephen Miller, the White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy.

World.title: Battery-only electric cars on the rise in Europe: Which countries lead?
World.content:
The number of newly registered battery-only electric passenger cars has risen rapidly across Europe in recent years. In the EU alone, around 1.9 million new battery-electric cars were registered in 2025.

 

As a result, battery-only electric vehicles are taking an increasingly large share of new car registrations. In 2025, they accounted for 17.3% of all new passenger cars registered in the EU. In several European countries, the share is higher than one in three according to Eurostat.

But the transition is far from even across the continent. Some countries are moving towards electric cars much faster than others.

So, how is the number of battery-only electric passenger cars evolving across Europe? Which countries have the highest shares? And how many battery-electric cars are now on the road in each European country?

Ten years ago, in 2015, only around 47,000 battery-only electric passenger cars were newly registered in the EU. The number passed half a million in 2020 and climbed to almost 1.9 million in 2025 according to Eurostat.

Their share of newly registered passenger cars has risen sharply as well. Battery-only electric cars accounted for just 0.4% of new registrations in 2015 and 1.9% in 2019. By 2025, the share had reached 17.3%.

Among 38 European countries, including EU members, EU candidate countries, EFTA members and the UK, Germany recorded the highest number of newly registered battery-only electric passenger cars in 2025, at around 545,000.

The UK followed closely with about 473,000, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).

France ranked third with around 331,000, followed by Turkey with 187,000.

Norway recorded around 173,000 new battery-only electric passenger cars, while the Netherlands had 156,000 and Belgium 144,000.

Denmark, with 126,000, and Spain, with 105,000, also surpassed the 100,000 mark.

By contrast, Italy, which is one of Europe’s five largest economies, registered only around 95,000 battery-only electric passenger cars in 2025.

Electric cars exceed one in three in several countries

Of course, the share of battery-only electric passenger cars among all newly registered cars provides a more meaningful picture of how quickly each country is making the transition.

Norway is a clear outlier: more than 95% of newly registered passenger cars in 2025 were battery-only electric. Two other Nordic countries followed, with Denmark at 67.8% and Iceland at 41.2%.

Battery-only electric cars also accounted for more than one in three new registrations in Malta (37.6%), Finland (37.2%), Sweden (36.4%) and Belgium (34.1%).

Among Europe’s five largest economies, the UK had the highest share of battery-only electric passenger cars in new registrations in 2025 at 23.4%.

France followed at 19.6%, just ahead of Germany at 19.1%.

Spain and Italy, however, remained significantly below the EU average of 17.3%. Battery-only electric cars accounted for just 8.7% of new passenger car registrations in Spain and 6.1% in Italy.

The share of electric cars remains particularly low in several Eastern European and Balkan countries, as well as in many EU candidate countries. Turkey is a notable exception, with battery-only electric cars accounting for 16.7% of new registrations.

The share is below 2% in Croatia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Electric cars remain a small share of Europe’s car fleet

When it comes to the share of battery-only electric cars in the total passenger car fleet, the picture changes considerably. No country exceeds one in three.

Norway remains the clear leader, with battery-only electric cars making up 32% of all passenger cars in 2025. Denmark follows at 17.9%.

Luxembourg (8.7%), Sweden (8.6%) and the Netherlands (7.2%) complete the top five.

Across the EU as a whole, however, battery-only electric cars account for just 2.9% of the total passenger car fleet.

Among the EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies, Germany has the highest share at 4.1%, closely followed by France at 3.9%.

The share falls to 1.1% in Spain and just 0.9% in Italy.

Overall, battery-only electric cars account for less than 1% of the passenger car fleet in 16 of the 37 European countries.

World.title: Space storms could put airline passengers at radiation risk, scientists warn
World.content:
Extreme space weather could expose airline passengers to high radiation levels and cause significant flight disruption, according to a new study by the University of Surrey.

 

The research, carried out by the Surrey Space Centre (SSC), found that this radiation could also affect onboard systems and flight crews.

Radiation levels can surge considerably at typical flight altitudes of between eight and 14 kilometres, the study found, while also triggering faults in aircraft electronics that could raise flight safety risks.

The study was published in the Journal of Space Weather and Space Climate.

Increasing frequency of high radiation events

Although the atmosphere shields against some radiation, passengers are still considerably more exposed to it on flights than at ground level. This exposure worsens during solar storms or events such as solar flares.

Solar storm events have surged in recent years, causing a corresponding spike in radiation.

In November 2025, a massive solar storm caused radiation to briefly jump to almost 10 times normal high-altitude flight conditions, according to calculations by the SSC.

Aircraft systems are also becoming increasingly vulnerable to these events, as high-energy particles from space can interfere with onboard electronics.

These interactions cause Single Event Upsets (SEUs), minor errors that can accumulate and eventually affect critical systems.

Last year, Airbus temporarily grounded 6,000 of its A320 planes after a vulnerability caused by intense solar radiation was found in a flight control computer.

The issue was discovered after a JetBlue flight from Cancún to Newark was forced to make an emergency landing in Florida in October 2025.

Beyond radiation exposure, such disruptions can also cause widespread operational challenges by increasing pilot workloads — in extreme scenarios, SEUs can surge from a few per hour to thousands.

The most severe risks are on polar flights such as London Heathrow to Vancouver International, where the effects can be felt much further south during severe geomagnetic storms, including over the UK.

"The recent Airbus A320 grounding linked to cosmic radiation shows that space weather is not a theoretical risk, it is already affecting aviation. As aircraft systems become more advanced and increasingly reliant on electronics, understanding and preparing for these events will be critical to maintaining flight safety," said Dr Fan Lei, senior research fellow at the Surrey Space Centre and lead author of the study.

Crucial gap in current aviation safety

The study points to a critical gap in current aviation safety frameworks. Most frameworks today focus mainly on routine radiation exposure and do not adequately account for extreme space weather events.

Better integration of space weather data into flight planning, along with clearer guidance, is essential to keep air travel as safe and reliable as possible.

"At the moment, there is no consistent way for the aviation sector to assess and respond to extreme space weather risks. We've introduced a clearer, aviation-specific radiation scale to help support more informed decision-making in aviation, helping operators act quickly to protect passengers, crew and critical onboard systems," said Professor Keith Ryden, leader of the Space Environment and Protection research team at the Surrey Space Centre and co-author of the study.

The scale is expected to provide clearer thresholds for when action such as increased monitoring, grounding flights or rerouting should be taken during particularly severe or disruptive space weather events.

"An atmospheric radiation scale has been needed for a long time, as current alerts based on low-energy proton events give at least 10 false alerts for every true alert," said Professor Clive Dyer, visiting professor at the Surrey Space Centre and co-author of the study.

"The new scale is based on high-energy proton measurements in space and ground-level neutron monitors, as installed at Surrey, Lerwick and Camborne, and scales human dose and avionics upset rates from the study on the February 1956 event. In combination with our radiation modelling (MAIRE) and monitors (SAIRA) on aircraft, this should provide the basis for a proportionate response," Dyer said.

World.title: Temples to Minoan palaces: Greece is opening 126 ancient sites for free under the August full moon
World.content:
If you’re heading to Greece at the end of August, there’s a nationwide event that should be on your radar.

 

Each year, the country’s Ministry of Culture unlocks over a hundred archaeological sites, monuments and museums after dark to coincide with the full moon and lets visitors in for free.

This year, it will fall on Friday 28 August. From around 7:30 pm until midnight, visitors can enjoy historical treasures from temples to Minoan palaces under the moonlight, several with live concerts, choirs or guided tours built into the programme.

See Greece’s most famous archaeological sites by moonlight

Of the 126 sites, several are some of the top visited attractions in Greece, so seeing them in a different light is extra special.

One not to miss is Delphi, a sanctuary and town on Mount Parnassus where the ancient world travelled to for the Oracle's word on wars, colonies and marriages. On 28 August, there is free entry to the site up to the Temple of Apollo terrace from 7:30/8 pm to midnight.

In the western Peloponnese of Greece, Ancient Olympia, the birthplace of the Olympic Games, will have free entry to both the site and museum, with guided tours by archaeologists, between 8 pm and midnight.

If you’re headed to Sparta, you can visit the medieval ghost town of Mystras, which will be open from 8 pm to midnight with a musical event.

In Athens, the Acropolis Museum remain open continuously from 9.00 am until midnight. Regular admission fees will apply to the permanent collections; ticket desks and shops will remain open until 11.30 pm.

Visitors will also be able to enjoy free admission to the temporary exhibition Inspiration: Ancient Greek Art in Italy, which runs until 30 August.

In Athens, the Acropolis Museum remain open continuously from 9.00 am until midnight. Luna Zhang

The exhibition brings together 38 significant works in ceramic, bronze and marble from museums across Italy, many of which have left their home collections for the first time.

A guided tour of the temporary exhibition, led by a museum archaeologist, will also take place at 6.00 pm on 28 August. Advance online booking through the museum’s reservation platform is required.

Lesser-known ancient treasures to have on your radar

There are also dozens of sites often overlooked in favour of the big hitters, which are well worth your time if you’re in the area, according to Yahya Dawood, founder of Bnbstay, a villa rental company across Greece and Cyprus.

He recommends the Nekromanteion of Acheron, in Epirus, an ancient sanctuary above the Acheron valley, believed by ancient visitors to be an entrance to the underworld where pilgrims consulted the spirits of the dead (free entry, 7.30/8 pm to midnight).

"Everything about this site was built around darkness and ritual, so visiting it after dark under a full moon isn't a gimmicky experience - it's actually one much closer to how it was meant to be experienced than a midday visit ever could be," he says.

One not to miss is Delphi, a sanctuary and town on Mount Parnassus where the ancient world travelled to for the Oracle's word on wars, colonies and marriages. Chad Little

Dodona in northwestern Epirus is considered to be Greece's oldest oracle site – older than Delphi – and was built around a sacred oak believed to speak for Zeus. You can visit for free between 8 pm and midnight.

On the island of Crete, Malia, a Minoan palace complex on the north coast, will open between 7.30/8 pm with a musical event featuring Greek singer Manolis Mitsias and a full choir.

Gortyna, also on Crete, will have free entry and a musical evening. The site is home to the Gortyn Code, the longest surviving ancient Greek inscription – 600 lines of 5th-century BCE civil law carved directly into stone.

Nafpaktos Castle is a Venetian castle overlooking the Gulf of Corinth from above the harbour town of Nafpaktos in Western Greece. "It's the water that will really make this one special, because you'll get the moon reflecting off the gulf as well as lighting the castle itself,” Dawood says.

For opera lovers, Dawood highlights the Sanctuary of Ammon Zeus in the village of Chalkidiki. The coastal sanctuary on the Kassandra peninsula is hosting a full staged opera performance of Orpheus and Eurydice this year.

The full list of sites can be found on the Ministry of Culture’s website.

World.title: US military pushes back on reports of mental health crisis aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln
World.content:
The US military is pushing back on reports of a mental health crisis among crewmembers on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which has been at sea for more than 260 days as it takes part in Washington's operations in the Middle East.

 

In a post on social media, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said there had been "several false claims" and "rampant misreporting" relating to the carrier's deployment and that the crew remained "resilient and resolved."

Concerns have been growing in recent days over the welfare of the crew and the conditions on the ship, the US's fifth Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and one of the largest warships in the world.

US Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, wrote to US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao on Wednesday listing the reported problems and demanding to know what action was being taken.

“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months,” Blumenthal wrote, adding that "recent carrier deployments have repeatedly stretched beyond their originally anticipated durations."

Speaking during a trip to Panama on Thursday, Hegseth said the conditions - many of which had been reported by the military outlets the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes - were "completely misrepresented."

"We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment," he said. "Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody.

CENTCOM has confirmed that one Sailor "fell overboard" on 3 August but said they were "quickly and safely recovered" from the water.

The USS George Washington aircraft carrier is reportedly now set to take over from the Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East.

An F/A-18 fighter jet taxis on the deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier in the Arabian Sea, Monday, June 3, 2019. Copyright 2019 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The US's Nimitz-class aircraft carriers are used to operate fighter aircraft and to help support ground troops overseas. They are also used for maritime security operations against terrorist threats or to protect merchant shipping.

The Abraham Lincoln has been taking part in Operation Epic Fury, US President Donald Trump's military campaign against Iran.

The operation began with a series of strikes in late February and aims to "dismantle the Iranian regime's security apparatus."

World.title: France wildfire forces 525 people to flee as Landes forest burns
World.content:
The fire broke out shortly before 2.30 p.m. on Thursday, 13 August, and was driven by strong, shifting winds, reaching within a few hundred metres of homes in Luglon. By Friday morning, the Landes prefecture said more than 1,100 hectares had burned. No homes had been destroyed, but residents and a nearby campsite were evacuated as a precaution and taken to a reception centre in Sabres. Two departmental roads around Luglon were also closed to traffic.

 

Around 500 firefighters were deployed alongside 40 forest‑fire vehicles, with aircraft including Canadairs, Dash water‑bombers and Air Tractors supporting the operation. Rising humidity overnight slowed the flames, but authorities warned that stronger winds could quickly worsen conditions.

The fire came during a severe heatwave, with temperatures above 40 °C recorded in parts of the Landes. It followed several major fires in south‑western France this summer, including a blaze near Biscarrosse that burned about 3,700 hectares and destroyed around 200 homes and buildings.

Skip next section Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Published 08/14/2026 Published August 14, 2026 Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.

"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.

"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."

Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.

Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."

"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.

The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.

"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."

World.title: Hunger stones: The history behind 'If you see me, weep'
World.content:
Centuries-old hunger stones are emerging as Europe's rivers recede. Among the most famous is the Děčín hunger stone in the Elbe River with its cryptic message.

As Europe's rivers recede during periods of drought, long-hidden traces of the past have resurfaced.

Alongside Nazi-era shipwrecks, unexploded World War II bombs and prehistoric mammoth remains, some rivers reveal history literally written in stone.

One such inscription, in German, reads: "Wenn du mich siehst, dann weine" — "If you see me, weep."

These words are etched on a hunger stone in the Elbe River near Děčín in Czechia, close to the German border.

The 2026 drought has revealed historical artifacts lying under Europe's rivers, like this shipwreck Image: David Jerkovic/Pixsell/IMAGO

Why 'hunger'?

Hunger stones, or "Hungersteine" in German, are riverbed boulders that usually stay underwater and hidden, but become exposed when river levels drop significantly during prolonged droughts.

Unlike a high-water mark, which records the highest water level, the hunger stone marks the lowest.

For centuries, communities carved dates or inscriptions onto these stones whenever the waters of rivers like the Elbe, Danube or Rhine receded dramatically. Some hunger stones bear lists of years, including 1616, 1746 and 1842.

The 2026 drought has seen water levels in the Danube river reach new lows Image: Cristian Cristel/Xinhua/IMAGO

In a 2019 study "Extreme Droughts and Human Responses to Them: The Czech Lands in the Pre-Instrumental Period," Czech historian and climatologist Rudolf Brázdil and his colleagues drew on chronicles, administrative records and other documentary sources to examine how drought affected communities long before systematic weather measurements existed.

For people living along rivers such as the Elbe, low water created a host of problems. Barges carrying timber, grain and other goods struggled to navigate shallow channels, disrupting trade along one of Central Europe's vital transport routes. In severe cases, shipping had to be restricted or halted altogether.

And drought also meant crop failure, rising prices — and hunger.

Hunger stones like this one didn't just commemorate years of drought; they also attempted to mark low water levels Image: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

More than just drought memorials

While hunger stones were often treated as symbolic reminders of drought, they've proven to be more than that.

A 2020 study published in the journal Climate of the Past found that many of the dates and markings on Elbe hunger stones closely matched documented periods of exceptionally low water. The researchers concluded that many of the inscriptions were intended to record how low the river had fallen, rather than merely commemorate drought years.

The study also documented drought year markings on the Děčín stone dating back to at least the 16th century, underscoring that the famous inscription "If you see me, weep" of 1904 represents only one chapter in the hunger stone's much longer history.

Hunger stones, like this one in Těchlovice, often bear years and water level marks Image: Wikipedia

A doomsaying stone?

Yet, its fame lies mainly in its seemingly foreboding message. Even its sighting during the more recent European droughts of 2020 and 2022 inspired media coverage, describing its message as "chilling", "grim" or a "harbinger of hard times."

In his 2019 study "Die Botschaft der Hungersteine" (or "The Message of the Hunger Stones"), Bernd Gross drew on newspaper reports, postcards and local historical records to reconstruct the history of the Děčín hunger stone and noted that its inscription may have been inspired by an older one.

Gross cited newspaper reports from the 1890s that described a hunger stone near Těchlovice, upstream from Děčín, that reportedly bore German inscriptions such as: "We cried — We cry — And you will cry."

The man most often associated with the Děčín stone's inscription is F. Mayer, a local innkeeper and boatman and member of the Elbe shipping community.

According to Gross, Mayer had the now-famous phrase carved onto the stone during the drought of 1904, dated July 18 along with his name.

Historical picture featuring the 'celebrity' Decin hunger stone Image: Wikipedia/Public Domain

A celebrity of its time

At the time, newspapers referred to it as the Bodenbach or Tetschen hunger stone, after the neighboring towns that today form part of Děčín. They reported on the exposed stone and its message, while contemporary accounts described thousands of visitors who went to see it.

Postcards featuring the hunger stone also circulated widely, spreading awareness of the site far beyond the Elbe Valley.

The Reichenberger Zeitung (1860-1938) for instance reported on August 28, 1904: "Day after day, groups gather on the rock; everyone wants to set foot on it at least once. However, the markings carved into the sandstone are likely to lose their visibility due to this frequent trampling."

Visitors were reportedly intrigued not only by the inscription but also the earlier dates carved into the rock, recording drought years stretching back centuries.

The stone that nearly disappeared

Ironically, the drought of 1904 that put the Decin stone and its inscription on the map, very nearly caused its destruction.

Local river authorities decided to remove rocks and other obstacles from the Elbe to improve navigation, and Gross' study states that there were concerns that the Decin hunger stone could be removed as well.

Following the intervention of the Tetschen Boatmen's Cooperative, which petitioned the imperial authorities, the stone was spared. News reports stated that officials agreed to route planned river works around it in order to preserve what was already regarded as a historic landmark of the Elbe.

Many hunger stones lying in the Elbe also bear later dates: this one has 1963 and 2003 on it Image: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

And while other obstacles were removed from the river, the Děčín hunger stone survived.

The stone's story did not end there. When another severe drought exposed it in 1911, Mayer's famous inscription was reportedly carved again, this time more deeply. Later in 1938, a Czech inscription was added alongside the older markings.

Together, these dates and inscriptions chart centuries of the stone's history and its role as a marker of exceptionally low water levels on the Elbe.

Edited by: Oliver Mojen

World.title: UK: Nigel Farage beats a trash can in Clacton by-election
World.content:
Nigel Farage reclaimed his Clacton seat with 63% of the vote, but his main rival, Count Binface, took over a quarter, as Farage skipped the count citing security concerns.

UK right-wing populist leader Nigel Farage won Friday's by-election in Clacton, regaining the parliamentary seat he resigned a month earlier to trigger the vote.

He took about 63% of the vote, while his main challenger, comedian Jon Harvey running as trash-can-costumed "Count Binface," secured roughly 27% — his best result yet in eight election attempts. The turnout was 44%.

What triggered the Clacton by-election?

Reform UK's Farage called the special election to prove his voter support amid a parliamentary investigation into an undeclared £5 million ($6.75 million, €5.85 million) gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Britain's major parties boycotted the race, calling it a self-serving stunt. This left Farage facing 33 mostly independent and novelty candidates.

Farage skipped the official vote count, saying police warned him of an "organized campaign to disrupt" the result. Essex police disputed reports of a credible threat but said a "proportionate and robust" security operation was in place. He also canceled a planned victory speech.

Count Binface's policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using their phone on speaker mode while on public transport Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," he told supporters.

What happens next?

The win doesn't resolve Farage's political troubles. The parliamentary standards investigation, paused when he resigned, is expected to resume and could still force him from his seat. Farage says the money was a personal gift he wasn't required to declare.

Last month, ​a Survation poll put Farage's share of the vote at 73%, a figure he fell short of. It comes as Reform UK's national polling is also slipping behind a resurgent Labour Party under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Who is Count Binface?

Count Binface is the alter ego of Harvey, a British comedian, writer and producer who uses the character to satirize UK politics.

He is a self-styled "intergalactic space warrior" who campaigns wearing a trash bin on his head. While he was expected to receive a large share of the vote, the figure was not expected to exceed 20 percent.

Binface has become somewhat of a serial candidate, challenging prime ministers past and present in line with a long tradition of novelty candidates in UK politics.

The satirical political character has challenged numerous UK prime ministers in past campaigns Image: Toby Melville/REUTERS

With the other parties boycotting the election, he became Farage's default rival with a comical platform vowing to "cut your taxes, and raise everyone else's," build one affordable home and nationalize singer Adele.

"The moral victory is already mine," Harvey, aka Binface, told the AFP news agency at the counting center ahead of the final count.

Skip next section Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

An Air India Airbus A320 that suddenly lost altitude on August 4 recorded losses in all three hydraulic systems, briefly losing crucial flight controls, media reports on Friday cited an initial Airbus analysis as saying.

Air India flight AI2379 from Thailand’s Phuket to New Delhi had dropped 300 feet during cruise over the Indian state of Odisha, before recovering and landing safely in Delhi.

Twenty passengers and four crew members were injured during the incident which was classified as "serious" by Indian aviation authorities.

India’s ​Aircraft Accident Investigation ‌Bureau is probing the incident with technical assistance from Airbus and France's BEA.

What do the Airbus findings say?

Airbus shared the technical evaluation after decoding the flight data recorder in a communication to Air India in response to the Indian flag carrier’s request for an assessment .

The plane’s elevators and ailerons, which control ​its pitch and roll, were unavailable for about four ​seconds, ‌during which the aircraft pitched upward, Reuters cited Airbus as saying in its preliminary findings.

The first officer applied a full nose-down input during the timeframe but ​there was "no direct response" from the flight-control surfaces, Reuters cited the assessment as saying, adding that the hydraulic systems recovered within seconds.

The initial analysis has not established a root cause and Airbus has asked Air India to conduct checks on ​the aircraft’s systems and sensors and to provide more information about the incident.

Airbus has also asked Air India to share the recent maintenance history of hydraulic systems along with more detailed accounts from the pilots.

There was no statement from the planemaker and Air India on the assessment.

Earlier this week, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

On Thursday, an internal communication from Air India showed that the carrier would now conduct a mandatory dope test for all its pilots, expanding checks beyond regulatory requirements.

Under the current rules, airlines in India randomly test at least 10 percent of their flight crew for psychoactive substances each year.

World.title: Can childhood trauma be prevented with a drug?
World.content:
Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.

Trauma is usually treated as something you carry, manage, work through and sometimes ease. Rarely as something that could be stopped before it takes hold. That is what a group of researchers in Munich and Stockholm set out to test .

They began by making the first days of life hard. Mother mice were given far less nesting and bedding material than normal. That was enough to make mothers erratic, and the first days of life unpredictable. The mice raised in that hardship grew up looking perfectly healthy — with no obvious illness or anything visibly wrong.

Then researchers put them in groups and watched what happened. Repeatedly, these mice ended up at the bottom. Pushed into the lowest ranks of their social hierarchies, first as adolescents, then again as adults. A difficult infancy had left no visible mark — but it had set the position they would occupy for the rest of their lives.

When the researchers gave some of them a drug, the pattern disappeared.

The study, published in June, was led jointly by Mathias Schmidt at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and Juan Pablo Lopez at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm .

How does childhood trauma affect the brain and body?

Start with cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. When something stressful happens, cortisol floods the system. This is a standard, protective response.

What matters just as much is the off switch. The body needs to register that the danger has passed and wind the response back down. It does this through cortisol receptors — the parts of cells that detect the hormone and signal the system to stand down.

A protein called FKBP51 controls how sensitive those receptors are. Early hardship, the research suggests, causes the body to produce too much of it. That makes the receptors harder to trigger, so the signal to stand down never fully lands, and the stress response stays switched on far longer than it should.

Schmidt's point is that none of this is something a person can feel.

"Your cortisol response is something you don't feel," he said. "You may think you're very stress resilient, but your body is pumping out cortisol, and you don't know."

Can a drug block the effects of a difficult childhood?

The researchers used a compound called SAFit2, which blocks FKBP51. Given to the mothers during the stressful period, it reached the offspring through breast milk.

The treated mice went on to perform identically, within their social groups, to mice that had experienced no adversity at all — the social cost of a hard start erased.

The effect showed up in the brain as well as in behavior. The team screened gene activity across six stress-related regions and found that early adversity had left a broad imprint across them. The drug largely reversed it, most clearly in two: the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens, regions involved in emotional control and reward.

Can childhood trauma be reversed?

Not on this evidence.

In the Munich study, the compound was given during the stressful period itself, not after. What the study demonstrates is prevention, not repair.

Other studies have shown behavioral effects when the drug is used in adult animals, but full reversal of trauma already in place remains unproven. And prevention only works if you can identify who's at risk before the harm is done — a problem this research doesn't address.

Would this drug actually work on humans?

It's too early to say.

The study tested male mice only, so it is not yet known whether the same holds in females. And SAFit2 remains a research compound 3 effective in animals but not yet developed or safety-tested for human use. Still, Schmidt sees a realistic path toward clinical application within the next decade, noting that stress mechanisms are "very, very similar in animals and humans."

War scars and genes: Can the impacts of trauma be inherited? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is trauma treated now, and why doesn't it always work?

Existing treatments for stress-related disorders, including PTSD and trauma-linked depression, rely heavily on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These drugs target serotonin pathways. They work for many patients, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and a significant portion of patients don't respond at all.

By contrast, targeting FKBP51 would mean treating the pathology at its source. "We would actually not only be treating the symptoms, but also the cause of the disorder by acting directly [on] a stress mechanism," said Schmidt. "These types of drugs are currently not on the market."

Longer-term, Schmidt envisions a more targeted approach: identifying individuals who are genetically vulnerable to stress, whose FKBP51 expression is already elevated, and treating that group specifically after acute traumatic events.

On the other end of the spectrum are people who, through genetics or prior experience, prove remarkably resilient even under extreme conditions, and may not need medication at all. Understanding who does need it, Schmidt said, and reaching them in time, is where the research is heading next.

What are the signs of unresolved trauma?

Schmidt is careful that trauma is highly individual, psychologically and physiologically. The rough guide he offers is duration, not intensity.

A strong stress reaction immediately after a car crash or a violent event is considered normal — the body doing its job. What concerns clinicians is when the response persists well beyond that: still unable to cross a street a month later, still unable to sleep six weeks on. Those are his illustrative examples rather than diagnostic thresholds, but the principle holds. If a stress response isn't fading, it's advisable to speak to a doctor.

That remains practical guidance for now. The drug, if it ever exists, is at least a decade away — and on current evidence, it would need to come before the damage, not after.

Editor: Kaukab Shairani

World.title: Four dead, thousands stranded as record rain lashes Japan
World.content:
Unprecedented rainfall in Japan's Chiba prefecture has stranded thousands of passengers at Tokyo's Narita airport and prompted authorities to issue the highest-level rain warning for the first time.

At least four people have died in eastern Japan as heavy rain flooded roads, cut power and left thousands of travelers stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport, authorities said Friday.

More than 36 centimeters (14 inches) of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of Chiba prefecture, which borders Tokyo, triggering landslide warnings and power outages for nearly 25,000 households.

Japan facing 'unprecedented' rain during busy holiday week

The downpour struck during one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks, prompting the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) to issue its highest-level heavy rain warning for the region for the first time.

A JMA official on Thursday said this was "shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain."

"This case was an extremely unusual situation, even ​by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters early Friday. "I have responded to many disasters in the past, but ⁠I ​have never experienced a case like this."

Several roads in the Chiba Prefecture were inundated Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

The Chiba Prefecture Disaster Management Office said those confirmed deaths included a man in his 60s or 70s found on a flooded road and a 66-year-old woman found in her submerged car.

A third victim was a man of unknown age found collapsed in the street, and a fourth was a person whose age and gender have not been determined, AFP reported. A fifth person is feared dead and a sixth remains unaccounted for. Soldiers have been deployed to help with relief efforts.

Thousands stranded at Narita airport

More than 6,000 people were stranded overnight at Narita, one of Tokyo's two major international airports. Many train services to and from the airport were also canceled into Friday afternoon.

"I never thought I'd spend the night at the airport but it is what it is and we are learning," a traveler told Japanese public broadcaster NHK. "We're never going to forget this trip."

Hundreds more were stranded at Chiba station after train services were suspended. Several people spent the night in shelters. NHK footage also showed cars submerged up to their headlights in Kashiwa city.

Hundreds were stranded at the Chiba Metro Station as weather authorities issued their highest-level heavy rain warning for the region Image: Philip Fong/AFP

Major highways in Chiba, including routes connecting Narita to central Tokyo, remained closed Friday, according to highway operator NEXCO East, forcing drivers onto alternate routes. Some train services connecting Narita to Tokyo had resumed early Friday.

An airport spokesperson said all flights were scheduled to operate normally, and Japan Airlines said some delays were possible, but no cancellations were expected.

The level-5 heavy rain warnings issued Thursday were downgraded to level 4 by Friday morning.

Scientists warn that human-driven climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and intense.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Romania shuts nuclear plant, Hungary dams dry Danube River
World.content:
Romania has shut down its only nuclear plant in a rare move prompted by the lack of cooling water from the Danube River. Hungary, meanwhile, is racing to dam the Danube, trying to keep its Paks plant online.

Romania shut down its lone nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare move amid the drought that has caused record lows on the Danube River and other major waterways in Europe.

The Danube is the sole source of cooling water for the Cernavoda plant, which usually generates around one-fifth of Romania's electricity.

The power station has only been shut down once before, in 2023, again as a result of drought and a hot summer.

Meanwhile, Hungary was scrambling to dam the Danube, as it tries to keep its Paks nuclear power plant at least running at the minimal levels that it has maintained in recent days, which are far below capacity.

Attempts to divert more water to Cernavoda earlier this month didn't prevent a shutdown Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance

What did the operator and authorities in Romania say about the shutdown?

Romania's Nuclearelectrica company had already shut one of the two reactors at Cernavoda last month.

On Thursday, it said it needed to shut the second "because of the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the Danube River."

The company tried earlier this month, with help from the Navy, to improve the plant's chances of staying operational.

Most memorably, it blew up a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels and strategically deposited the rocks on the riverbed in a bid to direct more water to Cernavoda.

But ultimately, continued dry weather and sinking water levels prompted the total shutdown.

"We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," the plant director, Romeo Urjan, told the AFP news agency.

Romania's Energy Ministry said it was procuring alternative power sources, including from wind power but also from energy imports, to try to ensure adequate supplies. Still it appealed to the public to consume responsibly.

It warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. Carmakers Ford and Dacia had already committed to pausing production until August 19 to save power.

Earlier in August, the Romanian Navy detonated submerged rocks as part of a bid to funnel more water to the power plant Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

What is Hungary doing to try to prevent a similar shutdown of the Paks plant?

Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Thursday visited Hungary's only nuclear power plant, the Paks facility that is also cooled by the Danube.

"We have begun construction of the low weir that will permanently contribute to raising the Danube's water level," Magyar told reporters at the site, roughly 100 kilometers (about 60 miles) south of Budapest.

Only one of Paks' four reactors is currently operational amid the drought.

Nine days ago, the plant was at risk of a complete shutdown, but the government was able to abort those plans at the last moment as the Danube's levels ended up being a few millimeters higher than forecast.

The unusually low river levels near the Paks plant are hard to miss at present Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance

Under normal circumstances, the plant is responsible for around half of Hungary's electricity generation, and about one-third of its consumption.

Before the completion of the weir, authorities plan to deliberately sink two 80-meter-long barges — placed end-to-end and perpendicular to the river's flow — to create an initial damming effect and raise the water level somewhat.

Magyar said that Hungarian soldiers were working round the clock on the construction, and that it should be completed in the next four weeks. He said the project should elevate water levels in front of the Paks plant cooling system by more than a meter.

The project might not be finished long before the summer starts to fade and the rains return, but the low water levels also provide a rare opportunity to undertake such construction projects relatively cheaply and easily.

World.title: Kennedy Center board approves Trump name on facade, renovation plan
World.content:
The move appears designed to circumvent a judge's ruling that the US president's name should be removed, potentially setting the stage for a new legal fight over the Kennedy Center's name and future.

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to add President Donald Trump's name to the building's facade, according to US Congresswoman Joyce Beatty.

The board also voted to proceed with a two-year closure of the performing arts venue in the US capital, Washington, D.C., for major renovations.

The decision comes after a federal judge in May ordered Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling that only Congress can change the institution's name or authorize major alterations.

"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty, a Democrat who is also an ex-officio board member, said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."

The latest vote revives a dispute that has been unfolding since Trump reshaped the center's leadership after returning to office.

Why was Trump's name on the building in the first place?

Trump became interested in the Kennedy Center's operations after winning the 2024 election. He installed a mostly handpicked board that named him chairman, and his name was added to the building's facade in December.

The move was part of a broader effort to overhaul the institution. At the time, the president also announced a two-year closure of the performing arts venue for renovations that were scheduled to begin in July.

That decision soon faced a legal challenge. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper said, "the Kennedy Center's organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so."

The Kennedy Center dispute became one of several obstacles to Trump's broader efforts to remake prominent Washington landmarks. An appeals court last week halted his planned White House ballroom after he demolished the East Wing.

His Reflecting Pool renovation also faced major problems, though he still plans to build a massive Memorial Arch.

How has the Kennedy Center board justified the move?

"In its meeting today, the board voted to change the front of the building's facade to read 'The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,' and renamed the physical site 'the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,'" Congresswoman Beatty said.

According to The New York Times, an inscription underneath the institution's name would read: "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

The newspaper said the wording appears intended to avoid a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that states "no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas."

World.title: El Gobierno amplía la vida de la central nuclear de Almaraz hasta 2030 por la “volatilidad de precios” originada en Oriente Próximo
World.content:
El principio del fin de la energía nuclear en España se gana una prórroga de dos años y medio mientras las guerras en Oriente Próximo y Ucrania se enquistan y no dejan de alborotar los precios energéticos mundiales. El Gobierno ha autorizado la ampliación de la vida útil de la central de Almaraz (en Cáceres), tal y como había recomendado el Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear hace un mes y habían solicitado desde el otoño pasado sus propietarias: Iberdrola, Endesa y Naturgy. Según se publica en el Boletín Oficial del Estado de este viernes, el Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico concede la renovación de la autorización de explotación de la Central Nuclear Almaraz, Unidades I y II, y prorroga “la vigencia de la autorización de explotación de ambas Unidades hasta el 8 de junio de 2030, teniendo en cuenta que la central nuclear cuenta con una Revisión Periódica de Seguridad (RPS) vigente hasta dicha fecha”. El apagado previsto debía comenzar en noviembre de 2027 y no se cambia el resto de apagados previstos hasta 2035. Desde el Gobierno se subraya que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se pretende defender al sistema energético y a los consumidores de la volatilidad de los precios internacionales.

El Ministerio justifica la decisión por el nuevo contexto energético internacional y la volatilidad del precio del gas derivada de la crisis en Oriente Próximo, según el texto de la orden. “La crisis en Oriente Medio ha supuesto una disrupción en el contexto energético global, incrementando y añadiendo volatilidad de forma significativa a los precios de los combustibles fósiles, entre ellos el gas natural. Según indican organismos internacionales, el contexto geopolítico y los daños en infraestructura de producción y exportación de combustibles extienden el riesgo y la incertidumbre a los próximos años”, indica el texto publicado en el BOE.

Según los cálculos incluidos en la resolución, mantener Almaraz hasta 2030 tendrá un efecto “acotado y poco significativo” sobre el despliegue renovable y contribuiría a reducir la dependencia del gas. El Ministerio no quiere que la decisión se entienda como un paso atrás y y deja clara cuál es su estrategia en la misma orden de prórroga de Almaraz: “La política energética aprobada y en ejecución en España, alineada con la normativa y objetivos europeos, tiene como base la apuesta por la generación renovable como forma más competitiva de producir electricidad, aprovechando asimismo las ventajas competitivas del país en términos de recurso, tecnología y capacidades. Esta apuesta ha permitido mejorar la posición de España en cuanto a costes energéticos en el contexto europeo, proteger a los consumidores ante subidas de precio, y generar un contexto inédito de atracción de proyectos industriales y de electrificación”.

Fuentes del Ministerio subrayan las “circunstancias extraordinarias derivadas del conflicto en Oriente Medio y de la continuidad de la guerra en Ucrania”. “Hay una situación energética internacional excepcional y sobrevenida que está generando un escenario de elevada volatilidad y precios altos de los combustibles fósiles, cuya duración es actualmente imposible de prever”, se subraya como punto de partida. Y como remate, se incide en que “la volatilidad y la incertidumbre son significativamente mayores a las anticipadas hace tan solo unos meses”. El cierre efectivo del estrecho de Ormuz provocado por la guerra de Irán ha hecho que se dispare el precio del gas en Europa.

Por lo tanto, se actúa en consecuencia: “En el contexto actual, la prórroga, coyuntural, puede contribuir a moderar la exposición de los consumidores a unos picos de precios de los combustibles fósiles no previstos anteriormente. Ello permite seguir protegiendo a la población ante la volatilidad de los precios y la incertidumbre en este periodo, mientras se sigue ampliando la respuesta estructural frente a la dependencia de los precios de combustibles fósiles: el despliegue de renovables”, explica el Gobierno.

La orden también señala que la continuidad de Almaraz aporta estabilidad al sistema eléctrico, según el operador del sistema, aunque la prórroga no “cambia la necesidad de continuar con las actuaciones ya encurso dirigidas a fortalecer la seguridad y estabilidad del suministro”.

Una extensión “acotada”

El Ministerio también subraya que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se otorga tras comprobar el cumplimiento de las tres condiciones que siempre exigió para concederla: que fuera segura para las personas (como avala el CSN en su informe preceptivo anterior), que no comprometiera la seguridad de suministro y que no suponga ningún coste para los ciudadanos. Es decir, no hay “ningún tipo de rebaja fiscal ni contraprestación económica para las empresas eléctricas”.

“La extensión solicitada del periodo de explotación para las Unidades I y II de la Central Nuclear Almaraz se limita en torno a 31 y 19 meses respectivamente, lo cual representa una proporción reducida de la vida media prevista del parque nuclear español, no alterándose el resto del calendario ni la fecha de cese definitivo del conjunto del parque nuclear a 2035. De acuerdo con los análisis realizados, dicha extensión tiene un impacto muy limitado sobre los objetivos de política energética del país”, explica la orden del departamento dirigido por Sara Aagesen.

El protocolo firmado en 2018 entre las propietarias del parque nuclear español y la Empresa Nacional de Residuos Radiactivos (Enresa), sociedad dependiente del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, contemplaba el cierre ordenado del parque hasta 2035, empezando en ese año 2027 que ahora se traslada a 2030 para el recinto extremeño. Las dos unidades de Almaraz eran las primeras en echar el cierre y, pese a contar desde 2020 con el visto bueno del CSN para funcionar durante 10 años (los permisos del organismo de seguridad se dan por una década), el calendario fijaba el cierre de las plantas cacereñas en siete y ocho años, respectivamente. Esto es, ya tenían permiso para funcionar 10 años, por lo que era de esperar que el CSN no se pronunciase en contra.

Finalmente, y tras muchos meses de debate soterrado, presión social en la comarca implicada, declaraciones públicas para testar la posición de la otra parte y negociaciones sobre el alcance de la posible medida, las eléctricas decidieron pedir la ampliación de la vida de ambas unidades de Almaraz hasta 2030, por mucho que su primera intención apuntaba a una extensión de diez años. Iberdrola, con una participación del 53% y Endesa con un 36%, eran partidarias de esta mayor ampliación, si bien, Naturgy, con un 11%, se opuso, y ganó la partida toda vez que, al estar constituidas las nucleares como comunidades de bienes, las decisiones deben adoptarse por unanimidad.

Además, Endesa e Iberdrola habían venido batallando para lograr un recorte de los impuestos que gravan a estas plantas, esencialmente, el del combustible nuclear gastado, que el Gobierno de Mariano Rajoy aprobó en 2013 para hacer frente a la deuda del sistema eléctrico. Pero, a medida que se acercaba el plazo límite para solicitar la prórroga al CSN (un año antes del cierre previsto), las compañías renunciaron a los recortes fiscales que venían reclamando y que el ministerio, y el Gobierno en su conjunto en no pocas declaraciones, siempre consideró “una línea roja”. Con todo, mantienen recurrido en los tribunales la tasa de gestión de residuos de Enresa.

La decisión del Ministerio pone fin al trámite y evita que el cierre escalonado de los dos reactores se active para sus fechas previstas: el 1 de noviembre de 2027 para la Unidad I y el 31 de octubre de 2028 para la Unidad II.

En cualquier caso, y según recoge la orden ministerial de este viernes, la prórroga de funcionamiento estará subordinada al cumplimiento estricto de las condiciones e instrucciones de seguridad dictadas por el CSN. El Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear emitió ya el pasado 16 de julio un informe favorable a la renovación solicitada, condicionado al cumplimiento de los límites y exigencias de seguridad nuclear y protección radiológica recogidos ahora en la orden. El aval técnico del organismo regulador certificó y acreditó que la instalación nuclear cacereña reúne las condiciones de seguridad necesarias para operar de manera segura durante dicho periodo de prórroga. Tras este pronunciamiento del CSN, el expediente fue remitido al Gobierno, abriendo un plazo para que el Ejecutivo tomara una decisión definitiva sobre su continuidad.

World.title: ¿Tienes un perro o un gato? Estas son las ventajas de usar un bebedero automático
World.content:
Está hecho de acero inoxidable 304, que es más higiénico que el plástico, y cuenta con un sistema de filtración para mantener el agua limpia y fresca todo el día

Cuando se trata de nuestras mascotas, cualquier cosa que mejore su día a día merece la pena. Y es que su bienestar y comodidad son una prioridad, de ahí que se preste tanta atención a la elección de la cama donde van a descansar, los juguetes con los que van a entretenerse o el transportín que van a utilizar.

La hidratación es otro de los aspectos clave, sobre todo en verano. Si bien un bol estático cumple su cometido a la hora de saciar su sed, un bebedero automático, como este que hemos encontrado desde EL PAÍS Escaparate en Amazon, ofrece una serie de ventajas que pueden hacer que la balanza se incline a su favor. ¿Por qué puede ser una opción más completa para nuestros amigos de cuatro patas? ¡Te lo contamos!

Tiene una capacidad de 2,2 litros y una ventana para controlar el nivel de agua. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Agua limpia durante todo el día

Esto es lo primero que agradecerá tu mascota. Pero ¿cómo lo consigue? A diferencia de un bebedero tradicional, este está equipado con un sistema de filtración avanzado que combina una capa fina de algodón, resina de intercambio iónico, carbón activo y esponja. Puede parecer mucho para un producto de estas características, pero cada una de estas capas está al servicio de un mismo objetivo: eliminar impurezas, pelos y partículas para que el agua esté más limpia. Además, al estar el líquido siempre en movimiento, no se estanca. Esto ayuda a evitar la acumulación de bacterias, ya que el agua se está renovando constantemente.

Tu mascota beberá más agua

Si alguna vez has visto que, al abrir el grifo de la cocina o del baño, tu gato o tu perro se ha quedado ensimismado, es una reacción completamente normal. Porque si hay algo que les atrae bastante, es el agua en movimiento. Esto es lo que estimula que beban más agua a lo largo del día, algo muy beneficioso para su salud renal.

Este bebedero tiene un diseño compacto que permite ubicarlo en cualquier rincón de casa y una capacidad de 2,2 litros. Así, basta con colocarlo en una zona accesible para tu mascota y enchufarlo a la toma de corriente para que esté en funcionamiento las 24 horas del día. “Yo compré este justamente porque mi gato estaba enfermo de los riñones. Necesitaba su agua, necesitaba incentivar que bebiera y que no hubiese ninguna impureza aunque beba varias veces. La fuente cumple todo eso”, dice una de las más de 17.000 valoraciones en Amazon.

El agua se mantiene en movimiento todo el día, lo que estimula que beban más. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Con luz LED para ubicarlo fácilmente por las noches

Frente al bol de siempre, este modelo cuenta con una ventana que permite controlar el nivel de agua. Esto que parece muy simple resulta muy práctico a diario para saber cuándo hay que rellenar el recipiente. Teniendo en cuenta su capacidad, el agua puede durar entre cinco y siete días, aunque esto varía según la cantidad que beban al día. “También es más cómoda para mí, que les cambiaba el agua dos o tres veces al día. Ahora la voy rellenando cuando veo que baja el nivel, cada dos días o así, ¡y siempre fresca!”, comenta una compradora.

Asimismo, incorpora una luz LED en la bomba de agua, otro aspecto muy útil, ya que consigue que tu mascota localice el bebedero con facilidad, especialmente por las noches. Si te preocupa que pueda ser molesto, puedes estar tranquilo: la iluminación que ofrece es suave y el sonido del agua al circular es agradable.

Elaborado con un material de calidad

Este bebedero no está hecho de plástico, sino de acero inoxidable de grado 304. La elección de este material se nota rápidamente en la durabilidad del producto, pero, lo más importante, en su higiene: no altera el sabor del agua y facilita su limpieza. “El acero me da mucha más confianza que el plástico”, añade otro usuario, que asegura que este fue uno de los motivos por los que decidió adquirirlo.

Sin embargo, hay algo que conviene tener en cuenta. Al igual que los cuencos estáticos, este bebedero requiere un mantenimiento básico. En este caso, además de lavar el recipiente y el depósito, hay que limpiar la bomba de agua y cambiar los filtros cada dos o cuatro semanas. Así, te asegurarás de que la calidad del agua que bebe tu mascota sea buena.

Es fácil de montar y requiere de unos cuidados básicos, pero esenciales. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Preguntas frecuentes sobre este bebedero automático

¿Qué nivel de ruido emite?

30 decibelios.

¿Cuáles son sus dimensiones?

11,5 x 19,5 x 19,5 centímetros.

¿Funciona con batería?

No, este artículo debe ir enchufado. Por eso, incorpora un cable de alimentación y un adaptador.

¿La luz LED se puede apagar?

No, permanece encendida mientras esté el bebedero en funcionamiento.

[Recuerda que si eres usuario de Amazon Prime, todas las compras tienen gastos de envío gratuitos. Amazon ofrece un período de prueba gratuito y sin compromiso durante 30 días.]
