World.title: UAE Coal Deal Highlights Why Foreign Investors Are Betting on Kazakh Coal Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – A United Arab Emirates company has secured a 25-year license to develop the Kenderlyk coal deposit in eastern Kazakhstan, expanding foreign investment in the country’s mining sector.

According to documents released ahead of public hearings in early August, MQ Emirates Group Ltd will develop Coal-Shale Field No. 1 of the Kenderlyk deposit using open-pit mining methods.

Coal production is scheduled to begin in 2028, following geological exploration and preparatory work planned for 2026 and 2027. Initial output is projected at 10,000 metric tons, increasing to the mine’s planned annual capacity of 50,000 metric tons by 2034. Recoverable reserves are estimated at 940,000 metric tons.

The Kenderlyk deposit is located around 70 kilometers from the town of Zaisan in the East Kazakhstan Region. It has been known since the late 19th century, when coal and oil shale were extracted through small surface mines. During the Soviet era, the area underwent extensive geological exploration for coal, shale, and hydrocarbons.

Several years ago, the Kazakh Industry Ministry offered parts of the Kenderlyk deposit for auction. According to the National Geological Service, the broader deposit contains 11.3 million metric tons of coal reserves across three coal-bearing formations. Coal at Field No. 1 has a relatively high ash content of 35% to 40%.

Coal remains key to energy security

Although many countries are accelerating the shift toward renewable energy, coal remains one of the world’s primary sources of electricity. It generates roughly one-third of global power. Demand continues to be driven largely by China and India. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan ranks 10th globally in proven coal reserves, with an estimated 33.6 billion metric tons, enough to sustain current production levels for more than three centuries.

The country’s largest coal-producing regions include the Karagandy and Turgai coal basins in central Kazakhstan and the Ekibastuz, Maikuben and Karazhyra deposits in the northeast. Kazakhstan exports coal primarily to Russia, Poland, Uzbekistan, Türkiye, India and Malaysia.

To support future growth, the Energy Ministry plans to auction 10 additional coal exploration blocks by the end of the year. The government has also approved the Coal Power Development national project, which includes investment projects with a combined installed capacity of around 7.8 gigawatts.

Investment in the sector continues to rise. Mining companies invested 305 billion tenge (US$654 million) in 2025, while investment is projected to increase to 553 billion tenge (US$1.2 billion) this year.

Kazakhstan is also expanding investment in its broader mining sector. The government plans to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits, among the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten reserves, into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation.

Highly concentrated market

While Kazakhstan is expanding coal production, a new report from the Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition (APDC) found that the country’s primary wholesale coal market remains highly concentrated.

The agency’s review of the 2024-25 market concluded that the sector continues to be dominated by a small number of producers operating in an essentially unchanged oligopolistic market. For coal supplied to households and municipal utilities, the ERG Group and Karazhyra company controlled a combined market share of 74.8% in 2024 and 67.9% in 2025.

In the power generation segment, Bogatyr Komir and Kazakhmys Coal accounted for 84.1% of the market in 2024 and 81.6% in 2025. For industrial coal, the ERG Group held a market share of 62.3% in 2024, increasing to 69.1% in 2025. The agency said Kazakhstan’s oligopolistic market structure has contributed to sustained price increases.

According to APDC, wholesale prices for coal supplied to households increased 30% to 35% between 2022 and 2025, while thermal coal prices rose approximately 45% over the same period.

To improve competition, the agency proposed introducing price regulation for household and thermal coal, increasing the share of coal sold through commodity exchanges to 52%, and moving off-exchange transactions to digital trading platforms.

The report also identified several structural barriers to competition, including differences in mining contract terms and limited transparency in granting exclusive coal export rights. It further highlighted concerns over the allocation of rail capacity by the national railway operator, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy.

APDC recommended establishing transparent criteria for coal export permits, ensuring equal treatment for producers and improving disclosure of available railway capacity.

The agency also identified companies that qualify as holders of key capacity in the coal market, including Shubarkol Komir, Karazhyra, Bogatyr Komir, Kazakhmys Coal and the Eurasian Energy Corporation. Once these companies are formally recognized as holders of key capacity, they will be required to sell coal under Kazakhstan’s Rules on Equal Access to Key Capacity, which are intended to promote fair competition and equal market access.

World.title: Tokayev’s G20 Invitation Reflects Broader U.S.-Kazakhstan Strategic Momentum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan confirmed that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit in the United States (US) in December, following a meeting on Aug. 12 between Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur to discuss expanding bilateral cooperation.

Although Kazakhstan is not a member of the G20, it is among the countries invited by the US to participate in this year’s summit.

The two officials discussed preparations for the summit. They expressed readiness to coordinate on its agenda, while reviewing broader prospects for strengthening the expanded strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and the US.

Kosherbayev briefed Kapur on Kazakhstan’s ongoing political and socioeconomic reforms, describing the country as entering a new stage of development. He said the Aug. 23 Kurultai elections will represent an important milestone in implementing the country’s new constitutional model.

Kapur reaffirmed its interest in expanding practical cooperation in energy, critical minerals, advanced technologies, digitalization, transportation and investment.

Growing strategic importance

According to Assylan Smagulov, Master of Political Science and director of the Voice of Youth Public Foundation, the timing of the meeting reflects Washington’s continued strategic interest in Central Asia.

“August is traditionally a period of diplomatic coordination before a busy fall schedule of international summits. When the US holds high-level meetings with the Central Asian countries during this period, it signals that the region remains an important strategic partner. That creates additional opportunities for attracting investment and advancing national interests,” Smagulov told The Astana Times.

Smagulov noted that Kapur’s participation was particularly significant because of his expertise on South and Central Asia.

“The US sent a senior official who specializes in this region and understands both its challenges and opportunities. That demonstrates Washington views Kazakhstan as an important partner,” he said.

He added that the country’s growing geopolitical importance stems from its strategic location, transportation links and abundant natural resources, including critical minerals. These factors have become increasingly important as prolonged geopolitical tensions reshape global supply chains.

“Participation in international platforms such as the G20 creates a window of opportunities for Kazakhstan to strengthen dialogue not only with the US but also with other major powers. The broader Kazakhstan’s international engagement becomes, the greater its diplomatic flexibility and its opportunities to expand economic cooperation,” Smagulov said.

Water cooperation moves from policy to practice

Water security has also become a growing pillar of U.S.-Kazakhstan cooperation. The officials reviewed Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization as a specialized United Nations agency. The initiative aims to create a platform for coordinating international efforts on water governance, facilitating data and technology exchange and developing joint solutions to global water challenges.

The proposal entered formal international consultations during the Regional Ecological Summit held in Astana in April. A summary report from those consultations is expected to guide further negotiations among UN member states ahead of the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi later this year.

On Aug. 10, representatives of Kazakhstan’s National Hydrogeological Service (Kazgidrogeology), U.S.-based IBL Elements, and Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector met in Astana to discuss technologies for treating and reusing industrial and produced water generated during oil and gas production.

The talks focused on wastewater treatment, water reuse and the recovery of valuable and critical minerals contained in produced water. Following the meeting, Kazgidrogeology, IBL Elements and Kazakhoil Aktobe signed a trilateral memorandum of cooperation establishing a framework for pilot projects in the country’s oil and gas industry.

Rather than viewing produced water solely as industrial waste, the initiative aims to assess its potential as both a water resource and a source of strategically important minerals.

“This meeting marks an important practical step in developing cooperation between the Kazakh and American sides. The signed memorandum creates the foundation for implementing a joint pilot project and scaling successful technologies to other oil and gas facilities across Kazakhstan,” said Bolat Bekniyaz, chairman of the board of Kazgidrogeology.

Expanding economic and technology partnership

Economic ties between the two countries continue to grow. Bilateral trade exceeded $1 billion during the first half of the year, an increase of about 10% compared with the same period last year. Cumulative U.S. investment in Kazakhstan has surpassed $60 billion.

Several high-level engagements this summer underscored the growing partnership.

In June, Astana hosted the C5+1 Critical Minerals Dialogue, where senior officials from the five Central Asian countries and the United States discussed cooperation on critical mineral supply chains, investment and technology. At the event, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor described Central Asia as an increasingly important component of U.S. foreign and economic policy.

Later that month, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative and the AI Opportunity Partnership, expanding cooperation in AI, advanced technologies and high-tech manufacturing. During the Pax Silica Summit, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev signed the declaration on Kazakhstan’s accession to the initiative.

On June 30, government officials and business leaders from both countries also reaffirmed their commitment to expanding trade, investment and technological cooperation during the Kazakhstan-U.S. Business Roundtable. During the event, the two countries’ business associations signed a memorandum aimed at strengthening long-term institutional cooperation.

World.title: Two Giant Tungsten Deposits Could Test Kazakhstan’s Push Beyond Raw-Material Exports
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to turn two of the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten deposits into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation, requiring ore to be processed domestically rather than exported as raw material as Astana seeks to capture more value from its critical mineral reserves.

The Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits are being developed by a venture between U.S.-based Cove Capital, which holds a 70% stake, and Kazakhstan’s state mining company Tau-Ken Samruk, with 30%. Cove Capital is expected to provide at least $1.1 billion in financing as well as processing technology and access to international markets.

The agreement was signed in November 2025 during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Washington D.C. The partners formalized the investment in February, signing a package of transaction documents, including a sale and purchase agreement and a shareholders’ agreement, for the critical minerals project.

The mines are located in the Shet district of the Karagandy Region, close to transport and transport and energy communications. Karagandy, the region’s administrative center, is around 130 kilometers from the deposits.

“The Northern Katpar project involves establishing a full production cycle in Kazakhstan, from ore mining and beneficiation to metallurgical processing, based on the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits. This is the first project of its kind to be implemented in Kazakhstan,” Tau-Ken Samruk told The Astana Times.

Its planned output includes ammonium paratungstate, or APT, a key processed product in the tungsten supply chain. The agreement envisages processing all extracted ore domestically and producing higher-value tungsten products in Kazakhstan.

The timeline

The project is currently in the Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) phase, meaning its final production capacity, economics and launch date have yet to be determined.

“This work will confirm and optimize the existing feasibility studies, and refine the project’s economic and technical indicators, as well as its mineral resources and reserves. As part of the project’s implementation, preparatory and technical work is scheduled to begin on-site, including topographic surveying, the construction of temporary access roads and fencing, the preparation of drilling sites, the opening of a field office, and other related activities,” said Tau-Ken.

The definitive feasibility study, which began in July, is expected to be completed before the end of 2027, Cove Kaz Capital told The Astana Times.

“The principal objective of this stage is to finalize the overall mine plan, define the parameters of the processing facilities and prepare the project for a Final Investment Decision, as well as for detailed due diligence by prospective financing partners,” the company’s CEO Dominic Heaton told The Astana Times.

The company said physical activity has commenced at the site in July, including surveying, access road and drill pad preparation, and establishment of field facilities.

Untapped potential

The two deposits are considered among the world’s biggest undeveloped tungsten deposits. Together, the deposits contain an estimated 410,000 metric tons of tungsten trioxide reserves under JORC standards, while total resources are estimated at 1.4 million tons, according to previous studies cited by Tau-Ken.

Cove Capital said a key distinction is between mineral resources and mineral reserves.

“The current figure represents JORC-compliant [JORC refers to an internationally recognized reporting standard used to classify and publicly report mineral exploration results, mineral resources and ore reserves] mineral resources, while the ongoing DFS [Definitive Feasibility Study] will further update the geological and technical data and optimize the development plan for the deposits,” said Heaton.

“Based on existing studies, Northern Katpar has the potential to support production of approximately 5,000 metric tons per annum, while Upper Kairakty has the potential to contribute approximately 7,000 metric tons per annum. Combined production of approximately 12,000 tons per year would be equivalent to roughly 15% of current global tungsten mine production,” Heaton explained. The company is also developing the Akbulak rare earth project in the Kostanai Region with Qazgeology national geological exploration company.

The financing

Under the agreement, the U.S. partner is expected to provide at least $1.1 billion in financing, introduce modern processing and beneficiation technologies, build a complex of production facilities and develop international sales channels for the output.

“The approximately $1.1 billion figure represents the current estimate of the total investment required to develop Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty, including the associated mining and processing infrastructure. It does not mean that the full amount has already been financed, committed or deployed,” said Heaton.

At this stage, Cove Kaz Capital Group has financed the acquisition of its 70% controlling stake in Northern Katpar, along with site preparation, drilling and work related to the definitive feasibility study.

“An important component of the prospective financing structure is the interest expressed by U.S. government-backed financial institutions. The Export-Import Bank of the United States has issued a Letter of Interest for financing of up to $900 million, while the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation has issued a Letter of Interest for up to $700 million, including project financing and development support,” Heaton explained.

Potential financing could reach $1.6 billion, but the figure remains indicative rather than committed, Heaton added. The amounts represent expressions of interest from prospective lenders, with the final financing package still contingent on completion of the definitive feasibility study, lender due diligence and a final investment decision.

Why it matters

What this project illustrates is that Kazakhstan is betting on higher-value domestic processing rather than remaining primarily a supplier of raw tungsten ore or concentrate. Cove Capital said it seeks to create an integrated domestic value chain in Kazakhstan, spanning mining, beneficiation and downstream chemical processing.

“The principal benchmark product currently planned for the Kazakhstan refinery is ammonium paratungstate, or APT, a high-purity intermediate product that is the internationally recognized benchmark product of the tungsten industry. The project may also have the potential to produce other tungsten compounds depending on the final technical configuration,” Heaton explained.

Deeper processing would allow Kazakhstan to retain more of the value generated from its tungsten resources rather than exporting mainly ore or concentrate.

“APT is subsequently used to produce tungsten oxides and powders, tungsten carbide, hard metals and other specialized materials used across advanced manufacturing, high-technology and defense-related industries,” said Heaton.

Global tungsten dynamics

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, tungsten is a strategically important metal used primarily in tungsten carbide for mining, construction and metalworking, as well as in electronics, aerospace, high-performance alloys and defense applications. Its combination of hardness, heat resistance and high density makes it difficult to substitute in many industrial uses.

Tungsten is relatively scarce in the Earth’s crust, ranking 57th among chemical elements by abundance. Its wide industrial use stems from a combination of distinctive properties. No other known metal matches tungsten in heat resistance, and its boiling point is close to the temperature at the Sun’s surface.

China has remained the world’s leading producer, importer and consumer of tungsten concentrates.

The project is advancing at a time when tungsten is taking an increasingly greater geopolitical importance as the U.S. and other economies seek to diversify critical mineral supply chains away from China. Beijing tightened controls on exports of selected tungsten products and related technologies in February 2025, adding pressure to already concentrated global supply chains.

The restrictions, alongside growing demand and trade tensions, helped push tungsten prices sharply higher in 2025. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, throughout 2025, prices went up from $266 to $551 per metric ton unit for 65% concentrate and from $331 to $675 per metric ton unit for APT.

“At the same time, the strategic importance of secure and diversified critical mineral supply chains is growing rapidly. The United States, the G7 and other advanced economies are actively seeking to reduce reliance on highly concentrated sources of supply and support the development of alternative supply chains. Tungsten is one of the critical minerals receiving particular attention in this context,” said Heaton.

Kazakhstan is emerging as a potential alternative supplier. Production began at the Boguty tungsten deposit in the Almaty Region in 2024, operated by Aral Kegen, a subsidiary of China’s Jiaxin International Resources Investment.

The project with Cove Capital is also emerging as part of a broader build-out of Kazakhstan’s tungsten industry, with additional deposits moving toward development. The country’s total tungsten trioxide reserves are estimated at more than two million metric tons. Esil-Mining, owned by Britain’s Resources Enterprise Limited, plans to begin developing the Aksoran deposit in northern Kazakhstan in 2027, with production targeted for 2028.

The planned development of Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty would take the country further downstream by combining extraction with domestic processing rather than exporting raw material.

“More broadly, our strategy is to build a portfolio of critical mineral assets in Kazakhstan and Central Asia supported by domestic processing and refining capacity,” said Heaton.

He emphasized this ambition is supported by the country’s substantial mineral resource base, a mature mining sector, extensive geological data and established industrial infrastructure.

“Just as importantly, Kazakhstan is increasingly focused on moving beyond the extraction and export of raw materials toward higher-value processing and manufacturing,” he added.

The project illustrates Kazakhstan’s broader effort to extract more economic value from its mineral wealth by pairing foreign capital with domestic processing. But major questions, including production capacity, final economics and the start of commercial output, remain unresolved while the venture completes its definitive feasibility study.

World.title: Investment Outlook for Kazakhstan Equities: Strategic Allocation to Eurasia’s Hidden Blue-Chip Market
World.content:
In life and on the investment journey, it is often said that it is the journey that counts, or it is the “journey” that is the reward.

Kazakhstan became the first country of the former Soviet Union to receive an international investment credit rating in September 2002.

According to Bloomberg data, tenge is the sixth best performing currency in the world so far this year, and the Kazakhstan equity market has outperformed global equities.

Next year, the IMF expects Kazakhstan’s economy to expand by 4.4% in 2027, while forecasting global GDP growth of 3.4%. This implies the nation would grow approximately 1.0 percentage point faster than the world economy, continuing to outperform the global average. Global investors should take notice.

Yet Kazakhstan remains one of the most attractive yet under-owned equity markets in the emerging and frontier investment universe. Despite its abundant natural resources, improving corporate governance and strategic location between Europe and China, it continues to receive only a modest allocation in most global strategic asset allocation portfolios. For long-term private clients and family offices willing to diversify beyond traditional developed and emerging markets, Kazakhstan deserves serious consideration.

While oil made Kazakhstan rich, today’s investment story extends well beyond oil. Kazakhstan is the global leader in uranium production, a significant producer of copper, zinc and ferroalloys, and is investing heavily in logistics, manufacturing and financial services. Government reforms are aimed at diversifying the economy, encouraging foreign investment and strengthening domestic capital markets.

Valuation remains one of the market’s greatest attractions. Leading local companies have often traded at attractive earnings multiples while generating robust cash flows and paying generous dividends. For value-oriented investors, this combination of reasonable valuations and strong profitability provides an attractive long-term entry point.

The financial sector is one of the strongest investment opportunities. Halyk Bank, Kaspi.kz and Bank CenterCredit have demonstrated strong profitability, healthy capital ratios and growing digital capabilities. Kaspi.kz has built one of the world’s most successful digital financial ecosystems, while Halyk Bank continues to combine market leadership with attractive shareholder returns.

The nation also occupies a unique position in the global energy transition. As the world’s largest uranium producer, the country is strategically positioned to benefit from growing investment in nuclear energy driven by electrification, artificial intelligence and expanding data-centre demand. At the same time, the Middle Corridor linking China and Europe continues to enhance the country’s role as a logistics and transport hub.

For international investors, tenge remains influenced by commodity prices, particularly oil, together with global risk sentiment and developments in neighbouring Russia. However, substantial foreign-exchange reserves and the National Fund of Kazakhstan provide an important cushion against external shocks.

Risks include commodity-price volatility, geopolitical uncertainty, lower market liquidity and evolving governance standards. Nevertheless, these risks are balanced by attractive long-term growth prospects and improving institutional quality.

For global investors and family offices, Kazakhstan remains one of the faster-growing upper-middle-income emerging markets. However, GDP growth alone is not sufficient for investment success. Investors should also assess:

Corporate earnings growth. Valuation of listed companies, Dividend yields, Corporate governance standards, Currency outlook for tenge (KZT), Liquidity on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange.

Given expected GDP growth of around 4–4.5%, Kazakhstan should continue to grow faster than the global economy, supporting a constructive long-term investment case—particularly in banking, energy, uranium, infrastructure, and selected consumer sectors.

Kazakhstan should not be viewed as a replacement for developed-market equities or large emerging markets. Instead, it can serve as a strategic satellite allocation providing exposure to return drivers that are often poorly represented in conventional global benchmarks.

For patient investors, this is precisely where the opportunity may lie. Markets that are under-researched, under-owned and occasionally misunderstood can offer attractive long-term opportunities when economic fundamentals and corporate performance continue to improve.

We therefore maintain a BUY recommendation on Kazakhstan equities as a strategic long-term allocation for globally diversified investment portfolios. Attractive valuations, world-class resource companies, strong financial institutions and ongoing economic reforms provide a compelling investment case for patient money and smart money investors and private clients alike.

The author is Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner & Portfolio Strategist at Das Family Office in Singapore.

World.title: Kazakhstan Powers Central Asia’s Economy, But Can Its Weight Drive Regional Growth?
World.content:
ALMATY – Central Asia’s combined economy has surpassed half a trillion US dollars, reaching an estimated $543 billion, with Kazakhstan accounting for more than half of the region’s gross domestic product, according to figures compiled by The Times of Central Asia.

Kazakhstan’s economy is estimated at $306 billion, representing nearly 56% of the combined GDP of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan. The figures highlight Kazakhstan’s continuing economic weight in a region where economic growth, trade links and international investment are increasingly reshaping Central Asia’s position.

Uzbekistan has the region’s second-largest economy at $147 billion, followed by Turkmenistan at $50 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic at $23 billion and Tajikistan at $18 billion. Kazakhstan’s position becomes even more pronounced when GDP is considered alongside trade and investment.

Kazakhstan accounts for two-thirds of regional exports

The five Central Asian countries generated a combined $139 billion in exports, of which Kazakhstan accounted for $92 billion, or 66%. Uzbekistan contributed $32 billion, representing 23% of regional exports. Turkmenistan accounted for $7 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic for $6 billion and Tajikistan for approximately $1.6 billion. The overview uses 2024 data for Kazakhstan and Tajikistan.

The figures point to a regional economic structure in which Kazakhstan remains the principal link between Central Asia and international commodity and trade markets. Its large energy and mineral sectors, as well as developed transport and industrial infrastructure, give it a substantially larger export capacity than its neighbors.

However, the concentration of exports also raises a broader question about the region’s future development. As Central Asian economies become more integrated through transport corridors and growing intra-regional trade, Kazakhstan’s economic scale gives it a major advantage, but also makes its diversification increasingly important for the region as a whole.

Nearly 70% of accumulated foreign investment is in Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan also dominates the region in terms of accumulated foreign direct investment. The combined stock of foreign direct investment across Central Asia is estimated at $220.5 billion, with $151.3 billion, or 68.6%, concentrated in Kazakhstan.

Turkmenistan follows with $44.6 billion, while Uzbekistan has accumulated $16.7 billion. The Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan each account for approximately $4 billion. This gap is significant because FDI is not simply a measure of capital inflows. Over time, accumulated investment can shape industrial capacity, infrastructure, technology transfer and a country’s ability to develop new sectors.

Kazakhstan’s share suggests that international investors continue to view the country as the region’s largest and most established investment market. At the same time, the figures illustrate how unevenly foreign capital remains distributed across Central Asia.

Economic weight exceeds Kazakhstan’s demographic share

Kazakhstan’s dominance is particularly notable given its population. Of Central Asia’s estimated 83.6 million people, Kazakhstan accounts for around 21 million, or nearly 25%. Uzbekistan, by comparison, has around 37 million people, representing 44% of the region’s population. This means Kazakhstan produces more than half of Central Asia’s GDP with roughly one-quarter of its population.

The comparison points to Kazakhstan’s considerably higher economic output per capita and reflects differences in economic structure, natural resources, industrial development and the scale of accumulated investment. Uzbekistan’s larger population and rapidly expanding economy, meanwhile, suggest that the balance of economic weight within Central Asia could gradually become more competitive in the coming years. For now, however, Kazakhstan’s economic lead remains substantial.

A stronger financial position

Kazakhstan also stands out through several financial indicators. Its reserves are estimated at $129.3 billion, while its state and state-guaranteed external debt stands at $34 billion. Reserves therefore exceed this debt by nearly 3.8 times, the highest ratio among regional countries for which comparable data were available.

Government debt amounts to 24.6% of GDP, while remittances from abroad represent just 0.1% of GDP and dependence on foreign aid is estimated at 0.03% of gross national income.

These indicators suggest that Kazakhstan’s regional influence is supported not only by the size of its economy, but also by relatively strong financial buffers and lower dependence on external income sources such as remittances or foreign assistance.

Central Asia’s economic center of gravity

Taken together, the figures reveal a clear pattern, as Kazakhstan accounts for nearly 56% of Central Asia’s GDP, 66% of its exports and nearly 69% of its accumulated foreign direct investment, despite representing only one-quarter of the region’s population.

That concentration makes Kazakhstan the region’s principal economic center of gravity. Its performance has implications beyond its own borders, particularly as Central Asian countries seek to develop new transport routes, energy links and industrial supply chains connecting the region with China, Europe and the Middle East.

But the data also point to a changing regional context. Uzbekistan’s $147 billion economy and large population make it an increasingly important second pole of growth, while other countries are seeking to attract investment and strengthen their roles in regional trade networks.

World.title: One Sea, Five Countries, Two Futures: Caspian Sea’s Next Test
World.content:
ALMATY – Caspian Sea Day is being marked on Aug. 12, the 20th anniversary of the entry into force of the Tehran Convention, the main regional agreement on protecting the Caspian Sea’s marine environment, as environmental concerns over declining water levels and the future of the world’s largest enclosed body of water continue to grow.

The anniversary coincided with the conclusion of the international Caspian Sea Action Week 2026, which brought together delegations from Azerbaijan, Iran, Russia and Turkmenistan, as well as representatives from Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan, alongside volunteers, environmental activists, scientists and young people in Aktau.

Held under Taza Kazakhstan environmental culture development concept, the week combined scientific discussions, environmental campaigns, volunteer initiatives and innovation projects aimed at drawing attention to the shared challenges facing the Caspian.

From regional agreement to environmental action

The Framework Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea, known as the Tehran Convention, entered into force in 2006. It created a regional framework for the five Caspian littoral states to cooperate on pollution prevention and the protection of the sea’s ecosystem. Two decades later, the nature of the challenge has become more complex.

Environmental cooperation initially focused heavily on managing pollution and protecting marine biodiversity. Today, the long-term decline in the Caspian’s water level has added another dimension to the region’s environmental agenda.

Laura Malikova, chair of the Association of Practicing Environmentalists, recently warned about rapid shallowing in the northern Caspian. She linked some of the concerns to dredging operations conducted by the North Caspian Operating Company and its contractors to support navigation and cargo deliveries.

“Photos and videos clearly show how far the water has retreated. The northern Caspian is becoming shallow at an extremely rapid pace,” Malikova said, as quoted by Kazinform.

According to Kazakhstan’s Ecology Ministry, climate change remains the principal driver of the long-term water-level decline. Precipitation in the Caspian region is decreasing while evaporation is increasing, making the region particularly vulnerable to rising temperatures.

The combination of climate pressures and human activity creates a more complicated policy challenge. As water levels decline, coastal infrastructure, shipping routes, ports and industrial projects may need to adapt, while efforts to maintain economic activity can themselves place additional pressure on an already changing ecosystem.

Science becomes central to the response

This growing complexity explains the emphasis on scientific cooperation during Caspian Sea Action Week. An international seminar and roundtable on Aug. 6-7 brought together scientists and experts from Caspian countries to discuss environmental monitoring technologies and ongoing research. The focus reflects an important question for regional environmental policy: whether countries have sufficiently coordinated data and scientific capacity to understand changes occurring across the entire Caspian basin.

The Caspian is one interconnected ecosystem, but environmental information, monitoring systems and policy responses are largely organized at the national level. More effective cooperation could therefore depend not only on exchanging research results but also on developing compatible monitoring systems and a clearer shared understanding of environmental risks.

The One Caspian – One Future session held during the week reflected this idea by bringing together volunteer communities from different countries to discuss common approaches to protecting the sea.

From environmental awareness to practical solutions

The week also demonstrated an effort to connect high-level environmental discussions with public participation. The Caspian Clean Challenge, held in Aktau on Aug. 8 with the participation of Kazakh Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Mansur Oshurbayev, brought volunteers together for a large-scale coastal cleanup and waste-sorting campaign. More than 80 trees were planted at the newly opened Friendship Alley of Caspian Region Volunteers, while participants also placed a time capsule with messages for future generations.

A cleanup campaign was also held on Aug. 9 in the Bozzhyra area of the Mangystau Region. The international hackathon also invited participants to develop projects aimed at protecting the Caspian ecosystem, while an open TED-style discussion brought environmental volunteers and experts together to exchange ideas. The event concluded on Aug. 12 with the Caspian Talks international volunteer summit, where participants discussed current environmental challenges and exchanged experiences.

A shared sea, facing two possible futures

The central difficulty of protecting the Caspian is that environmental consequences do not stop at national borders. Changes affecting one part of the sea can eventually influence fisheries, biodiversity, coastal communities, ports and economic infrastructure across the region.

Between 2006 and 2025, the shoreline in some areas retreated by 30 to 35 kilometers, according to officials. The average water level across Kazakhstan’s sector of the Caspian stood at –29.35 meters relative to the Baltic height system in 2025.

The longer-term outlook presents two possible scenarios. A forecast prepared by Kazhydromet outlines an optimistic scenario under which the sea level could fall to –32.4 meters by 2050. Under a more pessimistic climate scenario, it could decline as far as –34 meters.

Neither scenario points to a return to previous conditions. Instead, the difference between them represents two levels of adaptation that Caspian countries may have to prepare for. A decline toward –32.4 meters would require substantial adjustments to coastal infrastructure and economic activity. A fall toward –34 meters could bring far more profound changes, pushing the shoreline farther from existing ports and coastal settlements and transforming parts of the former seabed into land.

This changes the nature of the policy challenge. The Caspian countries are no longer dealing only with the task of protecting an existing ecosystem from pollution and overuse. They may increasingly have to manage the economic and environmental consequences of a sea whose physical geography is changing.

Twenty years after the Tehran Convention entered into force, this may be the next major test of Caspian cooperation. The region now faces two broad futures, neither of which assumes the sea will remain unchanged. The critical question is whether Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan can use scientific monitoring and shared data to anticipate the consequences of either scenario before environmental change turns into an economic and infrastructure crisis.

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU annual report: ‘serious problems’ in Azerbaijan and ‘serious restrictions’ on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.
