World.title: Quick hits: Tempers flare as Aussies wilt, Starc's heart-in-mouth moment
World.content:
Mitchell Starc vents his frustration at a Bangladeshi batter, while a star is born on treacherous Darwin turf.

Here are the quick hits from another torrid day for Australia against Bangladesh.

1. Smith grounds one

DARWIN, AUSTRALIA - AUGUST 14: Steve Smith of Australia looks on after an attempted catch during day two of the First Test Match in the series between Australia and Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Darwin, Australia. (Photo by Robert Cianflone/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There is toiling, and then there is whatever the Australian bowlers were doing during the first session of day two.

The much-vaunted Aussie quartet, with Cam Green and Beau Webster in support, combined for just a single wicket during the opening two hours of play.

The ball found its way past Bangladeshi willow on a few occasions, but for the most part, chances were at a premium.

So, it was far from an ideal time for the usually so-reliable hands of slipper-supreme Steve Smith to let him down.

But with rookie opener Tanzid Hasan already past 50 and Australia having just taken their first wicket of the day, Smith floored one.

Tanzid edged a Nathan Lyon delivery into the elbow of Alex Carey, the ball ricocheted towards slip, and a diving Smith was unable to gather cleanly.

It was far from a sitter, but one Smith will be disappointed to have missed.

Tanzid given a life on 62.

2. Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test ton

Coming into this series, there were serious questions surrounding Bangladesh's opening pair, with the Tigers having struggled to nail down a reliable top two in recent years.

Up steps Tanzid Hasan, the 25-year-old opener playing just his second Test match.

Tanzid was considered and composed against the much-vaunted Australian attack, providing the foundation for a brilliant Bangladeshi team effort.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

He already had an ODI century to his name, having scored 107 against Pakistan in Mirpur in March, and he also has scored five first class tons for an average of 39.60.

Talk about nervous 90s, though.

First, Pat Cummins whacked the 25-year-old on the arm with a vicious, 140km/h bouncer.

Then, Tanzid almost holed out to the substitute fielder at long off when on 96, skying a Lyon slower ball with a lofted drive that plugged in the outfield after falling just short of the fielder.

He moved to 99 with a neat clip, and then celebrated his century with a push down the ground off Lyon, a superb hundred celebrated accordingly.

3. The Darwin turf bites at the Australians

Starc got tangled in the turf while taking a catch. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, Tanzid was unable to turn his maiden Test ton into a truly big one, holing out to Lyon only a matter of balls later.

But Australian hearts were in Australian mouths as Mitchell Starc slid to make the catch and then flipped over ungainfully.

Starc, wincing as he got up, looked to be in some discomfort, and the replays showed that the Darwin turf may have been to blame.

The fast-bowler's knee had been caught in the grass, with a cloud of dust and thatch of grass disengaging from the ground.

Starc was tangled up awkwardly by the Darwin turf. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Thankfully, Starc appeared to recover well, but it wasn't the first time the Marrara Stadium outfield had appeared a little loose, with the ever-energetic Marnus Labuscagne ripping out his fair share of greenery.

With the surface only likely to disintegrate more dramatically over the coming three days, both teams should be wary of not getting twisted up in the outfield.

4. Steve Smith's hat-trick of slip catches

Australia desperately needed something to happen to interrupt the Bangladesh momentum — and it arrived with the new ball.

Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and then Pat Cummins all extracted edges with the new pill, claiming the wickets of Hossain Shanto (84), Litton Das (0) and Mushfiqur Rahim (36) as Bangladesh crumbled from 3-297 to 6-308.

And all three of them were caught by Steve Smith at second slip, making dramatic amends for his earlier fumble.

That trio of catches put Smith level with Joe Root with 218 catches, the most ever by a non-wicketkeeper in Test cricket.

Australia's pacemen are worth their weight in gold, but Smith certainly pays his way in the field to help them out.

5. 'Get off the wicket!'

Tempers flared late on it Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With that new-ball blitz an increasingly distant memory, and with the Australian bowlers beginning to wilt in the late Darwin sun, the hosts' frustration was on full display late in the evening session.

Into the 103rd over of the innings, Starc was bowling to all-rounder Mehidy, who was well set and intent on seeing the day through.

Mehidy set off for a single and came very close to colliding with the Australian spearhead.

Starc wasn't impressed.

"It's my follow through, not your follow through. Get off the wicket," Starc could be heard saying through the stump mic.

"I didn't see!" Mehidy could be heard saying during the next over, still perhaps apologetic about the near-collision.

But of course, the all-rounder shouldn't be taking the altercation personally.

The Australians' frustration was all of their own making.

6. You call that a knife?

Nathan Lyon used a knife to clean his spikes. (Supplied: Fox Sports)

There's nothing worse as an athlete than getting mud or grass caught between your cleats or spikes.

Nathan Lyon clearly had this issue during the second session, when going through his usual array of warm ups and stretches on the boundary at Marrara Oval.

But what can you do about it when in the middle of a Test match as you're about to prepare for a bowling spell?

Turns out, you ask someone in the kitchen if they have a spare a butter knife they don't mind soiling with some outfield dirt.

Much like the Northern Territory's best known international export, Crocodile Dundee, one can almost imagine one of the locals querying Lyon's choice of implement with quips like "you call that a knife …"

World.title: Gold Coast woman who helped dispose of alleged murder weapon walks free
World.content:
A woman who helped dispose of the weapon allegedly used to kill a "vibrant" young man on the Gold Coast has walked free from court.

In August 2023, 26-year-old Dylan McPadden was fatally stabbed at Robina's RQ's Tavern, allegedly by a complete stranger.

Tyler Rewi Malcolm Hailes was charged with Mr McPadden's murder and is set to face a trial later this year.

In the Brisbane Supreme Court, Mr Haile's then-partner Jade Brenda Laing, 33, pleaded guilty to helping him flee the scene and get rid of the knife used in the stabbing.

She was originally charged with being an accessory after the fact to murder.

Dylan McPadden died after he was stabbed at a Gold Coast tavern in 2023. (Facebook)

The charge was later downgraded to accessory after the fact with malicious intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

The court heard Laing picked up Mr Hailes from the tavern that night and drove him away from the scene knowing he had allegedly stabbed a man.

She also stopped the car so Mr Hailes could throw a knife into a body of water and later helped hide the clothes he was wearing.

Laing then told police officers the pair had not left their house that night and that she knew nothing about the weapon.

'Unbearable' loss of 'loving' son

Dylan McPadden's loved ones filled the public gallery as his father, mother and girlfriend read victim impact statements to the court.

His father Bruce described the loss of his "vibrant", "amazing" and "loving" son as "unbearable" and said it had left a void in his family.

He said his son had been taken in "the most violent and senseless way".

"Our beautiful boy was in the prime of his life," Mr McPadden said.

He said more than 500 people attended Dylan's funeral and that more than 1,000 watched on from around the world.

"He gave the shirt off his back, he helped the underdog, supported your dreams, was fun loving, risk taking, sporty, athletic," Mr McPhadden said.

"He lived large, laughed often, loved his family and friends."

Mr McPadden said Dylan was the kind of man who would be there for others, including previously helping a friend on the brink of taking their own life to find their way again.

"The world will never be the same," Mr McPadden said.

Carol McPadden saw her son hours before his death. (Supplied)

Dropped at tavern to wait for girlfriend

Carol McPadden said her son had been at a dinner in the hours before his death.

Later she went to drop Dylan to his girlfriend's place, but after he noticed she was still finishing up with a friend he asked to be dropped to the tavern while he waited.

At 3am the following day, police knocked on the family's door to inform them Dylan had died.

The incident took place outside RQ's Tavern in Robina in 2023. (ABC News: Danielle Maher)

"In just a few days it'll be three years since Dylan was lost," Ms McPadden said.

She said she would never be able to "watch him achieve his dreams".

'Dylan was my person'

Girlfriend Amara Pato said she and Dylan had been inseparable from the day they met.

"He was magic, he was witty, he loved hard," she said.

"He picked me flowers most weeks. Dylan was my person."

During Laing's sentencing Justice Peter Davis recognised the family's grief and "unimaginable loss".

"Mr McPadden was completely innocent in all of this," he said.

He noted Laing had also been a victim of sustained domestic violence at the hands of Mr Hailes, which he said had contributed to her offending that night.

Tyler Rewi Malcolm Hailes will face court in December, charged with murder. (Supplied)

The court heard she had allegedly been subjected to repeated abuse for a six-month period, including in the days leading up to the offence, and had been trying to "manage Mr Hailes behaviour".

"Our law has acknowledged the scourge of domestic violence," Justice Davis said.

"You were subject to domestic violence … your decisions were affected by the threat which he posed.

"What you did was not kill or directly contribute to the killing of Dylan.

"I have judged that the feature of domestic violence in this case is a particular pertinent one."

Laing was sentenced to four years' imprisonment, wholly suspended for five years.

Mr Hailes is expected to face trial for murder in December.

World.title: Major delays after overhead wires come down on Sydney passenger train
World.content:
There are major delays across Sydney's rail network after overhead wires came down onto a passenger train this evening.

The South Coast Line service was travelling between Redfern and Erskineville, in Sydney's inner west, when the wires came down on Friday afternoon.

Transport authorities have isolated power to the train and are working to safely remove passengers from multiple trains.

Sydney Trains' head of rail operations, Jas Tumber, said the cause was unknown.

"This is a really significant disruption that's causing really wide ripple effects," he said.

"We obviously don't know the cause of that at the moment, but we are working to understand and get response teams out to that particular train.

"That has resulted in us having to remove power between Central and Newtown on two of the six tracks that go in and out of the city."

Sydney Trains said there would be delays and gaps in services across the network for the rest of the day.

'Basically dead'

Train passenger Sean Murphy said he left Redfern for Sutherland on the Kiama train about 4:30pm and that "the engine just stopped" five minutes later.

"The train just went basically dead," he said.

Mr Murphy said staff announced that a train ahead of them "had brought down powerlines" and to await further instructions.

"Then they asked all the passengers to move to the centre of the train, so passengers came from both ends of the train to the carriage that I was in," he said.

"Then they got us to exit the train through the driver's compartment in the compartments in the middle of the train.

" We had to climb down a very steep ladder and then were taken to the side of the track. "

Mr Murphy said he was on the train for more than an hour.

"People were obviously delayed. They were calling people let them know that they've been late," he said.

"People were late for work, late getting home, but generally, people were reasonably calm and cool.

"The air conditioning went off, so starting it a little bit warm, but I wouldn't want to be in there for much longer."

Significant delays

It has significantly impacted the T2, T3, T8, T1, North Shore and the Western Line, as well as the T9 services.

"We also have an impact to our intercity customers who are leaving from Sydney terminal, so because of this power outage, we're not able to operate any intercity services that are going west or north," he said.

He recommended passengers catch a suburban train to Blacktown or Parramatta.

"Those trains that typically would have come in from the west and the north or into the city, they'll be turning around at Parramatta, Strathfield or Hornsby," Mr Tumber said.

Passengers are advised to allow plenty of extra travel time and consider alternative travel options.

World.title: Man critical after glass panel falls on workers near Albury
World.content:
Three men have been injured, with one in a critical condition, after a workplace accident in which a glass panel was dropped from a crane onto them.

A NSW Ambulance spokesperson said paramedics were called to Glen Park in the northern Albury suburb of Glenroy around noon today after reports of the panel being dropped at the worksite.

It is believed two sets of thick glass panels were being moved from a shipping container via crane to another area of the park.

All three men were sent via ambulance to Albury Hospital, with a man in his 20s sustaining critical injuries to his head, chest and leg.

Another man, also in his 20s, had injuries to his leg and back and was in a serious but stable condition.

Police cordoned off the park area where the incident occurred. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

A third man of unknown age had minor injuries.

A SafeWork NSW spokesperson said the organisation was investigating the incident.

"SafeWork NSW has been notified and is responding to an incident at a construction site at Glenroy … where three workers have been injured, " the spokesperson said.

"SafeWork NSW inspectors are on site and making enquiries.

"As enquiries are ongoing, no further comment is available at this time. "

NSW Police officers and forensic investigators were still at the scene several hours after the incident occurred.

World.title: China denies espionage and foreign interference in New Zealand
World.content:
The Chinese Embassy has rejected a report by New Zealand's top spy agency that includes what it says are multiple "false allegations against China".

In its fourth Security Threat Environment report released on Thursday, the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service said China was the sole nation pursuing espionage in New Zealand "at scale".

The report also said China remained the "most active" nation among several others involved in foreign interference in New Zealand.

In a statement today, the Chinese Embassy said the NZSIS report included baseless and fabricated accusations.

"Its false allegations against China either smear normal exchanges and cooperation as so-called espionage or interference, or are entirely groundless and fabricated out of thin air," the statement said.

" We firmly oppose this and will never accept it. "

The embassy said the China-New Zealand relationship was one of mutual benefit, with progress in recent years in areas such as trade, people-to-people exchanges, tourism and international education.

It said the Chinese community in New Zealand had played a positive role in this process.

Since China implemented a unilateral visa-free policy for New Zealanders, a growing number of New Zealanders have visited China, and goodwill towards China, as well as support for China-New Zealand relations, has continued to grow, the embassy said.

Chinese state-linked observatory sought NZ site A Chinese state-linked observatory has sought to install infrastructure at a New Zealand site.

"That this report is released at this particular juncture is no coincidence — it forms part of a new wave of attacks, slander and vilification against China orchestrated by certain international forces, and may well itself be a product of foreign interference," the statement said.

It claimed "anti-China forces" were seeking to drive a wedge between the people of both countries, creating a chilling effect on the public, undermining mutual trust and obstructing the growth of the relationship.

"Our message to those forces and individuals attempting political machinations is this: do not sacrifice the hard-won, mutually beneficial China-New Zealand relationship for selfish gain, and do not act against the interests of New Zealand and its people," the embassy said.

"Serving as a pawn for anti-China forces will ultimately backfire.

"Manufacturing distractions in foreign relations will not solve New Zealand's own problems — it will only prove counterproductive.

" We urge these forces and individuals not to quench their thirst with poison, and not to lift a rock only to drop it on their own feet. "

The embassy also said China valued its relationship with New Zealand and stood ready to work with New Zealand to advance exchanges and cooperation for the benefit of both peoples.

This story was first published on rnz.co.nz

World.title: Youth who assaulted woman sleeping rough admits to breaking into businesses
World.content:
A teenage boy who assaulted a woman sleeping rough has pleaded guilty to serious criminal trespass in South Australia's Youth Court.

The now-18-year-old pleaded guilty in June to causing harm with intent against the woman, which was today accepted by the prosecution.

The prosecution had applied for the matter to be dealt with in the District Court, with the defendant to be sentenced as an adult given the "extremely serious" nature and "harrowing nine-minute-long footage" of the offending.

That application is to be fought by his defence lawyers, who are seeking to have the matter remain in the Youth Court.

The lawyer for the defendant said documentation from the centre where he has been remanded in custody reflected "very positive reports from youth justice" and addressed his "complex mental health issues".

The court heard the youth had a long-standing ADHD diagnosis and undiagnosed autism spectrum disorder.

At the time of the attack, police said the 64-year-old victim had been sleeping in the vicinity of Mitcham Memorial Library on Belair Road at Hawthorn.

Police said she had been kicked and punched to the head and body in the early hours of November 13, 2025.

Paramedics treated the woman before taking her to hospital where she was reported to be in a serious but stable condition.

The incident took place near the Mitcham Memorial Library. (ABC News)

The teenager was also accused of breaking into nearby businesses on the same night and subsequently charged with serious criminal trespass.

Magistrate John Wells today urged counsel to consider that the matter involved "highly vulnerable" parties and that it would be "unfortunate" and time-consuming for the case to be referred to the District Court, only to be sent back to the Youth Court.

"I want to say to everyone, I urge you all to do your best to try and resolve it," he said.

"We have a highly vulnerable victim — her interests are important.

"We have a highly vulnerable child in custody, and his interests are also important.

"Please don't let anyone ignore those paramount considerations."

Magistrate Wells told the defendant that he was "very keen to finalise" the matter.

"I'm sure you are, I'm sure your parents are and those who support you are, but we are moving in the right direction," he said.

The 18-year-old remained in custody and would appear in court next month.

World.title: Wind farm workers detail photo with accused farmer after alleged triple murder
World.content:
The trial of a Queensland cattle farmer, charged with murdering three people and attempting to murder a fourth has heard from workers who spent the day of the alleged shooting with the accused.

Darryl Valroy Young, 63, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder during the ongoing Supreme Court trial in Townsville.

He is charged with the murder of married couple Mervyn Schwarz and Maree Schwarz, and Mrs Schwarz's son Graham Tighe.

He is also charged with the attempted murder of Graham Tighe's brother Ross Tighe.

Mr Young's lawyer said his client never saw the family at the gate of his Bogie cattle station on the morning he was accused of shooting them.

On Friday, the court heard renewable energy workers Liam Parnell and Matt Garbutt estimated arriving at Mr Young's Bogie property in a ute at about 7:30am on August 4, 2022.

Liam Parnell gave evidence in the triple murder trial on Friday. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The trial has previously heard that Ross Tighe, who said he and his family were shot by Mr Young, estimated the incident occurred at the farmer's front gate after 8am.

Mr Parnell and Mr Garbutt told the court after meeting Mr Young, they left him at the gate and drove to the property homestead before splitting into separate vehicles.

Mr Parnell said he continued to scout a high-altitude location and saw Mr Young again after 8:30am.

Mr Garbutt was shown a video he had taken at 8:11am that morning.

Matthew Garbutt also gave evidence in the Supreme Court trial on Friday. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

He said he saw Mr Young more than 10 to 20 minutes after he had taken that video.

The colleagues said they learned there had been a shooting after 11am when they were installing equipment on a ridge with Darryl Young, his stepmother and son close-by.

Police asked group for 'selfie'

Mr Parnell said he was initially contacted by his boss, then police who advised the group to stay in place.

"We spent the whole day up there," Mr Parnell said.

" I was asked to take photos and send them across — a selfie of all of us up there. "

Mr Young has taken notes through the trial. ( ABC News: Carole Howlett)

The court was shown photos taken by Mr Parnell.

The group of people, including Darryl Young wearing a dark navy shirt, could be seen giving a thumbs up in one photo.

Earlier the trial heard Ross Tighe describe Darryl Young wore a fluorescent work shirt during the alleged shooting.

Another photo shown to the jury showed all in the group smiling except Darryl Young.

Mr Parnell said during the afternoon he saw Mr Young appearing "relaxed in the ATV" and said he noticed no change in his demeanour.

He and Mr Garbutt said police eventually told the group to travel in one car to the property gate.

Mr Parnell said he drove, and the group was met by a specialist policing unit.

Neighbour missing gun

The court heard from grazier Brett Stagg, a neighbour of both the Schwarz's and Tighe's Sutherland Station and Mr Young's Shannonvale Station.

Mr Stagg told the court he had an "up and down relationship" with Mr Young but would "keep the peace" as they were neighbours.

Crown prosecutor David Nardone asked Mr Stagg about a fire at his house on his property in 2011.

Prosecutor David Nardone (right) is appearing on behalf of the crown. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

"During the time of the fire some guns went missing? A .30-30 and a .223?" Mr Nardone asked.

"Correct," Mr Stagg said.

The grazier confirmed that of the missing firearms the .223 was recovered but the .30-30 rifle never was.

Prosecutors have told the trial that .30-30 ammunition cartridges were found in Mr Young's kitchen and work shed and had the same markings as the spent cartridges found at the scene of the alleged triple murder.

"Those markings were '30.30 WIN RP'," Mr Nardone told the jury in his opening address on Monday.

"Darryl Young was licensed to possess six firearms — none of those were .30-30 rifles."

Mr Nardone said that in a search of Mr Young's dwellings, "no firearm capable of discharging .30-30 cartridges were found".

The trial continues.

World.title: Being the PM and dealing with the paradoxical art of strategic defeat
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A prime minister shouldn’t need to be stubborn (“PM’s fatal flaw spooks his colleagues”, August 14). They need universal appeal. That’s what Albanese was seeking by appearing on Bush Deep. And how easy it should have been to bat away all the innuendo in the interview while still remaining witty and likeable. The fact that he couldn’t shows (large) gaps in his social and emotional intelligence. The lack of apology (yes, there was innuendo in his melon “joke”) is compounding that. James Massola recommends that Albanese learn the art of strategic defeat. Most of us are thinking that it’s too late and/or the brief is too big. A PM doesn’t have to be perfect, nor barren-dry formal. But when the ego takes over, it’s the beginning of the end. For me, Albo’s always been that way. Ted Bush, North Epping James Massola, in the context of the prime minister’s Melongate dilemma, advises that Albanese “needs to learn the art of the strategic retreat”. I suggest that he should avoid ever being placed in a position of having to use this skill. The prime minister is not an entertainer. Leave that to other politicians – no names. In negotiating the media minefield, where every misstep becomes a public gaffe, he should treat each question as a “verbal Rorschach test”, where each response will be analysed by political commentators of all persuasions from every possible angle. He needs to be more prudent both in the media company that he keeps and his attempts at humour. Paul Casey, Callala Bay The PM denied any innuendo around his gesture during the podcast. And what of the media adviser(s) who no doubt counselled it would make Albo look cool and an “ordinary bloke” if he went on that podcast? As for strategic retreat, when do politicians actually think strategically? James Mahoney, McKellar (ACT) James Massola nails Albanese’s fatal flaw, but where we part company is in his assertion that it’s probably too late to apologise. Yes, the longer we take to apologise, and the more we justify our actions, the harder it is to apologise. But the harder it is to apologise, the more respect you gain when it’s done. It’s never too late. And so it is for the PM, regardless of all his obfuscating over recent weeks. The list of people he embarrassed during Nikki Osborne’s podcast is endless, but the political pain will be endless, too, unless he shows a bit of courage and decency and acknowledges his error. Prue Nelson, Cremorne Point One aspect overlooked in the melon debate is how the melons passed quarantine. Keith Masnick, Woollahra A haiku titled Melancholy:

So embarrassing

Aussie obsession with boobs

Maintain dignity.

Neil Reckord, Gordon (ACT)



I have always admired politicians – not all, but a great many over the years. Their job is highly scrutinised and, when compared to chief executives in the commercial world, poorly remunerated; the hours are long; and the workload is unforgiving. Governing responsibly is a serious task. Our representatives are elected to stand up for all Australians – not to perform stand-up. In my view, sharing “fruity” asides with a precocious podcaster is a waste of time that could be spent addressing significant issues. Then again, I’ve been watching the political cycle for many years. Maybe I’m just feeling a little melon-choly. Janet Argall, Hurlstone Park Surely it’s time, especially for the Coalition, to take a few breaths, get a grip on itself, and drop its carping hype on this topic. Albo’s comments may have been in poor taste but they were hardly a hanging offence. If you ask me, Taylor et al are making a mountain out of melons. Edward Loong, Milsons Point James Massola calls our PM’s inability to admit to missteps “stubbornness”. I’d call it ODD – opposition defiance disorder. Melongate was far from a minor misstep, far more serious than prevarication over slipping off a stage. Thankfully, our Japanese friends have gracefully excused his discourtesy. Brian O’Donnell, Burradoo Gourd, what a week. The ICAC wrestled with amnesia while the House suffered from melon-oma. Les Shearman, Darlington Please, don’t appease In the words of the African-American Nobel laureate, the late Toni Morrison, “The very serious function of racism is distraction. It keeps you from doing your work. It keeps you explaining, over and over again, your reason for being.” This is happening now, with One Nation running the agenda (“Labor plan migration cut in visa crackdown”, August 14). Against the intensifying right-wing siege, we see people striving to defend migrants’ contribution to Australia. Plus, the PM plans a crackdown on so-called undocumented migrants via “farms, hotels, restaurants and construction sites”, where their work input is obviously needed. Who will replace them if there is an ICE-style hunt and expel program? Dr Abul Rizvi, a former immigration department official, stresses the costs would “run into many billions”. What of the human consequences for these disadvantaged people and the families they support? Before any such exercise to appease the Hansonites, Australia should learn from the cataclysmic damage in the US. Bruce Springsteen catalogues this in his protest song Streets of Minneapolis, where “King Trump” and his “private army” of federal ICE “thugs” targeted “black and brown” people, with two protesting Americans killed: Renée Good, a mother and poet, and intensive care nurse Alex Pretti. Barbara Chapman, South Yarra (Vic) Dog gone



It is indeed good news that the whistleblower David McBride has been released on parole after two years in prison and is now looking forward to seeing his dog (“Whistleblower released on parole now faces battle with lung cancer”, August 14). I hope he doesn’t have the same luck as Odysseus upon his return home after 20 years away: his dog Argos died as soon as he arrived. More importantly, as with many, I’ve been greatly disappointed by the Labor government not passing any substantial laws to protect whistleblowers, as it had promised when in opposition. It is a disgrace that whistleblowers could face years of prison for exposing corruption. Con Vaitsas, Ashbury David McBride arriving at the ACT Supreme Court, in Canberra Andrew Ellinghausen Regardless of what we think about the whistleblower laws, why should the power to release on parole be in the hands of a federal politician? Michael Blissenden, Dural Last may be first Stephen Bartholomeusz’s article (“Wall Street firms to chip in billions for Nvidia AI bonds”, August 14) on the extraordinary financial acrobatics that are happening in the AI sector to keep it afloat is enlightening. It makes you wonder if Australia is too late to “take advantage” of our “strategic” position. Maybe we should be grateful that we were one of the last to be tapped on the shoulder by Big Tech, and make a subtle but hasty exit. Elizabeth Darton, Lane Cove West Confidence trips It seems to me from emails and courtroom behaviour that the Reformers went about their grubby business with the usual confidence of young men raised to believe their privilege is a result of merit. Sadly for these would-be political conspirators, the ICAC has instead exposed a sorry band of bumbling amateurs (“How McInerney went from helpful to hot under the collar”, August 14). Colin Stokes, Camperdown



Megan Herbert Fishing for COD Once bitten, twice shy. Given the uncertainty about the delivery of the US nuclear subs, more purchases (“Australia urged to buy US missile interceptors”, August 14) should strictly be a cash-on-delivery transaction. Steve Ngeow, Chatswood Lesson for private school road hogs Imagine if your local public school needed more room and proposed buying a street to expand it (‴⁣⁣Gets up everyone’s nose’: Private school in talks to buy whole street”, August 14). It would never happen, as public schools are too busy trying to fund the basics for education and correct possible structural problems, such as cracked and uneven (trip hazard) paths, broken sewer lines etc from 90 and more years ago when the school was built. But here we are in 2026, Redlands wants to use its federal income tax revenue to buy a street. If they can even dream of buying a street, they obviously have far too much money. Stop their federal funding immediately; they really don’t need it. I’m sure a fete with cashed-up alumni would whip up the funds over a weekend. Then redirect their funding to public schools that struggle to do the basics because of socioeconomic disadvantage, isolation and population size. Fund the extra teachers and the infrastructure needed to keep them, rather than let a private school expand its campus by buying a road. This has to stop. If you want to send your kids to a school that isn’t public, you pay the whole cost, as they do everywhere else in the world. Ridiculous state of affairs. Geoff Holmes, Woonona Redlands School Flavio Brancaleone Once again private schools demonstrate the obscene amount of cash they have and add fuel to debate over government funding. It comes as no surprise that North Sydney Council is interested in the sale, as the well-documented cost blow-out of more than $50 million for the new North Sydney Pool would leave the coffers thin –the sale of the street would be a very welcome cash injection. In my own area I have seen a private school buy many of the shops and some houses near Croydon station. Another large private school used a public park near my house for sport at various times throughout the year. Private schools can certainly choose what to spend their money on, but I look forward to the day when their government funding is greatly reduced or stopped altogether. I certainly won’t be holding my breath. Peter Miniutti, Ashbury



How is eating a suburb creating “opportunities to further enrich learning, wellbeing and co-curricular activities”? Private schools used to coexist with their suburb. Students took public transport, teachers parked on school grounds, nobody needed a wellness centre, a cricket ground to rival the SCG or a state-of-the-art drama theatre. Their learning was based on self-reliance and using their ingenuity, imagination and co-operation to get the best results out of co-curricular activities. They also realised the world, starting with their neighbourhood, did not revolve around them. Resilience was fostered so their wellbeing, in most cases, was just fine. If these schools really cared about their students, they’d opt out of this infrastructure race to the bottom. It’s counterproductive for the students and is a misery for anyone unfortunate enough to live or work in the school’s vicinity. It’s a disgrace that ratepayers and taxpayers are funding these educational travesties. Elisabeth Goodsall, Wahroonga Now who came up with that idea? Why don’t we just buy a few more roads to expand our schools and also make it easier for the lads and staff to park their limos? It is only a little cul-de-sac and we need it more. As a private school, we always need more land and this suits us fine. I note one of the reasons is to “enrich learning” and what better way to teach privilege than to commandeer public property? Nola Tucker, Kiama Does the avarice of Redlands know no bounds? The school uses parks for play, but does not pay rates. Its website names itself as an independent school, however it accepts large amounts of public money. It now wants to purchase an entire public road, to convert to private space. The inequity between public and (misnamed) private education could not be more stark. The so-called land of the “fair-go” fades inexorably into oblivion. Graham Fazio, Cootamundra Smelting point I am disappointed that some groups are invisible in the Tomago aluminium smelter subsidy story (“Will bailout stave off One Nation in the Hunter?” , August 14). Where are all those people who demanded that we keep manufacturing jobs in Australia? Where are the supporters of not just selling raw minerals, but getting into processing? Where are those opposed to rolling out renewables that would make electricity cheaper? Where are the people complaining about increasing house costs because we have to import raw materials like steel and aluminium? Waiting for another more suitable story, I guess. Neville Turbit, Russell Lea Tomago Aluminium: An Open or Shut case? James Brickwood Global transport issues have coined a fashionably parroted, half-thought-through, hope-and-a-prayer, financially and sustainably dubious rationale: “Australian self-sufficiency imperative for national security.” It’s another name for our nation’s historic, abiding doctrine of capitalising profits and socialising losses. The aluminium smelter bailout is just a virtue signal likely going to prove a hopeless money pit like Snowy 2.0. That wonderfully reassuring, disingenuously paraded word, security, now outdoes even “a green future” for political propaganda value. Alex Mattea, Kingston

World.title: Billy Slater rules out Storm job after quitting as Maroons coach
World.content:
Billy Slater has quit as Queensland Origin coach, but insists he has no plans to succeed Craig Bellamy at the Melbourne Storm. Slater confirmed on Friday afternoon he would step down as Maroons coach after three Origin series wins from five attempts. Loading Queensland Rugby League officials will commence an immediate search for his successor, with Ben Te’o and Matt Ballin among the early candidates. Next year’s series will have a fresh look all round, with NSW also under new leadership after Matt King replaced Laurie Daley as Blues coach. Speculation had been swirling that Slater was being groomed to take over from Bellamy after the long-serving Storm mentor indicated he was likely to step aside at the end of 2027. Slater, who currently works with the Storm in a part-time consultancy role, has been spotted deep in conversation with Cam Munster and Harry Grant in the Melbourne dressing room at NRL games recently.



But just hours before the news of his Maroons departure broke, Slater was at Royal Randwick for a charity lunch – where he maintained he had no appetite to be a club coach. When asked by Andrew Johns on stage about the possibility of succeeding Bellamy becoming the next Storm boss, Slater said: “That won’t happen. I never say never, but, ‘never’. That’s a 365-day job. You have to be all in for it.” Billy Slater has become a wonderful coach at Origin level. Getty Images Slater said he had only taken on the Queensland job after being talked into it by Maroons legend Paul Vautin during a round of golf. “Fatty said, ‘You have to do it, it will be the best thing you’ll do in your life’,” Slater said. “I was waiting for him to laugh, but he didn’t. And he was right. The reward you get when you help guys achieve something for a mass of people you really care about, it’s such a rewarding and fulfilling job.



“I won’t sign a long-term deal [with Queensland]. If I’m the right person for the job, I’ll consider it, if I’m not, I’m all for the right person. That’s where I see the role.” Related Article Wallabies ‘First-world problem’: Why Wallabies star says Suaalii shouldn’t be pigeonholed The Storm will ramp up plans to lock in Bellamy’s successor once their season finishes, with 2026 the first year they will miss finals since the club’s 2010 salary cap scandal. Slater has long been high on their list of eventual replacements when Bellamy steps away, though Slater has regularly dismissed interest in a full-time NRL role. Melbourne rate Bellamy’s current assistant Ryan Hinchcliffe especially highly and he has broadened his coaching experience in recent years by working with Samoa and the NSW Origin side.

Long-time assistant Marc Brentnall has previously indicated little desire in being an NRL head coach.



All indications are that Slater will continue in his part-time consultancy role – which includes one-on-one work with star fullback Sua Faalogo – with Melbourne next season. Slater said via a press release on Friday he felt the time had come for him to step away after with eight wins and seven losses as Maroons coach, following a playing career which spanned 31 appearances across 15 years. “From being a boy who idolised this team, to a player, to guiding a group that has inspired our state, this has been one of the most rewarding things I’ve done in my life,” Slater said. “I want to thank the players, this group gave everything for the jersey, for each other and our state, and I’m proud of what we’ve built together.” The QRL confirmed the search for Slater’s successor would soon begin. Ballin and Te’o, Slater’s assistants for the 2026 series, are likely to come under consideration having both also played for Queensland.



Ballin is currently serving under Michael Maguire at the Brisbane Broncos. Te’o was at the Broncos before his sudden departure after the club’s round three win against the Storm. Te’o has been linked to a potential South Sydney homecoming under Wayne Bennett. Former Broncos and Maroons coach Kevin Walters, who coached the state from 2016 to 2019, is contracted to the Kangaroos until June 2028. World.title: Scots boys allegedly captured on CCTV on night of sexual assault
World.content:
Detectives have seized CCTV of Scots College students from the evening they allegedly sexually assaulted a 14-year-old girl in an eastern suburbs alleyway, as parents express shock and sound the alarm on what they say is a culture of toxic masculinity at the school. Investigators on Thursday seized several items of interest from the boys’ homes, including electronic devices, which are being forensically examined for links to the alleged attack and crime scene. The college, Sydney’s most expensive private school, has refused to say whether it will suspend the trio. Scots College parents have sounded the alarm on what they say is a culture of toxic masculinity at the school. Steven Woodburn The girl and the boys, who cannot legally be identified, were known to each other and are believed to have arranged to meet on the night of the alleged assault. The boys, a 13-year-old and two 14-year-olds, have been charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others, and aggravated sexual touching of another person over the alleged attack on July 22. All three boys were granted conditional police bail on Thursday and are due to face Surry Hills Children’s Court on August 25.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Three Scots College boys charged with rape of teenage girl Detectives also seized two replica firearms, a “Glock-style” BB gun, three laser pointers and a number plate, which is believed to have been stolen, during searches of the boys’ homes on Thursday. The school has refused to answer repeated questions about the students’ enrolment status, when it became aware of the alleged incident, or what measures were being taken to address wellbeing and safety at its Bellevue Hill campus, where parents say a culture dismissive of women is rife. “There’s a culture in the school of inequality of genders that is part of the boys’ everyday lives,” one Scots College mother, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect the identity of her family, told the Herald. “There’s little representation of women at a senior management level. It’s just tokenistic. You feel that as a mother, you feel that as a woman stepping onto campus.”



Conversations of consent at the school, she said, were limited and have little impact on students. “There’s this ambiguity about what consent means … That sends a really bad message to the boys,” she said. Females make up 39 per cent of staff. There is one woman on the Scots College Council and 10 men. Another parent, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, said: “By and large, the school community is shocked as you would expect.” He said the alleged crime was an “abhorrent thing” but had occurred outside of school hours and off school premises.



He believed the school had done a good job when it came to teaching consent in the years after Chanel Contos launched her campaign for mandatory sexual consent education. The former Kambala student’s 2021 petition for earlier sex education in schools received hundreds of testimonies alleging that boys at several Sydney private schools had been perpetrators of sexual assault. Former Kambala student Chanel Contos campaigned for mandatory sexual consent education. Alex Ellinghausen Noting some had called for the students to be expelled or suspended, the father said the boys should be given the presumption of innocence. The Scots Student Discipline Framework categorises student misbehaviour ascending in severity, from level zero to level three. Level three is behaviour that poses a “significant risk to the safety, dignity or rights of others”.



Across the country, instances of child sexual abuse perpetrated by adults had declined, the 2024 Australian Child Maltreatment Study found, but rates of peer to peer abuse among adolescents had increased. Teenagers have now overtaken adults as the now most likely perpetrators of sexual violence towards other young people. Australian Bureau of Statistics data from 2024 found victims of sexual assault increased by 10 per cent from the previous year, to 40,087 victims nationally. Separate Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data shows 92.3 per cent of women did not report an assault by a male perpetrator to police in 2021-22. Sexual assault victims were most commonly aged between 10 and 17 at the time of offending. Public schools have also had to grapple with handling the fallout of sexual assault allegations. Anna Coutts-Trotter, founder of The Survivor Hub, called for “a general statement of support for survivors and a condemnation” of alleged acts of violence. Louise Kennerley An ombudsman report into the handling of an alleged sexual assault at an unnamed public high school between a male and female school student found the NSW public system had no consistent or clear way to deal with criminal matters involving students, and provided little guidance on what to do when the victims of a crime and its perpetrator attended the same school.



The Department of Education subsequently provided updated advice on how to best manage the safety, wellbeing and educational risks for the students involved in sexual assaults. Options available include managing students within a school. “If this is not practicable, a suspension may be required to allow the risk management plan to be put in place,” the advice says. Anna Coutts-Trotter, a victim-survivor and founder of The Survivor Hub, said she would like to see a “strong stance” from Scots College. “The person who used violence against me went to a prestigious school in Sydney,” she said. “It definitely speaks to a wider problem.” She said Scots was “evading responsibility” by noting the alleged assault was outside school hours, and called for “a general statement of support for survivors and a condemnation of acts of violence”.



Angelique Wan runs workshops in high schools across the country aimed at preventing sexual violence. Angelique Wan, co-founder and CEO of Consent Labs, which runs workshops in high schools across the country aimed at preventing sexual violence, said parents also play a role in consent education, both in terms of explicit conversation, and modelled behaviour. “It’s often said that young people are influenced by social media and what they see online, and to some extent that’s true,” she said. “But parents and carers are still a massive influence and source of information for young people.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
